en: Preface to the *Commentary on the Essentials of the Abridged Explanation of Amitābha* (Mida lüjie yuanzhong chao), composed by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi on Mount Tiantai.
Now, the secret oral teachings of the Tathāgata contain manifold meanings. This is illustrated by the analogy of the king requesting *saindhava*, which has a single name yet possesses four meanings.

Truly, it was because that wise minister well understood its meaning. Whether the king was about to go out, eat, drink, or engage in battle, as soon as he uttered this single phrase, the minister would provide him with horses, salt, water, or vessels;
everything accorded with the king’s heart and suited his intentions. The Bodhisattva, the wise minister, is also like this, for he well understands what the Tathāgata has taught.

Regarding the Dharma: within shallow teachings, one provides profound explanations; within profound teachings, one provides shallow explanations; within teachings that are both shallow and profound, one provides explanations that are neither shallow nor profound;
and within teachings that are neither shallow nor profound, one provides explanations that are both shallow and profound.

In composing treatises to propagate the sutras, one adjusts the extent of detail to suit the occasion, ensuring that the intelligence of the listener is not discouraged and that no meaning is omitted. Only then can it be said:
To ascend its hall and enter its chamber—this is the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Smaller Amitābha Sūtra).
It is that which Śākyamuni Tathāgata provided as a simplified exposition within the midst of profound teachings, and as a concise summary within the midst of extensive teachings.

Since the explanation was already concise, even when the wise minister composed this commentary, he could not help but remain brief. Since the meaning was already profound, even when the wise minister composed this commentary, he [could not help but remain concise].
It is not excessively profound; its concise explanations do not cause wisdom to regress, and its deep principles do not leave the meaning deficient.
By using the concise to explore the expansive, it proceeds with ease along the Middle Way. I have seen Master Quan’an’s *Brief Commentary* at Wumen; its preface states:
"The jade groves and jeweled ponds directly manifest the source of the mind; the lifespan and radiance fully reveal one's own nature. Furthermore:

It is said that once one realizes the fundamental endowment of mind-only, billions of lands are not distant; knowing that the Great Vow can be relied upon, the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are traversed in a single stride.
Alas! To encompass the entirety of the whole scripture, how brief are these words! Yet the nature of the mind is its very essence—how profound is its meaning!
How could a minor Bodhisattva or a wise minister ever reach such a state? Now, I have made an abridgment of this for them, specifically titling it "The Perfect within the Middle.
My intention is that the environment and inhabitants of Sukhāvatī constitute the wondrous existence of the One Mind; the practice of holding the Name is the true emptiness.
Without the subtle true emptiness, one cannot realize the wondrous existence of Sukhāvatī; and without the subtle, wondrous existence, one cannot manifest this [emptiness].

The true emptiness of the mind is what is called inconceivable provisionality; it is not partial provisionality. True emptiness is not empty [in the sense of mere nothingness], nor is it merely empty.
When one practices by unifying these two, then the perfect Middle is fully realized, and the Way of the Middle is accomplished. For this reason, I have titled this work "A Commentary" (*Chao*).
It is my intention that those who read this sutra and practice accordingly will look to the meaning of its name and truly apply themselves to it. One should surely do so.
When the mind is undistracted and all worldly concerns are forgotten, the principle of True Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is revealed.

When one holds the Name for seven days with mindfulness succeeding mindfulness, the principle of Wondrous Existence (*prabhāsvara*) is manifested. Practice perfected, one beholds the Buddha; the mind purified, the lotus flower blooms.
The seal of the Sahā world is destroyed and the inscription of Sukhāvatī is formed. The seal is destroyed in order to empty the emotions; this is what is called "True."
Emptiness. This is the reason Wen Cheng established his doctrine; this is what is called "wondrous existence.

When both [emptiness and existence] are simultaneously forgotten and simultaneously preserved, the words of the Amitābha Sūtra are therefore concise, while its meaning is profound. Thus, in the course of compiling these excerpts, I have set forth the meaning of the title and composed this preface at length.
Preface to the *Brief Commentary on the Buddha-Spoken Sutra of Immeasurable Life: An Extract from the Round Center*,
written by hand on the first day of the waxing moon of the twelfth month in the inaugural year of the Ming Emperor’s reign.
Recorded by the Śramaṇa Dayou of Wu Commandery;
Transcribed by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi at Mount Tiantai.
△ Next, the person who composed [this work].
The Master’s courtesy name was Qúān (蘧菴) and his given name was Dàyòu (大佑). He served as the abbot of Beichán Tiāntái Jiǎngsì (北禪天台講寺) in Suzhou.
He was profoundly learned in the principles of the doctrinal teachings (*jìào lǐ*), and regarding the single gate of the Pure Land, he attained its very essence.

His work, the *Jìngtǔ Zhǐguī jí* (Collection on the Pointing-out of the Return to the Pure Land), circulated widely throughout the world. His secular surname and native place remain to be examined in detail.
The preface to the three [sections] consists of two parts. First, the preface explains the origin of the sutra; second, the preface briefly explains the reasons for the commentary.

The first part has two sections: first, the introduction to the causal conditions (*nidāna*); second, the introduction to the exposition of the sutra. The first of these also has two sections: first, tracing back to the source and flow;
second, the formal introduction to the causal conditions. The first of these further has two sections: first, the non-duality of the true source; second, how the deluded branches become diverse.
In short, when speaking of the true source, within the single nature there is originally no distinction between suffering and pleasure;

thus, why would it be necessary for the Tathāgata to appear in the world to preach the sutras? It is only because delusive streams have formed distinctions that our Buddha manifested birth and expounded the teachings.
Now, we shall first clarify that the true source is non-dual.
[Commentary]: Now, the tranquil light (sukhāvatī) is truly pure; from the beginning, there has been no distinction between suffering and pleasure.
[Sub-commentary]: "Tranquil light" is one of the four kinds of pure lands (*śuddhakṣetra*). The four pure lands are: first, the Pure Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages;
second, the Pure Land of the Remaining Traces of Expedient Means; third, the Pure Land of True Retribution Without Obstruction; and fourth...

The Constant Quiescent Light Pure Land each possesses both purity and defilement; only the Supreme Grade Quiescent Light is the truly real pure land, for all other pure lands are, to a greater or lesser degree, provisional constructs.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the term "true purity" does not imply that the Quiescent Light exists apart from the three lands as something else to be attained;
it simply points to the fundamental essence of the three lower lands, which is ultimately grounded in principle.

It is no different from the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*). Therefore, the Venerable Ziming’s *Miaozongchao* states: "One must know that the four lands have both horizontal and vertical dimensions;

yet one must also know that these horizontal and vertical aspects exist within a single location. For example, the Land of Common Residence (*sahāloka*) is itself the Land of Real Reward (*bhūtakoṭi-vipāka*) when one reaches that very place.
If one breaks through ignorance and enters by transforming the body, this is the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). It is the same.
Regarding the essence and function of the Buddha-body, which is the wondrous true retribution, even those with the six sense-faculties purified cannot participate;
how much less could those of the Two Vehicles? This is a vertical discourse on the true land of retribution from a single perspective.

If one has not yet shattered ignorance and still possesses the view of a self, it is for the sake of such a "capable seer" that the Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas bestow upon them [this vision], enabling them to see the land of true retribution.
Generally speaking, there are those with the karmic conditions who, although they have not yet destroyed their delusions, have already practiced Madhyamaka;
such is the case for the various assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other lecture halls, where beings of diverse capacities all perceive the inconceivable nature of the bodies and lands.

Since this is true for the Land of Real Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*), it is likewise so when discussing the horizontal coexistence of the Lands of Expedient Means (*upāya*) and Peaceful Light (*śānta-prakāśa*). Within the Land of Shared Residence (*sahā-loka*), one may discuss the horizontal and vertical dimensions of these three lands.

In the stage of skillful means (*upāya*), the treatise discusses the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the two lands; in the stage of true retribution (*vipāka*), it discusses the horizontal and vertical dimensions of the single land;

and upon reaching the stage of quiescent light (*śāntaprabhā*), there is neither horizontal nor vertical, nor even the presence of such categories in that very place. Now, when it says "quiescent light is truly pure," this directly indicates the true essence itself.
From the outset, there is no distinction between suffering and pleasure, which demonstrates its transcendence of faults and severance of non-virtue. This is because of the four... [text truncated]

Speaking in terms of the purity or defilement of lands: in the Sahā world of common residence, there is only suffering and no bliss; in the Pure Land of Tranquil Security, there is only bliss and no suffering.
Speaking in terms of the land of skillful means in contrast to the land of common residence: in the land of common residence, there is only suffering and no bliss;
in the land of skillful means, there is only bliss and no suffering. Speaking in terms of the land of skillful means itself: in this defiled realm of skillful means, there is only suffering and no...

Regarding the ease and purity of bliss: in the Pure Land, there is only bliss and no suffering. When comparing the land of true retribution (*vipāka-bhūmi*) with the land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*), the land of skillful means consists only of suffering and no bliss, whereas the land of true retribution consists only of bliss and no suffering.

When speaking specifically of the land of true retribution, the defiled realm of true retribution consists only of suffering and no bliss, while the pure land of true retribution consists only of bliss and no suffering. If one were to further consider [the land of true retribution]...
Speaking in terms of the retribution of karmic response, the Realm of True Reward consists only of suffering and no joy, while the Realm of Quiescent Light consists only of joy and no suffering.
Speaking in terms of the lands themselves, within the Realm of Quiescent Light, the defiled realm is only suffering and no joy, while the pure land is only joy and no suffering.
All of the above is spoken according to the non-duality of the two [realms] as manifested through cultivation; therefore, they exist [as distinct].

Regarding the distinction between suffering and pleasure: when the present preface states that "from the beginning there has been no distinction between suffering and pleasure," it refers to the ten realms (daśadhātu) and the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) as inherently possessed by nature (*prakṛti*).

It means that within these there is only the nature in which the suffering and pleasure of the ten realms are perfectly interfused, and not the distinct characteristics of the suffering and pleasure of the ten realms.
That is to say, both sentient beings and Buddhas equally possess the essence of the unchanging *tathatā*, which fundamentally lacks [such distinctions].
Since there is no distinction between purity and defilement, how could there be any difference between suffering and joy?

Therefore, this single phrase is categorized as "the True Source is Non-dual," serving as the foundational basis for the subsequent elaboration on how the deluded streams become differentiated. This is precisely what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to when it says, "The nature of awakening is wondrously luminous;
fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous," and further states, "Pure and inherently so, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm. This applies to all four kinds of pure lands.
This is fully explained as follows.
△ Next, the false branches become distinct.
[Commentary]: As deluded consciousness proliferates in confusion, there subsequently arises the distinction between the holy and the ordinary.
[Commentary] "Deluded consciousness" (*wangshi*) is the general designation for the three delusions.

That is to say, since beginningless time, sentient beings have suddenly become obscured within the wondrous clarity of intrinsic awakening and the inherent clarity of fundamental awakening, thereby falsely producing the notion of "luminous awareness."

Based on this, you establish the "object. Once the object is falsely established, it gives rise to your false "subject. Within that which is devoid of sameness or difference, a blazing diversity is formed.
Consequently, the three subtle afflictions of ignorance arise like dust and sand; consequently, the six coarse afflictions arise.

Through the first transformation, the delusions of views and the delusions of thought become the Land of Tranquil Light and the Impure Lands. Through the second transformation, they become the Land of Real Reward and the Impure Lands. Through the third...
It transforms into the defiled land of skillful means; fourth, it transforms into the defiled land of cohabitation.

Thus, for the sake of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and the sentient beings of the six realms, it is said that as deluded consciousness proliferates, the distinction between the holy and the ordinary arises.

This is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to when it says, "In accordance with the minds of sentient beings, responding to the measure of their cognition," and what the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* [describes].
That is to say: according to the conditions of defilement or purity, the ten dharma-realms are subsequently differentiated; therefore, they are categorized as divergent branches of delusion.

Furthermore, one should know that although the first phrase speaks of the "tranquil light" (寂光) as truly pure and originally devoid of any distinction between suffering and joy, this does not preclude the fact that while there is no difference, there is nonetheless differentiation—this is precisely the ten realms inherently possessed by nature. Although the second phrase speaks of the deluded consciousness being chaotic...

Thus, there arises the distinction between the holy and the ordinary; yet, this very distinction does not obstruct their non-distinction, for they are without difference within the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*).
This is because, although True Suchness (*tathatā*) is unchanging, it does not obstruct its capacity to adapt to conditions (*pratyaya*) while remaining unchanging;

and although deluded consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) follows conditions, it does not obstruct its capacity to remain unchanging while following conditions. Because it functions through conditions, it is therefore not different.

It is extraordinary because it is unchanging; thus, it is different yet not different. Only one who can know this is able to fully comprehend the present mind of nianfo (buddha-recollection), which is the complete manifestation of the nature through pure cultivation, and the total presence of cultivation within the single nature.
△ Next, the formal sequence of the *nidāna*.
[Commentary]: Because they are thus adrift in the five turbidities and unable to return to the single truth, our Śākyamuni Buddha manifested birth in this Endurance World (*sahā-loka*).

[Commentary] This correctly sets forth the circumstances for the Tathāgata’s preaching of this sutra. For although Śākyamuni Tathāgata had long ago realized the true and eternal, how could he have undergone birth in a royal palace?
It was solely because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have fallen into decline.

Therefore, there is the emergence of this Sahā world. Those who drift in the five turbidities refer to sentient beings who, since beginningless time, have stirred the waves of consciousness from the ocean of the nature of nirvāṇa, thereby disturbing its clarity and perfect stillness.
They have defiled its luminous subtlety and submerged its true nature. This truly stems from first losing [the nature] through movement; hence it is called "drifting. (The Śūraṅgama Sūtra)
This refers to what is called: "Awakened clarity and empty dullness interact to produce agitation. Next, one loses this through obscurity; hence they are called the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
This is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* means when it says that "obscure dullness becomes space. However, obscurity necessarily entails motion, and motion necessarily entails obscurity.
Thus, flow is itself turbidity, and turbidity is itself flow. Once the delusions of obscurity and motion have taken form, [the process continues].
The truth of clarity and stillness is immediately lost. However, these five turbidities differ in their coarseness and subtlety.

As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*): "When you perceive empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions, space and seeing are not distinguished;
there is space but no substance, and there is seeing but no awareness. These interweave to falsely form [this state]. This is the first layer, called the turbidity of the eon. This, then—

This refers to the three delusions collectively. If one were to speak according to the common explanation—that the kalpa-turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) enters only when the human lifespan is twenty thousand years—this would refer exclusively to the two delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*), speaking of them at their time of greatest intensity.
However, while there may be instances where the subtle does not include the coarse, there has never been a case where the coarse does not include the subtle; thus, for now, [we shall] merely...
This refers precisely to the time when the World-Honored One manifested birth in this Sahā world. What is described here as "coarse" is appropriate to that context;

even the statement "do not return to the one true [reality]" is spoken with reference to the subtle as well. His manifestation of birth in the Sahā world was precisely an act of compassionate response within the impure land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together;
it specifically refers to his inferior response body, the physical form of an old bhikṣu six feet tall.

[End. If one speaks of this while also including subtle afflictions (*anuśaya*), then the meaning encompasses the "hanging response" [of the Buddha's descent], which refers to the two aforementioned lands.

△ Regarding the sequential exposition of the sutra, there are two parts: first, the sequence of the dwelling place and the suitability of the audience; second, the sequence of the essential teachings expounded.
Now, first is the sequence of the dwelling place and the suitability of the audience.
[Commentary] At the auspicious assembly in Jeta’s Grove, Śāriputra’s sharp faculties were addressed.
[Sub-commentary] "Jeta’s Grove" refers to the location where this sutra was preached; "Śāriputra’s sharp faculties" refers to the primary audience for whom it was intended.
Regarding the specific capacities of those to whom this sutra is addressed, there are three categories: first, bodhisattvas; second, followers of the two vehicles.
Third, regarding ordinary beings: generally speaking, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is never mentioned in the various sūtras of the Hīnayāna.

This is because, once the seeds and fruits [of existence] are exhausted, one's body is reduced to ashes and wisdom extinguished; they do not speak of rebirth after death. That this is now extensively discussed is precisely the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattvas.
If one traces the origin of this sūtra, it was preached during the Vaipulya period, when the biased views were being refuted and the Hīnayāna disparaged, and its excellence praised.
When [the Buddha] extensively praised the Perfect [Vehicle], he refuted the Lesser Vehicle by stating that [beings] are not born outside the [Buddha-]field;
thus, he spoke of "birth" while specifically indicating that in that land there are immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples.

Furthermore, when he extolled with utmost fervor the subtle and wondrous adornments of both the environment and its inhabitants in that realm, his praise for the Great and Perfect [Vehicle] was implicitly contained therein. How much more so, then, [regarding] Śākyamuni...
"Ānanda, furthermore, because he is the foremost among the assembly of disciples, I have addressed him to cause him to turn away from the Small Vehicle and head toward the Great Vehicle.

If one is truly a candidate for this teaching, even while remaining at the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), by holding the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction for seven days, one will immediately attain rebirth.
Upon entering this sublime assembly once, one attains non-retrogression. Viewed in this light, although one may still be an ordinary being,"
The meaning belongs to the Perfect and Sudden [teachings], which can likewise be understood.

Next, the essential points of the Dharma taught consist of four parts: first, the sequence of the scripture’s title; second, the sequence of the scripture’s essence; third, the sequence of its fundamental tenets;

and fourth, the sequence of its power and function. Since the means of expression (*nirukti*) and that which is expressed (*vācya*) do not exceed these four, they are summarized and presented in this introductory sequence.
Thus, having exhausted the essential purport of this single sutra, he may be called one who is well-versed in the Mahāyāna. Now, first, the title of the sutra is introduced.
[Commentary: It opens the gate of vows for the treasury of Dharma and points toward the wondrous land of the Land of Bliss.
[Commentary] This sutra fully explains both the primary and secondary rewards (the environment and its inhabitants), as well as the retinue, serving as the means of expression (*nāman*).
Yet, the title of the sutra simply says, "The Buddha Speaks of Amitābha. This is what is meant in Master [T'an-luan’s] *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*:

"By citing the primary reward, one encompasses the secondary fruits; by describing the transformative master, one includes the retinue. Thus, while the title speaks only of the primary [reward], it is precisely by citing the primary that it achieves this inclusion.

Regarding the inclusion [of the *pratītyasamutpāda*], the introduction mentions only the "basis" (*āśraya*). This employs the basis to include the "principal" (*pradhāna*), expressing them as mutual reflections;

this is a refinement of literary technique. This treatise contains no text concerning the opening of the gate of vows (*praṇidhāna-mukha*) for this sutra; because it is explained in detail in the *Mahāvaipulya* (the Great Root), it is omitted here and not discussed.
△ The Essential Body of the *Anupūrvi-sūtra*.
[Commentary] The jade groves and gemstone ponds directly reveal the source of the mind; the lifespan and radiance fully manifest one's own nature.
[Commentary] "Jade groves and emerald ponds" briefly cites the description of the *nirmita-pratītyasamutpāda* (the environment).

From the passage on the sevenfold railings up to the jeweled trees and jeweled nets that emit subtle and wondrous sounds constitutes one section of the sutra text. "Life span and radiance" briefly cites the description of the *svasaṃbhoga-nirmāṇa-kāya* (the primary retribution).
From the passage beginning with "For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha" up to "can only [be described as] immeasurable and... constitutes the second section.
The "Infinite" (*asaṃkhyeya*) section explains a single passage of scripture that directly reveals the source of the mind and fully manifests its own nature (*svabhāva*).
Two lines of verse correctly set forth its essence: for this sutra takes the Seal of True Reality (*bhūtatathatāmudrā*) as its primary essence.

It is neither characterized nor uncharacterized; being characterized yet without characteristics, it is called True Reality. Indeed, the jade groves and jeweled ponds, the lifespan and the radiance—[all these are manifestations thereof].
This is indeed the characteristic of all dharmas. Thus, it is directly revealed in the source of the mind and fully manifested within one's own nature;

what characteristic, then, could possibly be apprehended? This is precisely the non-characteristic that is not without characteristic, the true essence of characteristics being without characteristic.
It is the wondrous Dharma of the Mind-only Pure Land and the Original Nature Amitābha; yet, though it is easy to speak of it, it is difficult to realize.
The principle is likewise difficult to refine; to profoundly awaken to its ultimate aim, there must necessarily be that which is most correct.
If one attempts to clarify this, it cannot be done except through the Tiantai school’s doctrine of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). Why is this?
For the Land of Ultimate Bliss lies far beyond ten trillion *kṣetra*s, and Amitābha Buddha is a perfected being whose wisdom and severance are complete and whose purity is fully realized. Broadly...
Ordinary beings on this earth are defiled by the three delusions and submerged in the two deaths; they create inexhaustible karmic bonds and act as the cause for endless births.
How could they suddenly respond to Amitābha and be reborn in the Pure Land, crossing the five paths of existence horizontally and immediately attaining the stage of non-retrogression?
This is precisely because, according to the discourse of our school, there is a specific meaning regarding the *dharmatā* (intrinsic nature) of sentient beings.
Third: First, as for the extent of one's nature, it pervades the ten directions, mutually penetrating without exterior.

The Land of Ultimate Bliss beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of lands exists within the extent of my own nature, being but a single corner of that which is already near and close. This is the essence of one's nature.
That which is eternally abiding, firm, and solid is pure and radiant—the enlightened essence (*bodhi*) of Amitābha’s perfected wisdom and severance (*jñāna-prahāṇa*).
This is precisely identical to my own nature-essence, without any difference. One term for this is "nature-inclusion" (*xingju*).

However, if one merely says that there is nothing external and no difference, yet remains ignorant of the Dharma-gate of nature-inclusion, then although one speaks of "no exterior," it ultimately results in [the existence of] duality.

Externally, although it is said there is no differentiation, in the end differentiation is established. Furthermore, one does not know from what cause the virtues of the nature’s capacity and the nature’s essence are all-pervasive, nor upon what dharma they depend for their purity; one should know that these exist as inherent within the nature.
Thus, what was previously stated regarding the substance of virtue and the measure of substance both take my nature’s inherent possession as their foundation.
The principles of the three natures are fully elucidated in the *Treatise on Birth and Non-Birth* (*Sheng wusheng lun*); they are not listed here at length.
△ Third, the Essential Summary of the Preface.
[Commentary]: That the various sages dwell together is not attained through minor merit. Holding the Name for seven days depends upon the non-distraction of a single mind.
[Commentary] In the five chapters explaining the title below, faith, aspiration, and pure practice are established as the essential core of this sutra.
Now, summarizing the scriptural text, I shall provide a brief exposition. While the text simply mentions "pure practice," this is because it occupies the central position among the three essentials.
The first phrase corresponds to the scripture which says: "That Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are..."
The Arhats cannot be known by means of calculation; the assembly of Bodhisattvas is likewise so.
It is further said that those beings born in the land of Sukhāvatī are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive), and among them there are many.
Those who are in their final birth before attaining Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) are so numerous that they cannot be known by calculation;
they can only be described as immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*). Furthermore, it is said that sentient beings who hear this should make a vow to be born in that land.
Why is this? Because one will be able to dwell together in one place with such superior and virtuous people.
The second phrase corresponds to the Sūtra’s statement: “One cannot be born in that land by means of a small amount of roots of goodness or causes and conditions of merit.
Therefore, it is said that the various sages dwell together; one is not born there through a small amount of goodness. The third and fourth phrases correspond to the Sūtra’s statement:
“If there be good sons or good daughters who, upon hearing the name of Amitābha Buddha, uphold his title—even if only once...”
Whether for one day, two days, or even up to seven days, with a single mind free from distraction, the jade groves and jeweled ponds directly reveal the source of the mind;

the lifespan and radiance fully manifest one's own nature. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have drifted through the five turbidities due to the causes and conditions of delusion and movement, unable to return to the One True Reality. Now, they shall return to their origin and restore their fundamental state.
The Source: Nothing precedes illuminating the darkness and stilling the movement. Holding the Name for seven days is the means by which one illuminates that darkness;
single-mindedness without distraction is the means by which one stills that movement. If darkness and movement are truly forgotten, what need is there for "not being real"?

It is like dust clearing so the mirror becomes bright, or the wind subsiding so the waves become calm. That holding the Name for seven days allows one to immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression precisely demonstrates this.

This teaching belongs to the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle]. It does not depend on the power of vows over a single lifetime; rather, its compassion that grants rescue and relief and its fundamental power of merit are inconceivable.
It is truly the essential ford for swiftly emerging from birth and death, and the great thoroughfare for practicing the Bodhisattva path.
△ Section Four: The Power and Function of the Four Periods, divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation of the power and function.
[Commentary]: The phenomena and principle are of one essence; sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally identical. Through unconditioned compassion, the response occurs without deliberation.
[Commentary] This sutra takes the departure from suffering and the attainment of happiness as its function. As the sutra says:
"When that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy ones, appears before them.

At the time of death, this person’s mind is not inverted, and they immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha. This is precisely the power and function of this [sutra].
It concerns bestowing and extracting. The merit of bestowing and extracting lies in resonance and response. Sentient beings take the single-minded holding of the Name as the stimulus;
Amitābha takes the extraction of suffering and the bestowal of joy as the response. The way to extract suffering is rooted in compassion (*karuṇā*);
the way to bestow joy is rooted in loving-kindness (*maitrī*). These are entirely matters of natural affinity and are by no means forced. As for the practitioner:
Because the essence of phenomena and principle is one, the Way in which the sentient being and the Buddha are fundamentally identical constitutes the "inspiration" (gan).
Amida, for his part, constitutes the "response" (ying) through the Way of responding without deliberation by means of unconditioned compassion (muryō-jizai). Is this not Amida coming from nowhere?
He comes to this Sahā world to guide and receive practitioners. By not going yet going, the practitioner reaches that Land of Ultimate Bliss to behold and pay homage to Amitābha.
This is indeed the fundamental principle upon which the power and function of this single sutra rely.
△ Next, regarding the meritorious achievements thus generated:

[Commentary] Having realized that the fundamental endowment is solely mind, billions of lands are not remote; knowing that the Great Vows can be relied upon, the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are traversed in a single stride.

[Commentary] Since the preceding text has already clarified that the principle of the power and function is fundamental, if one relies upon this to practice nianfo (recitation of the Buddha's name) with the aspiration for birth [in the Pure Land], one can realize that the essence of phenomena and principle is one, and that the living being and the Buddha are originally identical.

Thus, even the distant lands of ten million *koṭi* worlds are all inherently possessed within my own mind; though far away, they are not remote. One is thus able to know the unconditioned compassion (*amogha-maitrī*), which responds without prior deliberation.
Thus, the forty-eight great vows have no further conditions upon which to rely, and the flow of consciousness can be severed. Is such power and function not indeed supreme?

Regarding the statement that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are "transversely" traversed, this clarifies the transcendence of the triple world (*tridhātu*). There are two meanings: transverse and vertical.
According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, it explains that the *Tripiṭaka*-bodhisattva cultivates the six [perfections] for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Having completed the myriad practices and planted the causes for the marks and signs over a hundred kalpas, one then attains the stage of non-retrogression and acquires the fivefold Dharma-body;
this is the "vertical" progression, ascending from below to above, like a rabbit or a horse crossing a river, which is circuitous and takes a vast amount of time.
However, if one relies on this sutra to seek birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—whether already born, currently being born, or yet to be born—all shall attain it.
They do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, it is said that all beings who are born are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).
This is to emerge directly and transversely; it is to reach that [state] right here, like a fragrant elephant crossing a torrent.
It can be attained in a single thought-moment; therefore, this power and function are most preeminent.

[Commentary]: To explain the fivefold profound meaning of the title of this sutra, following the Master of Gushan, one takes the realized beings (*phala-pudgala*) of the two lands...

Its name is "The Great Vaipulya. Its essence is the true reality (*tathatā*) of the *vaipulya* sūtras. Its fundamental principle is faith, aspiration, and pure karma. Its function is the relinquishing of suffering and the attainment of bliss.

[Commentary] The "fivefold" refers to name (ming), essence (ti), doctrine (zong), power (li), function (yong), and the characteristics of the teaching (jiao xiang). "Profound" (xuan) means that it is subtle and difficult to perceive;
"meaning" (yi) means that there is a deep underlying reason for it. This Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai deeply grasped the Buddha’s mind and thoroughly clarified the purport of the scriptures.
Before commenting on the scriptural text, he first [addressed] those points within the scripture that are subtle, difficult to perceive, and possess a deep underlying reason.

This is the purport for interpreting the title of the scripture. It enables a person to understand the meaning of the scripture at a mere glance of its title. Generally, "Name" (Ming) refers to the title of the scripture.
"Essence" (Ti) refers to that which is elucidated by the title: the essential nature of the mind of sentient beings. "Principle" (Zong) refers to practice.

It is the essential core of taking the entirety of the essential nature as the basis for initiating the principle of contemplation, and taking the entirety of contemplative practice as the means for returning to the essential nature of the mind.
As for "power and function," this refers to the essence and fundamental principle of the sutra, as well as its great function of generating goodness and extinguishing evil.
As for "the characteristics of the teachings," this clarifies the progression and stages of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma over five periods.

The intent is to enable students to seek the essence of the mind by means of names, and to establish the essential tenets by means of that essence; thereby severing doubt and engendering faith, generating goodness and extinguishing evil, so that they may come to know them well.
Regarding the categories of Great, Small, Partial, and Perfect, there shall be no error or confusion concerning the intent of the scriptures.

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts. First, the explanation of Amitāyus, in two parts. First, the citation of the sūtra for explanation.
[Commentary]: The sūtra says: "The lifespan of that Buddha, as well as that of his people, is immeasurable and boundless, spanning asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
[Commentary]: Regarding "the lifespan of that Buddha," this refers to the sovereign who transforms [beings]. Regarding "its people," this refers to the sentient beings.

Although that land is a pure land and possesses its inhabitants, it has no king; because the people are each self-disciplined and dwell in goodness, there is no need for governance by both civil and military means, and thus there is no king. There is only the Buddha as the sovereign who transforms [them], and the Dharma...
It is simply the king. Generally speaking, the lifespan of a transformative leader follows that of the people of his land in its length or brevity.
Since the people of that country already possess immeasurable lifespans, how much more so must the Buddha’s lifespan be without limit?
This is an instance of illustrating the leader by means of the people; thus, the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable.
△ Third, the explanation by way of analogy regarding superiority.

[Commentary] Since the number of *saṃbhogakāya* (response bodies) is immeasurable, and even gods and humans cannot know their count, how much more so for the *dharmakāya* and *svābhāvikakāya* (dharma and reward bodies).

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the fact that each of the three bodies—the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*—has its own measure of lifespan: lifespan is established based on life-force (*jīvitendriya*), and life-force depends upon the body.
[The text] maintains that since the sutra speaks of "life-span" (*āyus*), there must also be a "body and life.

Therefore, the Great Master Tiantai, in his *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* (*Guanjing shu*), explains the title "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*) by clarifying the three bodies and the three lives. He states: "The Dharma-body takes the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) as its model;
it takes the Dharma-nature itself as its body. This body is not material substance, nor is it mind or consciousness; it is not comprised within the aggregates (*skandha*) or the realms (*dhātu*)."
This is merely a forced designation of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as the *dharmakāya*. Regarding the "life-span" (*āyus*) of the *dharmatā*:

it is not a life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) obtained through karmic retribution, nor does it possess any continuity or maintenance. It is merely a forced designation of that which is non-transmigrating and immutable, named "life-span.
This life-span is neither long nor short; it neither extends nor contracts. It is a forced designation of the *dharmadhātu*, equal in measure to empty space. This, then, is not a body.

This body is the longevity of that which has no longevity; it is the measurement of that which cannot be measured. As for the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), it is what is evoked by spiritual cultivation.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that it is "attained through long-cultivated practice. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that it is "the Great Parinirvāṇa, because it is attained through the cultivation of the Path."
The wisdom of suchness illuminates the realm of suchness. The wisdom of bodhi is in resonance with and merged with the dharma-nature.
"Resonance" is like the fit between a box and its lid; "mergence" is like water and milk merging together. The dharma-body is no body.
It is not that there is no body; since wisdom and [the object] are already merged, it is neither body nor non-body.

We provisionally name this wisdom the "Reward Body" (saṃbhogakāya). Its Dharma-life is neither life nor non-life; since wisdom and [the object] are already merged accordingly, it is neither life nor non-life.
We provisionally name what is not life as "life. Its Dharma-measure is neither measure nor immeasurable; since wisdom and [the object] are already merged accordingly, it is neither measure...
It is not that the immeasurable is called "immeasurable" by way of a mere designation; rather, it is measured as immeasurable. As for the *saṃbhogakāya* (Response Body):
it accords with all things in its lifespan; it accords with the continuity of existence in its lifespan; it accords with length and brevity in its lifespan.
Wisdom merges with the essence, enabling the arousal of great function, just as mercury mixed with pure gold can coat all manner of forms. Thus, merit blends with the Dharma.
The body manifests and proceeds everywhere; it can be both body and non-body. It can manifest as eternal life or as impermanent life.
It can manifest as immeasurable or as measurable. Regarding the measurable, there are two meanings: first, it is the measure of the immeasurable.
The second is the measure of that which is finite. For example, seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, as well as eighty [kalpas] and so forth, are measures of the finite.
As in the case of Amitābha, there is indeed a definite limit; though humans and devas cannot count it, it is a finite measure within the infinite.

These responsive Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya*) all employ these two types of measure. Following things and according to conditions, they appear with varying degrees of length and brevity. Yet, regarding these three bodies...
The three types of lifespan cannot be categorized as either identical or distinct; for if they were identical, they would contradict the nature of the Dharma-body.

It is precisely by being three that it is one, and precisely by being one that it is three—only thus does one accord with the profound text. In the present passage, this refers to the "responsive" (nirmāṇa) lifespan, let alone the manifest "Dharma" and "recompense" (dharmakāya and sambhogakāya) lifespans.
For this reason, the title of the sutra is called "Immeasurable Life" (Amitāyus).
△ Second, the explanation of Amitābha (Immeasurable Light). First, the individual translation.
[Commentary]: Also called Immeasurable Light.
△ Second, citing the sutra.
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "The light of that Buddha is immeasurable; it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without obstruction.
[Sub-commentary] This is also the light of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) of Amitāyus Buddha. By analogy with the light, one may also discuss the lifespan of the response-body.
That is to say, the Dharma-body is neither body nor non-body; thus, the Dharma-light is neither light nor non-light.
...and so forth. Now, even the light of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) is thus immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions without obstruction;
how much more so the lights of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body)!
△ Second, the explanation according to the general and specific names, in two parts. First, the direct explanation.
[Commentary] Furthermore, "Buddha" is a general title, while "Amitābha" is a specific title.
[Sub-commentary] All Buddhas possess both general and specific titles. In the title of this present sutra, Śākyamuni is mentioned only by his general title.
Amitābha mentions only his specific [name].
△ Second, resolving doubts.
【Commentary】 Śākyamuni is the Teacher of this world; all beings know him well, so his general title is cited. Amitābha is...
The Guide of the Land of Ultimate Bliss must logically be made manifest; therefore, his specific title is displayed.

[Commentary]: Some may raise the doubt: "Since all Buddhas possess both general and specific titles, why does the title of this sutra not list both the general and specific names of the teaching lords of the two lands?
It should rather state: 'Spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha, the Sutra of Amitābha. Thus, it is explained.
The commentary therein resolves this doubt, stating: Śākyamuni is the teacher of this world; there are no sentient beings who have not heard of or known him.
Therefore, he is referred to solely by his general title to encompass his specific attributes. Amitābha, however, is the guide of Sukhāvatī; his specific attributes are not explicitly indicated here.

If only the general name were used, it would not be manifest; therefore, a specific title was displayed to encompass its universal meaning. The translator, wishing to avoid redundancy and prolixity, adopted this concise approach, which aptly captures the essence of the matter.
△ Second, the explanation of the title, in two parts. First, the explanation by way of the permanence of the Dharma.
[Commentary]: "Sūtra" means the Dharma and it means permanence. It is universally observed by the ten realms and remains unchanged throughout the three periods of time.
[Commentary] The interpretation of *fǎ* as "constant" is based on the *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra).

Furthermore, according to the *Miaozong chao*, it is said that in the exegesis of Confucian classics, there are these two meanings [of "law" and "constancy"], which serve as a model for ten thousand generations; thus, it is interpreted as "law. It has remained unchanged through the reigns of a hundred kings.
"Gu" (故) means "constant. The Buddhist scriptures are likewise: they serve as the universal standard for the ten realms and remain unchanging throughout the three periods of time.
2. Explanation by way of the meaning of "you" (由).
[Commentary]: Because they were proclaimed from the golden mouth of the Sage, they are called "jīng" (scriptures).
[Commentary] The *Myōshūshō* states: Because the Great Sage Buddha proclaimed with his golden mouth the Dharma he himself realized, it is called a *sūtra*.
△ Second, the combined explanation of the general and specific [names], in two parts: First, pointing out the two names, general and specific.
[Commentary] Furthermore, "sūtra" is a general name, while "the Buddha’s teaching" and so forth are specific names.

[Sub-commentary] The *Miaozong* states: As for the general name, it includes both sudden and gradual teachings, as well as the provisional and the disclosure of the provisional; these exist outside of the Vinaya and the Śāstras.
Since all are called "sūtras," they are termed "general" (pāṭha). As for their specific names, the individual characteristics are numerous;

however, we shall now follow three types—namely, those based on persons, dharmas, and similes—which consist of three single [categories], three double [combinations], and one complete [set], thus forming seven distinct types. Regarding the three single [categories]:
Single [categories] include: the person, such as in the *Amitābha Sūtra* and others; the dharma, such as in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and others;
and the simile, such as in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and others. Regarding the threefold [combinations]: person-and-dharma, such as in the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and others;
dharma-and-simile, such as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and others; and person-and-simile, such as in the *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda Sūtra* and others. Person...
Regarding the "perfection of both the Dharma and its analogies," this refers to such texts as the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Ekayāna Mahā-upāya Vaipulya Sūtra*.
By means of these seven specific categories, together with the general [classification], they collectively characterize the Buddha-dharma of the entire dispensation.
△ Second, explaining the reason for the general and specific [teachings], in five parts. First, a general discussion of the single transformation.
[Commentary]: There are three kinds in the sutra, namely: teaching, practice, and principle. One practices according to the teaching, and through practice, one manifests the principle.

[Commentary] The *Miaozong* states: When our school explains the title by discussing it in terms of the general and the specific, it is because each of these two names possesses both teaching (*jiao*), practice (*xing*), and principle (*li*).
If these three were absent, then to discuss the general and the specific in vain would be without foundation. Why is this so?
This is because one practices based upon the teachings, and through practice, one subsequently manifests the principle.
△ Second, specifically indicating the present title:
[Commentary] “Buddha” has the meaning of awakening; since this refers to what is accomplished through cultivation, it belongs to practice. “Teaching” (shuo) is the doctrine itself. Amitābha...
This "Ta" (陀) is the principle.

[Commentary] Now, regarding the character "Buddha" (佛) in the title, it is judged to belong to the practitioner. This is because "Buddha" carries the meaning of "awakening," encompassing the senses of self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of the practice of awakening.
Since this is explained from the perspective of that which is accomplished through cultivation, it belongs to the category of "practice. As for the character "shuo" (說):
The classification according to teaching is most clear. As for the judgment that Amitābha belongs to the principle (li): it is because he is the Amitābha of the fundamental nature;
it is precisely through the practitioner’s invocation and cultivation that he is seen. Therefore, he is judged to belong to the principle.
△ Third, the judgment of their general and specific natures.
[Commentary]: If contrasted with other scriptures, then all three sutras are specific; if contrasted with the word "sutra" (jīng), then all three sutras are general.

[Commentary] It differs from other scriptures; thus, not only do the five characters constitute a distinction, but the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle in these three sutras are all distinct.

Conversely, when contrasted with the word "sutra" (經), not only does the single character constitute a commonality, but the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle in these three sutras are all common.
△ Fourth, the conclusion as the Secret Treasury.
[Commentary]: Principle is the Dharmakāya; practice is Prajñā; teaching is Vimukti. These three are perfectly interfused in an inconceivable manner;
this is called the Secret Treasury (Guhyakośa).

[Commentary] When our school explains every sutra title according to both its general and specific meanings, it is precisely because we wish to clarify that each [title] possesses three aspects of the sutra.
That each possesses three aspects of the sutra, in turn, is intended to clarify that they possess the secret treasury (guhyagarbha).
For example, the three characters "A-mi-t'o" (Amitābha) are the Dharma-body nature of our own practitioners. As for the character "Buddha" (Butsu)...

This is precisely the Prajñā-wisdom that arises from the entirety of nature (*xing*). The single word "expounding" (*shuo*) is the liberation attained through wisdom and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, principle (*li*) is the entirety of the path of suffering, which is the Dharma-body and the *tathāgatagarbha* as the direct cause (*zhengyin*).
Practice (*xing*) is the entirety of the path of delusion, which is Prajñā and the *tathāgatagarbha* as the cause of realization (*liaoyin*). Teaching (*jiao*) is the path of karma.
This is liberation itself; it has the Buddha-nature as its causal condition. These three virtues are like the three dots of the world-sign *i*, or the three eyes of the Heavenly King:
they are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor separate, and are thus inconceivable—the secret treasury.
The meaning and principles of the sutra’s title are as subtle and profound as this. How could those who lecture or listen to it afford to treat it with negligence?
△ Fifth, the conclusion on the resulting merit.
[Commentary: Therefore, by hearing even the names of the opening titles, one attains immeasurable merit.
[Commentary] As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* and various other Mahāyāna sūtras, this is frequently taught.
△ Second, the original title.
[Sub-commentary] The original title of this sūtra is "Praise of the Inconceivable Merit Protected by All Buddhas."
Recitation of the Sūtra.
△ Third, distinguishing the differences in translation, in three parts. First, the general heading.
[Commentary]: Transmitted to China, there have been two translations in total.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the two versions. First, the Tang translation.
[Commentary]: The Tang translation is titled *The Sūtra on Praising the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Acceptance*.
△ Second, the Qin translation. First, distinguishing it from the Tang version.
[Commentary] Now, the Qin version omits and abbreviates the title of the sutra; it appears after the section on the Buddhas of the Six Directions, stating simply:
"You sentient beings, you should believe in these [Buddhas].

[Sub-commentary] Whereas the Tang translation preserves the original name, the Qin translation does not, because it was omitted and abbreviated in that [latter] version, appearing [only] after the six directions.
This is because it appeared after the Buddha’s passing.
△ Second, praising the skillfulness of the Qin translation.
[Commentary]: This sutra correctly demonstrates the method for upholding the Name; moreover, the sacred title of Amitābha is something that all people delight in hearing.
By employing this to establish the title, many people have come to believe and accept it; thus, it has been universally observed throughout the four seas and its circulation remains inexhaustible.
This is the skillful artistry of the translator.
[Commentary] Generally speaking, in establishing a name, one values that which gives rise to goodness. Regarding the goodness now produced, there are two kinds. First, by...
This sutra correctly demonstrates the method for upholding the Name. First, because the sacred name of Amitābha is what all people delight in hearing, it was used to establish the title;

thus, many people believe in and accept it. For this reason, the Tang dynasty translator kept it secret within the Great Canon so that it was neither seen nor heard, whereas the Qin dynasty translation is universally followed throughout the four seas and its circulation is inexhaustible. This is due to the skillful artistry of the translators.
This is indeed trustworthy and verifiable.
△ Second, the discernment of the essence (tattva), in two parts. First, the heading.
[Commentary]: Second, the discernment of the essence.

[Commentary] Second, regarding the clarification of the essence (*tattva*): as stated in the preceding general enumeration, "the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of the Vaipulya [sūtras] constitutes its essence.
The true reality of the Vaipulya has two meanings. First, this sūtra was preached during the third period of the Vaipulya, when all four teachings were discussed together;
this sūtra belongs to the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) teaching. To distinguish it from the true reality of other sūtras, it is not the [true reality] of the *Avataṃsaka* or the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

It flowers forth the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the three periods; hence it is called *vaipulya* (extensive). As for the true reality of the One Perfect Teaching (*ekayāna*), every gate leads into the Cool Lake;

hence it is "square" (*fang*). It is "equal" (*pingdeng*) because both sentient beings and Buddhas equally possess it, being non-dual and impartial. The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states:
The "essence" (*tǐ*) is the primary substance. The *Miaozongchao* states: "Names are secondary and thus guests; essence is primary and thus the host.

Names are provisional designations, while essence is the actual substance. Under every name, there exists its corresponding substance; here, we are discerning the actual substance underlying a provisional name.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, citing treatises to clarify the essence.
[Commentary]: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All Mahāyāna sūtras universally take the single true reality (*eka-tattva-lakṣaṇa*) as the primary essence of the sūtra."
[Commentary] The *Myōshūshō* states: "All phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing; they are neither existent nor non-existent; they have no subject and no object;
they are free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental conditioning.

To be free from these characteristics is called the 'characteristic of the signless true reality' (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-asallakṣaṇa*). If one applies this principle to interpret this sutra, then the preceding section consists of seven layers.
From "The railings depart" up to "Those who hear this sound all give rise to the thought of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha," this clarifies that the Pure Land is mind-only (*cittamātra*).
This corresponds to the preface which states, "The jade groves and emerald ponds directly manifest the source of the mind.
From the middle section, "For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha? up to "But can only be described as immeasurable and boundless," [the text continues].
The *Śāṅgī* [commentary] states: "This clarifies the Original Nature Amitābha. The preface says, "Life-span and radiance fully manifest the self-nature," which is precisely this point.
"Jade groves and crystal ponds" clarify the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment or dependent retribution), encompassing the four kinds of pure lands.
"Life-span, radiance, and so forth" clarify the *sambhoga-kāya* (the primary retribution), encompassing the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and those of the nine grades who attain rebirth. This...
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is said that only Buddhas, together with Buddhas, are able to exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
What Tiantai calls the "inherent possession of the three thousand [realms]" (*xingju sanqian*) is none other than the essence of this true reality.
△ Second, the conclusion regarding the expressed meaning.
[Commentary]: This refers to the principle that is the expressed meaning.
△ Third, the two aspects of the thesis. First, the heading.
[Commentary] Third, the clarification of the central tenet.
△ Second, the explanation [of the tenet], which has two parts. First, citing a sutra to establish the proof.
[Commentary] The Sutra says: "If there are those with faith, they should make a vow to be born in that land."

[Commentary] In the previous general enumeration, it was stated that "faith, aspiration, and pure practice constitute the core doctrine. Therefore, I now cite the scriptures to establish this as proven.

"If there is one who has faith" refers to the gate of faith; "one should generate an aspiration" refers to the gate of aspiration; and "if one wishes to realize [this]" [refers to the gate of practice].

The Gate of Pure Karmic Practice should be fully cited from the text below: holding the Name for seven days with a single mind without distraction, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land—this constitutes the gateway of the three essentials.
As for faith: one must believe that there is a Pure Land of Mind-Only, the Amitābha of one's own original nature, and that through the power of the Tathāgata’s vows, all shall attain rebirth.
This corresponds to the first of the ten practices, the contemplation of the inconceivable.
This concerns the realm of deliberation. Although one may possess faith, if one lacks aspiration, rebirth will not be attained.
Since Amitābha has already gathered sentient beings through the power of his vows, I must seek to go there by means of my own vow; only then will our natures be in accord.
Spontaneous extraction is like a magnet that naturally attracts; according to the tenfold classification, this corresponds to the second:
the genuine arousal of the bodhicitta. Among the Four Great Vows, it corresponds to the vow: "To bring the unsurpassed Buddha-way to fulfillment."
One should attain the first three vows. Although these vows exist, if there is no practice, the vows will be mere delusions;

therefore, one must for seven days hold the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction, gathering [the mind] through the ten modes of practice. This corresponds to the third [of the ten modes]:

the skillful application of calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) to settle the mind. Holding the Name for seven days is *vipaśyanā* (contemplation), and single-mindedness without distraction is *śamatha* (calming).

Only when one holds the name with single-mindedness can one be single-minded while holding the name; this constitutes the simultaneous illumination of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as their simultaneous negation.
Through such skillful settling of the mind, one achieves success. This briefly indicates the three dharmas for those of superior faculties;
the remaining seven vehicles are all contained therein.
△ Second, the conclusion of the essential tenets.
[Commentary]: This is the essential tenet of this single sutra.
△ Fourth, clarifying the function; first, the restatement of the topic.
[Commentary] Fourth, the function of the treatise.
△ Second, the explanation, which has two parts. First, citing the sutra to provide proof.
[Commentary] The sutra says: "One immediately attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where all are non-retrogressive regarding unsurpassed bodhi."
[The commentary] states: "The first two phrases indicate the practice of holding the Name for seven days with a single mind without distraction;
the subsequent two phrases refer to the passage in this preceding sutra which says: 'All sentient beings who are born [therein] are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive).'"

In the previous general enumeration, it was stated that its function is "to abandon suffering and attain happiness. This refers to the scriptural passage stating, "One immediately attains rebirth," and so forth.
If one takes the latter [text] to corroborate the former, then all sentient beings who are reborn there are those from the Sahā world who practiced *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation);
they will certainly attain non-retrogression in their bodhi. By combining these two passages as mutual proof, one understands the power and function of this sutra.
△ Second, the conclusion regarding its power and function.
[Commentary] To leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of liberation—this is the power and function of this sutra.
[Sub-commentary] Among all other dharma-gates, there is none that does not cause sentient beings to emerge vertically from the triple world and leave behind the suffering of birth and death.
One attains the bliss of liberation. It is like a nine-storied tower: one ascends from the bottom to the heights; if one’s strength prevails, one advances, but if the feet grow weary, one falls.

Such an ascent is difficult. Only the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land enables sentient beings to exit the triple world horizontally, leaving behind the suffering of birth and death to attain the bliss of liberation.
It is as close as one's own home; from east to west, it can be beheld at a mere glance.
With a snap of the fingers, one arrives; how easy it is to depart! Is not the power and function of the sutras truly great?
△ Five: Judging the Characteristics of the Teachings (2). First: General Statement.
V. Judging the Characteristics of the Teachings.

[Commentary] "Teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the words spoken by the Sage for those below him. "Characteristics" (*xiang*) refer to the discernment of differences and similarities. The Tathāgata established teachings across five periods, advancing according to the needs of the time;
the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as the Gradual and Sudden approaches, each have their distinct divisions. Tiantai categorized these based on the five periods.
Yet, when analyzed, each has its own distinct place. Therefore, in the interpretation of all sutras, it is necessary to provide a doctrinal classification (*p'an-chiao*).
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics.

[Commentary] This section belongs to the Mahāyāna Vaipulya teachings. Regarding the meaning clarified by the two baskets (*piṭaka*), it is subsumed under the Bodhisattva basket. It is categorized as both gradual and sudden.
[This is] divided [into categories]. This belongs to the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*).

[The *Chao*] states that there are three explanations for judging the characteristics of this teaching. Regarding its classification as being subsumed under the Mahāyāna Vaipulya (*fangděng*) teaching, the first is a judgment based on time.
As previously listed in general terms: "Mahāyāna 'fresh butter' (*shēng-sū*) constitutes the teaching characteristic. Fresh butter is...

This is the period of the Vaipulya. The Great Master Tiantai employed the five periods of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as a sequence of development to judge the teachings of the Tathāgata throughout his entire life.
First, "milk is produced from the cow," which is a metaphor for the Buddha’s very first teaching: the preaching of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* during the seven days following his enlightenment.
Next, "curd is produced from milk," which is a metaphor for the emergence of the ninefold canon (*navāṅga*) from the twelvefold canon (*dvādaśāṅga*).
For twelve years, he preached the four Āgamas of the Hīnayāna. This is like producing fresh butter from curds; it is analogous to how the Vaipulya sutras emerge from the Āgamas.
For eight years, he preached the Vimalakīrti, Mahāsaṃnipāta, Śūraṅgama, Laṅkāvatāra, and the Sixteen Contemplations, as well as this present sutra and others.
He refuted the partial and rejected the small, praising the Great and extolling the Perfect. As for the śrāvakas—
One attains the benefit of censure: feeling shame for the small and aspiring toward the great, one enters and exits without difficulty.

This is precisely what is meant when it is specifically told to Śāriputra that Amitābha has a land and Bodhisattvas have bodies, and that those sentient beings who are born there all attain non-retrogression—this is exactly that matter. Next, from the "fresh butter" (piṇḍa-sarpis):
The production of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is like the emergence of the *Prajñāpāramitā* from the Vaipulya sūtras.

In the twenty-second year, he preached various sūtras such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, using the water of the wisdom of emptiness to cleanse the attachments of the followers of the two vehicles, causing Subhūti and others to turn and teach the *Prajñāpāramitā*, thereby entrusting them with the wealth of the Dharma in its integrated entirety.
Next, the production of the finest essence (*sarpis*) from clarified butter is like the emergence [of the Lotus Sūtra] from the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the nine realms and the three vehicles are brought together; provisional teachings are granted predictions of enlightenment, such that there is neither "small" nor "great," and all are made to become Buddhas.
This is now the third stage, the "fresh butter" (*navanīta*). Therefore, it is said that this section belongs to the Mahāyāna Vaipulya teachings.

As for the statement that "its meaning is clarified within the two piṭakas and it is subsumed under the Bodhisattva Piṭaka," this is the second classification according to the piṭakas. Generally, among the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, there are...

Regarding the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, which is taught for the sake of those of the two vehicles: it clarifies principle only as far as the ultimate truth; it clarifies delusion only as the breaking of view-delusions and thought-delusions;
it clarifies wisdom only as the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness; and it clarifies that the fruit consists of neither body nor land.
Now, since this sutra clarifies that outside the Sahā world there exists a distinct pure land, it follows that the retributive fruit includes both body and land. Is this not logical?
The fruits of both delusion and wisdom are all subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. When divided into the gradual and the sudden, this belongs to the Sudden Teaching;

this is the third [criterion], the judgment according to the teaching. Within the teachings of the transformative ritual, there are both the gradual and the sudden. The gradual involves practicing over the course of kalpas.

The gradual approach leads to the stage of non-retrogression; the sudden approach accomplishes it in this very life, reaching the rank of *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive). Thus, the conclusion states:
"By causing ordinary beings not to retrogress from Bodhi, and enabling them to reach the rank of non-retrogression in this very life, this is truly the Perfect-Sudden Dharma-gate.
Furthermore, one must first open the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhimukti*) and subsequently cultivate the perfect practice to shatter the three delusions.

Only then will they realize the perfect fruit and ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. For now, however, I shall merely describe the two types of retribution—the environment and the inhabitants—of that land, so as to open their understanding and engender faith;

and I shall explain how, by reciting the Name for seven days with a single-minded lack of confusion, one establishes the gateway of practice, whereby at the moment of death, one immediately attains rebirth there and ascends to the stage of *avaivartika*. This would not be possible were it not for Śākyamuni...
The skillful means of this [sūtra], the vow-power of Amitābha, and the past roots of the practitioner—these are the three essentials for manifestation.

By maintaining "one mind without distraction," the three delusions are thoroughly suppressed and the roots of karma are suddenly severed; thus one proceeds directly forward without hindrance. How could one achieve this without it?
Therefore, know that this sūtra is the unsurpassed *amṛta* (clarified butter) for the world of the five turbidities, even as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* [declares].
It is said: "If poison is placed within fresh butter, it will kill a person upon consumption; how can this not be believed?

[Commentary: Ānanda is translated here as "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi). He was the son of King Śuklodana and the cousin of the Buddha.
He was born on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment; because the entire nation rejoiced, he was given this auspicious name. He was foremost among those of great learning.
△ Explanation of the Name Rāhula. [Commentary]:
Rāhula means "obscuration" or "covering. This was originally the name of an asura who was able to obstruct the sun and moon.
Because the Buddha was being obstructed by him and thus could not immediately leave the household life, he was given this name.
△ 11. Explanation of Gavāmpati. [Commentary]:
Gavāmpati means "the Cow-Chewer. In a previous life, he was an ox; because he would chew the cud after eating, he received this name.

An alternative translation renders it as *Piṇḍola-bharadvāja*.

The Buddha [has been] for ninety-one kalpas; his retribution is fully perfected, and he is foremost in the divine eye. [Commentary]:
In various sūtras, when the assembly is enumerated, there is always a praise of their virtues, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*; these are examples thereof.

That this sūtra alone lacks such a passage is not that it does not exist; rather, it is because the translator was skillful, intending to cause one to contemplate the meaning by looking at the name itself.
As for the Greatly Wise Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others—considering what virtues of theirs were not manifest?

Yet, when various sūtras praise their virtues, they necessarily do so in accordance with the specific conditions that arose. For example, because Ānanda was prompted by the condition of his improper attachment, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* praised his virtues specifically, saying:
"The Buddha’s son maintains [the Dharma], skillfully giving rise to all existences," and so forth. It is the same here.
As for this assembly of followers, since they already possess such virtues, it clearly demonstrates that they are the appropriate recipients [of the teaching].
Although they rely upon conditions of false defilement, they are in reality free from such faults. As for the other disciples in this sutra, there is no need to discuss them for now;
even Śāriputra of Great Wisdom, who occupies the foremost position, followed by Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, and Mahākapphiṇa...
Candana, do these three individuals lack intention? It is simply that regarding the Dharma-gate of Ultimate Bliss, none can believe it without the true wisdom of a Bodhisattva;
none can go there without the great supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva; and none can shake off the three delusions without [such power].
Yet none are able to purify it; were it not for the subtle, fourfold unimpeded eloquence, none could discourse upon it.

This sutra is taught within the Vaipulya (fangdeng) class, intending to cause śrāvakas to turn their minor wisdom into great wisdom, their minor supernormal powers into great supernormal powers, their minor dhūta practices into great dhūta practices, and their minor discourses into great discourses, thereby purifying the buddha-lands.
That which is expedient yet real, and real yet expedient—by this one may clearly perceive the true mark (*dharmatā*) and, with faith and acceptance, practice accordingly.
That which is near yet distant, and distant yet near—by this one may travel swiftly without haste; in the snap of a finger, one arrives.
When the mind is pure, the land is pure. That which is defiled yet pure—by this one realizes that birth is non-birth; though born, one is not born.

He transforms the two obscurities; wondrous existence is itself emptiness, and true emptiness is itself existence. In this regard, he can employ his wondrous function and eloquence to analyze these matters without obstruction.
As for the other disciples, each possesses a particular virtue, and their virtues are praised according to their respective categories.
One dedicates merit through these very activities. Within this Dharma-gate, one achieves the benefit of the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings:
realizing non-arising yet arising, one brings forth birth beyond the realms; attaining bodilessness yet possessing a body, one receives the transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
To emerge vertically from the three realms is already inconceivable; moreover, to emerge horizontally from the three realms is even more inconceivable.

Those whose ignorance is not yet exhausted are called *sattva* (sentient beings).
*Mahāsattva* is translated here as "beings with the mind of the Great Way. [Commentary]: The two characters "bodhisattva" are an abbreviation of the Sanskrit term.
If expressed in full, it should be *mahā-bodhi-citta-sattva*. *Mahā* is translated as "great"; *bodhi* is translated as "way" (*mārga*); *citta* is translated as "mind"; and *sattva*...

"Sentient beings" (*zhòngshēng*) is also translated as "sentient entities" (*yǒqíng*). Taken together, they constitute "sentient beings with the mind of the Great Way. The "mind of the Great Way" distinguishes them from ordinary sentient beings below;
"sentient entities" distinguishes them from the Buddhas above. This is because they have already departed from this shore, yet still dwell in the middle of the stream.
These bodhisattvas are further distinguished as "Great Beings" (mahāsattva) because they occupy the highest rank among them.
