△ Second, the explanation of the meanings is divided into five parts. First, the explanation of Mañjuśrī.
【Commentary】 Mañjuśrī is translated here as "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode). This is because his three subtle and wondrous virtues are identical to those realized by the Buddha.
He is also called Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Having entered the correct position of the Dharma, he is named a "Dharma Prince.

[Commentary] Regarding the three subtle and wondrous virtues (triguṇa) that are identical to those realized by the Buddha: in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), from the first stage (prathama-bhūmi) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samābodhi), one gradually breaks through a portion of the ignorance of each stage and thus partially shares in the Buddha’s realization of the three subtle and wondrous virtues. If we speak of Mañjuśrī in terms of the textual tradition...
The Bodhisattva thus possesses the distinction between his fundamental essence (*hon*) and his manifested trace (*seki*).

Regarding his fundamental cause, as recorded in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Pao-tsang ching), he made great vows before the Buddha Ratnagarbha and received a prediction of enlightenment from that Buddha, being named Mañjuśrī.

Furthermore, at the abode of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, he served as the teacher of the Eight Princes; he is the ancestor of nine generations of Śākyamuni’s lineage. In the past, he attended various Buddhas; now, he assists [Śākyamuni].

Śākyamuni, if one discusses his fundamental fruition: in the present, he acts as a Buddha in the northern world-realm of *Ānanda*, named *Ānandagarbha-maṇiratna-akṣaya* (Joyful Treasury Maṇi Jewel Accumulation).
In the future, he will attain Buddhahood in the southern world-realm of *Vimalā* (Stainless), named *Samantamukha-tathāgata* (Universally Manifesting Tathāgata).
Such are his fundamental and manifest traces; they are identical in what has been realized by the Buddha, their rank is equal, and he is also called *Miaoji* (Wondrous Auspiciousness).
"Xiang" (Auspiciousness) refers to the three—delusion, karma, and suffering. As long as even a fraction of these remains, one has not yet attained auspiciousness.

Only when one's stage reaches the ultimate and the three virtues are fully manifested is one called "Miaojixiang" (Wondrous Auspiciousness). The Buddha shattered the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), attained the King Samādhi, and entered the correct position of the Dharma;
thus he is named the "Dharma-King Who Shatters Existence. Mañjuśrī likewise occupies a rank adjacent to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and serves as the Buddha’s [crown prince].
The eldest son is named Dharmaputra (Dharma Prince).
△ Next, the name Ajita is explained.
[Commentary] Ajita means "Unconquerable. Because he transcends both the partial and the small [vehicles], he bears the name Maitreya (Kindly One).
[Commentary] In Sanskrit, his name is Ajita, which translates as "The Invincible. He is also named Maitreya, which translates as "The Compassionate One" (Maitri).
The *Siddhārthasādhana-sūtra* states: "If sentient beings behold him, they immediately attain the samādhi of the compassionate mind."
Taken together, this means that this bodhisattva has entered the stages of realization and is adjacent to the ultimate;
because his compassionate heart extends to all beings, he is given this name.
△ Third, the explanation of *Gandhahasti*.
[Commentary] *Gandhahasti* means "unresting" (*aviśrānta*), because one diligently practices without indolence. [Sub-commentary] The *Siddhārthasāgaramatiparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"A period of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas constitutes one day and night; thirty such days constitute one month."
Twelve months constitute one year. After passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one may encounter a single Buddha.

Encountering Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in this manner, one practices various pure conducts (*brahmacarya*) and cultivates meritorious virtues; only then does one receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Because the mind never rests, it is called *gandhahasti*.
△ Fourth, the explanation of Constant Diligence (*nityavīrya*).
[Commentary] "Constant diligence" refers to the fact that the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is eternally abiding, thereby accomplishing effortless right effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-samyakprahāṇa*).
[Sub-commentary] The *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states: "This bodhisattva, for the sake of all sentient beings, pursues them throughout immeasurable kalpas."
He does not abandon them; yet they do not receive transformation. Without a single thought of renunciation, he advances with both body and mind, which is called "constant diligence.

It is simply by seeing that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally abiding that he achieves effortless right effort (*anabhisaṃskāra-samyakpradhāna*); though he is diligent, there is no mark of diligence.

In various sutras, when listing the assembly of bodhisattvas, there are also praises of their virtues, as seen in the *Lotus Sūtra* and others—this is the general rule. That this sūtra alone lacks such praise is not because it does not exist; rather, it is intended to cause those who read this sūtra to contemplate its meaning by reflecting on the names and to receive and practice the teachings by looking up to their virtues. Why is this? As the text states: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, with his great compassionate heart, universally delivers all sentient beings. If there are sentient beings who suffer from various afflictions, and they single-mindedly call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara will immediately perceive their voices and deliver them from suffering. If there are women who, having reached the age of marriage, desire sons or daughters, and they single-mindedly call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall obtain what they seek. When their pregnancy reaches full term, they shall give birth to a son or daughter who is handsome, upright, and intelligent, and they shall not experience the suffering of childbirth. Furthermore, in that household, there will be no fear of fire, water, wind, or thunderbolts; nor will there be any fear of kings, thieves, or robbers; nor will there be any fear of poison, weapons, or calamities. Even if one were to fall into a great fire, by calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, one would immediately be extinguished and cooled. If one were adrift on the great ocean, surrounded by waves and facing the threat of death, by calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, one would immediately reach the shore of safety. If one were bound in shackles or fetters, by calling upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the bonds would immediately loosen and fall away. Maitreya and Gandhahasti possess self-mastery and tireless vigor, cultivating with diligence and without slackening, always being energetic so as to awaken to the permanence of the Dharma and achieve effortless right effort (*anābhoga-samyak-pradhāna*).

For one who practices the Pure Land, they first take the three subtle and wondrous virtues—which are the three truths of my own mind—as the foundation for the three contemplations that serve as the subject of observation; this is what is meant by "first contemplating the inconceivable realm.

For those who seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, their primary aspiration should be to transform sentient beings, sever afflictions, study the Dharma-gates, and realize the Buddha-way.

the remedial teachings spontaneously assist in their unfolding. One may ascend the nine grades, no longer dwell in the city of doubt, and give rise to no attachment to the Dharma;

[Commentary] Jingjue says: There must be four intentions for not addressing the bodhisattvas, devas, and nāgas.

First, because he was a left-hand disciple (*vāma-pārśva-śiṣya*), and in both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna assemblies, he frequently occupies the foremost position. Second, because his wisdom is supreme, none among the fourfold assembly or the eight classes of beings fail to revere and look up to him.
Third, it is to cause the fourfold assembly, upon hearing of the Buddha’s Pure Land, to feel self-reproach.

Because it severs [the bonds] completely; and because those who still desire the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) but have not yet attained realization may turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).

Whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he invariably brings about the benefit of the four *siddhāntas*. Now, among the twelve divisions of the scriptures preached by the Buddha, this should be classified as the *avyākṛta-svayambhāṣita* (unasked spontaneous discourse), for the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is not within the realm of the Lesser Vehicle. Furthermore, it is intended to...
Because they turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, this sutra lacks only the *geya*, *gāthā*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa* [of the twelvefold division].
However, the *sūtra*, *vyākaraṇa*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *udāna* are all clearly present here.

If the Jātaka and Itivṛttaka have not yet been translated, they can be sought through their brief summaries in the extensive versions; these are likewise fully contained within the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra*.
△ Third, the explanation of the number of sections.
[Commentary]: One great trichiliocosm is called a single Buddha-field. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* states: "The Western Land is ten thousand billion lands away from here;
this is spoken merely in relation to the physical eyes of ordinary beings and the mental capacity of those in the cycle of birth and death.
It means that as long as sentient beings achieve pure karma, their mind of meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the rebirth in the Pure Land.
The mind: the very movement of thought is the moment of birth in the Pure Land; it is truly not far away.
[Commentary] In the explanation, first the distance is clarified according to the sutra, and next the lack of distance is clarified according to principle. One great trichiliocosm.

Regarding the term "one Buddha-field": it is so called because ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion great oceans, and ten billion Cakravāḍa mountains constitute one Buddha-field.

As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "One thousand sets of four continents, suns and moons, Mount Sumerus, the six heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds, is called a small chiliocosm. One thousand times this small chiliocosm [is a medium chiliocosm]."
This is called a medium chiliocosm; a thousand times this is a great trichiliocosm, all of which share the same process of formation and destruction.
Viewed in this way, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is extremely distant from here. Next, the Great Master Tiantai is cited from his *Ten Doubts* (*Shi yi lun*) to clarify that it is not far away.
This is because ordinary people, due to the delusions of their afflictions and the karmic retributions of their good and evil deeds from previous lives, [perceive it as distant].
One obtains this fruit of suffering, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of this life. All ordinary people with their physical eyes do not see what is distant;
thus, they take that which is unseen to be distant. All that pertains to the mental scope of birth and death is unknown when it is distant;

likewise, they take that which is unknown to be distant. It is no cause for wonder. If a person who recites the Buddha’s name maintains single-mindedness without distraction, then delusions will be severed.
I prostrate. When pure karma is accomplished, the path of karma becomes clear. At the time of death, when the seal of *Sahā* is destroyed, one is liberated from the path of suffering.
At that moment, the physical eye is transformed into the divine eye, and the ordinary mind is transmuted into the sacred mind.
Therefore, the mind abiding in meditative concentration at the time of death is precisely the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land; a single movement of thought constitutes birth there.

Regarding the phrase "at the time of the Pure Land" and "moving thoughts": this refers to the moment of impending death when one is able to behold the Triple Gem, as well as seeing light, flowers, and so forth.
Any such vision is termed "moving thoughts," yet it is not a thought of delusion.

Although one is still in this world, having already attained such a vision is the very moment of rebirth in the Lotus Pond; therefore, it is said that it is truly not far off. Furthermore, [the *Pǎn*...]
The *Zhongjing* (Commentary on the Sutra) states that sentient beings possess three powers by which they are able to see Amitābha.
First is the power of samādhi, which is precisely what is explained in this treatise. Second is the power of the Buddha, namely the Forty-eight Vows. As the sutra says:

"If, when I have attained Buddhahood, sentient beings of the ten directions should with sincere heart believe and rejoice, desiring to be born in my land, and should even recite my name ten times, yet [not attain birth]..."
I shall not attain perfect enlightenment until [all beings] are born [in the Pure Land]. Third is the power of fundamental merit. This has two meanings.
First, sentient beings have, since beginningless time, possessed the seeds for mindfulness of the Buddha and seeking birth in the Pure Land; at that time, however, these had not yet sprouted.
Now that the seeds have ripened, one should attain rebirth there. Second, the nature and mind of sentient beings inherently possess all lands and kalpas;
although they may be as distant as ten million billion *yojanas*, there is nothing that is not inherently possessed. This is the very substance and magnitude of the nature itself:

like a single jewel in Indra’s net, its reflection contains all other jewels; like a single wave in the great ocean, it fully possesses the entire body of the tide. It is not merely a matter of mutual possession.

They are, moreover, mutually identical. Thus, Siming said: "If the nature of the mind did not inherently contain the dust-motes and lands, then birth would lack the efficacy of evoking vision, and there would be no principle for the Buddha’s manifestation in response."
△ Fourth, explaining "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
[Commentary]: The Sanskrit term is *Sukhāvatī*. This is translated here as "Peaceful Nourishment" (Ān-yǎng), or "Pure Tranquility" (Qīng-tài). It is also called "Ultimate Bliss."
This refers to being "most supreme.

[Commentary] "Peaceful Nurturing" (An-yang): in contrast to the eight sufferings that seethe together in this Sahā world, that which is nurtured therein is not peaceful. "Pure Tranquility" (Qing-tai):
in contrast to the five turbidities and evil conditions of this Sahā world, the place where one dwells is not tranquil. "Ultimate Bliss" (Ji-le): in contrast to this Sahā...
The multitude of sufferings among the *pāpa* (evil) is most severe; that which is experienced therein is not pleasure.
△ Five: Explaining the Four Lands, Part Two. First, the general heading. [Commentary]:
All lands are manifested according to the capacities of sentient beings; there are four such types.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the four [lands] has four parts. First, the Land of Tranquil Light.
[Commentary]: 1. The Land of Constant Tranquil Light is the ultimate abode of all Buddhas, where they dwell as the fruit of the supreme realization.

[Commentary] The *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra) states: "The 'Eternally Quiescent Light' (*chang-jiguang*)—eternity is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), quiescence is liberation (*vimukti*), and light is wisdom (*prajñā*).

These three points form the syllable *ī*, which is neither vertical nor horizontal; it is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). The *Miaozong chao* (Exegesis on the Sublime Topic) states: "The previous three [lands] pertain to phenomena (*dharma*);
therefore, their names as lands are established based on the causes and effects of cultivation and severance for those who dwell therein. This land, however, pertains to principle (*li*)."

Therefore, it is named after the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of its fundamental substance. I [the commentator] say: since the name "superior-grade *śānta-prabhāsa*" (tranquil light) already appears in the *Chao*, one knows that that land is also divided into nine grades.
Only the "superior-of-the-superior" grade is the dwelling place of those who have attained the ultimate fruit;

the remaining eight grades are all the dwelling places of the sages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) who have attained partial realization, and thus they constitute the "partially realized *śānta-prabhāsa*. As the *Shu* says:
This is the partial realization of the ultimate, wherein the tranquil light is both pure and impure.
△ Second, the Land of Real Reward.
[Commentary]: The second is the Land of Real Reward, which is the dwelling place of the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body.
[Commentary] The *Guanjing shu* states: "The realm of true recompense without obstruction" means that by practicing the true Dharma, one elicits a superior retribution;
because matter and mind do not obstruct one another, it is called "without obstruction. It is pure of Bodhisattvas alone, with no followers of the Two Vehicles. As the *Renwang jing* says:
"The Three Sages of the Stage of Merit and the Ten Sages of the Stage of Wisdom dwell in the fruit-recompense"—this is precisely its meaning. The *Śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva is superior..."

The exquisite five sensory desires are capable of causing Kāśyapa to rise and dance. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of "immeasurable pavilions of fragrant clouds," which refers precisely to the pure and exquisite five objects of sensory experience (*pañca-viṣaya*) in that land.
I privately maintain that Buddhas also possess lands of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*); why must these necessarily be the dwellings of Bodhisattvas?
They may likewise be categorized into nine grades: the highest of the high grades is where Buddhas reside, while the remaining eight grades are for others.

The differences in their respective levels correspond to the greater or lesser extent of ignorance eliminated by each Bodhisattva. The commentary states that "gradual and sudden entry" refers precisely to the distinctions between the Real Reward Land (*sambhoga-kāya*) and the Pure or Impure Lands.
△ Third, the Land of Expedient Means.
[Commentary] The third is the Land of Expedient Means, where those of the Three Vehicles reside.

[Sub-commentary] The *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra) states: "Regarding 'the land of expedient means with remainder,' this refers to having cultivated the path of expedient means and thereby severed the delusions of the four abodes."
It is said that because their skillful means (*upāya*) remain and their ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet exhausted, they are called "those with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). The *Śāstra* states:

Outside the triple world (*tridhātu*), there are pure lands where Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are born; having been born therein, they receive the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatākāya*), which is not a birth through the breaking up of the aggregates (*bheda-utpatti*).

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "If, after my parinirvāṇa, there are those who have truly attained the state of an arhat, yet do not believe in this Dharma, they shall attain definitive understanding upon encountering another Buddha.
Within this, there are further distinctions of sharp and dull faculties, where the former is designated as pure and the latter as defiled.
I privately remark that since it is said there are such distinctions of sharpness and dullness, purity and defilement within [the ranks of] these practitioners, this must be understood accordingly.

These are also divided into nine grades: the Perfect Path of Expedient Means (*pariniṣpanna-upāyamārga*) occupies the upper three grades; the Distinct and Common Paths of Expedient Means (*pratyeka-sāmānya-upāyamārga*) occupy the middle three grades;

and the Secret Store Path of Expedient Means (*guhyakośa-upāyamārga*) occupies the lower three grades. The *Śū* (Commentary) states: "The distinction between skillfulness and clumsiness in essence and analysis constitutes the remaining purity and impurity.
This is precisely what is meant.
△ Four: The Land of Common Dwelling (Sahā-loka). Part Two. First, the naming [of the land].
[Commentary] The fourth is the land of common dwelling (*sahā-loka*). This is the place inhabited by the six classes of ordinary beings.
[Sub-commentary] The *Amitābha Sūtra Commentary* states: "The Sahā world is a mixture of evils; it is filled with thorns, rubble, and impurities. It is a land of common dwelling."

It is free from defilement. The ponds flow with the eight virtues, and the trees are arrayed with the seven treasures. Following this is the Nirvana [Pure Land], where all belong to the stage of right determination;
it is a superior pure land where ordinary beings and sages dwell together.
△ Next, the explanation of the meaning. [Commentary]:
Based on the relative gravity of the five corruptions (*pañca-kaṣāya*), lands are distinguished as pure or defiled. In the Sahā world, the five corruptions are heavy;

therefore, it includes the four evil destinies, and the cycle of rebirth does not cease. In the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), the five corruptions are light; therefore, there are only humans and devas, all of whom attain non-retrogression.
Therefore, it is named "Ultimate Bliss.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Because of the five turbidities," this indicates the Sahā world. To explain it briefly:

because the causes of the five turbidities are heavy for the sentient beings of the Sahā world, it is called the "Defiled Realm of Co-residence. Consequently, their retributive experience encompasses the four evil destinies. This...
Within the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), one is drawn into the four realms of rebirth by whichever of the five dull fetters (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*) is most predominant.

Since humans and devas arise through the goodness of ethical discipline (*śīla*), their afflictions are relatively slight; however, the five turbidities in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*) are lighter than those in this Sahā world.
By single-mindedly cultivating pure karma and regarding the five turbidities as light, one attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and receives the rewards of humans and devas.

Moreover, upon reaching that land, the sensory environment is serene and pure, and afflictions do not arise; thus, even those among the ranks of humans and devas all attain the stage of non-retrogression.

Therefore, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). To speak further, even the Land of Ultimate Bliss is divided into the pure and the defiled, as seen in the nine grades of the *Contemplation Sūtra* and the three classes of the *Large Sūtra*.
Since these ranks and positions are distinguished by high and low, what is perceived naturally differs accordingly. Thus, the *Miaozongchao* states:
"The first [grade] has light five turbidities and constitutes the 'pure' of the Shared Residence. One must understand that this "purity" is extremely broad in scope.

This refers to a different intention. For example, regarding those with virtuous precepts, those in the ordinary stages of the four teachings are all able to cause the five turbidities to become light and thin, thereby inducing a pure shared realm (*sahā-loka*).
However, through the perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*) of lightness and turbidity, one induces a pure shared realm where both the environment and its inhabitants (*yi-zen*) are most pure.

As stated in the sutras, from the stage of earth-contemplation (*di-guan*) onwards, each and every characteristic, when compared to other sutras, involves the cultivation of various wholesome practices that induce peace and security.
The Land of Nurturing. Its characteristics differ from those of heaven.
△ Sixth, the distinction. [Commentary]:
To speak exhaustively according to principle, it is only the Ultimate Land of Tranquil Light that is the true and ultimate Land of Bliss.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "to speak exhaustively according to principle," this is a progressive differentiation based on the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*).
Thus, the partially realized *sambhogakāya* land of tranquil light (*śānta-prabhāsvara*) is still like a defiled land or a realm of suffering;

only the land inhabited by those who have attained the ultimate fruit can be called the truly real *Sukhāvatī*. Therefore, the preceding preface first clarifies that the true source is non-dual, stating: "The tranquil light is the true..."
"Purity. This refers to the fact that, from the very beginning, there was no distinction between suffering and pleasure.
△ Second, the adornment of the primary retribution (vipāka), in two parts: first, the citation of the section heading;
second, the adornment of the primary retribution itself.
△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra, in two parts. First, the listing of the sūtra:
In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who is currently preaching the Dharma.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts. First, the explanation of the three bodies (trikāya), in two parts. First, the general heading.
[Commentary] The Buddha has three bodies.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of two [bodies]. First, the Dharma-body.
[Commentary] First, the Dharma-nature body. It dwells in the Land of Tranquil Light; body and land are of one suchness, named the Secret Treasury.
[Commentary] The *Guanjing shu* states: "As for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the teacher takes the Dharma-nature as his model and likewise takes the Dharma-nature as his body.
This body is neither material substance nor mental consciousness; it is not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or sense-bases (*āyatana*).

It is merely a provisional designation of the Dharma-nature as the 'Dharma-body. The *Miaozong chao* states: "The teacher’s interpretation of the term 'Dharma' abandons the general sense for the specific. If taken generally..."

Both sentient beings and Buddhas take the *dharmatā* as their guiding principle; however, while the nine realms of existence follow this principle, they act in opposition to it, like a person who relies upon a teacher yet does not comply with the teacher’s instructions.
Only the Buddhas, from the first generation of the bodhicitta, practice by following the *dharmatā*, and are now able to bring it to ultimate perfection.
This is the profound legitimacy. Thus, the Great Sūtra says: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is what is called the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.
Because they accord with the nature of the Dharma, the Dharma is named 'Teacher. Yet in reality, it is not that which is taught, for it is distinct from the subject who teaches.
Therefore, the very Dharma that is the Teacher constitutes their body. Although it is called a 'body,' it has already transcended the five aggregates."
Therefore, it is neither material substance nor mental consciousness. Material form is the first aggregate (*skandha*); mental consciousness consists of the [remaining] four aggregates.

Since it is not an aggregate, it is also not an entrance (*āyatana*) or an element (*dhātu*). Thus, it is not included within the three categories (*trivarga*). Its maintenance and subsumption have already been excluded by this.

To demonstrate birth and death through the distinctions of the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) types, it may also be appropriate to exclude material substance from the category of mental consciousness, as it is subsumed under the aggregates and so forth.
Brief Report. A brief analysis of the causes for the three categories: since [the Buddha] is not any of these, by what means is he designated?

For the sake of sentient beings' capacities, the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is forcefully pointed to and termed the "Dharmakāya. This is the body that dwells; as for the land in which it dwells, it is as explained previously.
△ Second, the Reward Body (*sambhogakāya*).
[Commentary] The second is the Reward Body, which dwells in the Land of True Reward.

[Sub-commentary] The *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra) states: "The Reward Body is that which is evoked by the practice of cultivation. The *Lotus Sutra* says: "That which has been cultivated through long-term practice..."
It is attained. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that it is attained through the cultivation of the path. Suchness-wisdom (*tathatājñāna*) illuminates the object of suchness;
the wisdom of bodhi is in mutual resonance and union with the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). As for "resonance," it is like the fit between a box and its lid.
"Mutual merging" means merging like water and milk. The Dharma-body is neither body nor non-body; since wisdom should likewise merge with it, it is also neither body nor non-body.
This wisdom is provisionally named the "Reward Body" (*saṃbhogakāya*). The *Miaozongchao* states: "Reward" means recompense. Practice is the cause;
one elicits a wondrous reward and thus repays that cause. This refers to the realized wisdom of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Regarding virtue: the Sūtra states that the light of wisdom shines immeasurably; this is obtained through long-cultivated practice. It refers to the realization of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) within the Great Parinirvāṇa.

These two fruits of virtue are the recompense for having cultivated the causes; therefore, they are called "retribution" (*vipāka*). At the time of receiving this retribution, what are its characteristics?
Thus, it is revealed by means of one dharma and two metaphors. As with the name, there is no difference, yet there is a distinction in what is observed.

It is not called "conformity to the object" because there is an object external to the wisdom. It is not called "conformity to the wisdom" [for the same reason]. Regarding the two types of conformity for each:

the conformity of the object is like the wisdom, and the conformity of the wisdom is like the object. Because this object and wisdom are thus, they attain a state of profound resonance. Wisdom is termed "penetration";
therefore, it is distinguished by the awakening to the fruit, which is the wisdom of unsurpassed bodhi. This [wisdom] accords with the realm of *dharmatā*.
The characteristics [of the beginning and the fundamental] should merge in obscurity. First, the metaphor of the box and its lid is raised to illustrate their correspondence.

Fearing that one might think that although the edges of the box and lid meet perfectly, two distinct characteristics still ultimately remain, the metaphor of water and milk is further raised to illustrate their merging in obscurity.

This causes one to know that the beginning and the fundamental are both the same awakened nature (*bodhata*), their substance being utterly dissolved, exactly like water and milk. Thus it is revealed that there is no wisdom outside the realm, and no realm outside wisdom.
There is no objective realm. Water and milk can be seen [as distinct]. To say it is "not the body" means that it is not the delimited body of the *nirmāṇakāya* (Response-Buddha).

To say it is "not non-body" means that it is not the undelimited body of the *saṃbhogakāya* (Reward-Buddha). Furthermore, "not the body" means it is not existence; "not non-body" means it is not emptiness.

The Dharma-body of the Middle Way is the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Initial enlightenment merges with this; when that which is able to merge is also forgotten, it becomes [suchness].
Because it manifests through accomplishment, it is conventionally termed "retributive wisdom" (*vipākajñāna*). The meaning of its land is the same as before.

△ Third, the Response and Transformation Bodies (*nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*). [Commentary]: The third, the response and transformation bodies, dwell in the non-dual land; according to the capacities of the nine grades of beings, what they perceive differs.
[Commentary] The *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra) states: "The Response Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) means that it responds by taking on a body identical to the myriad things.
Wisdom is in profound union with the essence (*dharmatā*), enabling the arousal of great function. It is like mercury mixed with pure gold, which can coat various forms and images;

when merit is blended with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), it manifests and appears everywhere. It can act as both body and non-body. Nevertheless, these three bodies are neither identical nor distinct."
To be either identical or different contradicts the very nature of the Dharma. To be three while being one, and to be one while being three, is to harmonize with the profound text.
The *Miaozongchao* says: "It is like a valley responding to an echo; the magnitude follows the sound. It is like a mirror manifesting forms; the beauty or ugliness resides in the substance."
In response to the myriad things that evoke it, the [Buddha] manifests superior and inferior bodies. Wisdom is the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), and the essence is the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).

When these two are merged in profound unity, their application is boundless. Just as high-quality gold requires mercury to be able to coat objects—if this one condition is lacking, the gold has no function for coating—so too the merit of the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* must accord with the *dharmakāya*; then, according to the presence of those with capacity, it responds.
There is nowhere it does not reach. What has been explained above concerns retribution, which refers solely to the subtle dharma—that is, self-enjoyment.

Now, we clarify the manifested response, which is other-enjoyment. By contrasting the eternal response with the impermanent response of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), two traces of activity are shown.
Therefore, both types of bodies and so forth are clarified together. "Body" here refers to the birth-body, which possesses limited characteristics; hence, it is so named.

The body is not a body; it is a retribution-body. Because it lacks the characteristics of spatial limitation, it is called "not a body. The *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā* states: "What the Buddha calls 'not a body' is named the 'Great Body.
This Great Body is the *parabhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others). As for this "body of others," it manifests through transformation according to the capacities of beings at a single moment.
In meaning, it is identical to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), though there is a slight difference between them in terms of essence and function.
The *saṃbhogakāya* (response body) arises from the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, which are bodies of profound union, to initiate its function of response.
The *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), in turn, arises from the substance of the *saṃbhogakāya* to initiate its function of transformation; thus, it functions by means of function.

Furthermore, if it transforms through further transformations, then these transformations are infinite. The *saṃbhogakāya* represents the beginning and end of the eight phases [of a Buddha’s life], whereas the *nirmāṇakāya* appears and vanishes in an instant.
Extinction. Those who dwell in the land of non-duality: the *saṃbhogakāya* is the wisdom that realizes, and the *dharmakāya* is the principle realized.
Thus, both the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*) and the Land of True Reward (*vipākaphala*) are the essence capable of responding.

The Land of Other-Enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga*) and the Land of Expedient Co-residence (*upāyasahabāsa*) are all lands where the *nirmāṇakāya* dwells. Due to differences in the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, there are nine grades; therefore, one observes them...

As for these differences, the Buddha’s response must be without distinction; thus, the Land of Quiescent Light and the Land of True Reward exist simultaneously across the three grades. Therefore, it is said they are "non-dual.
One should consult the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* to determine those who attain rebirth in the nine grades; those in need should look this up. Furthermore, regarding the four lands:

Each of the lands is divided into nine grades; according to the response of the land, there are differences in the three bodies. According to the capacity of the response, the four lands are not the same.
Next, the distinctions are explained and clarified.
[Commentary] "Teaching the Dharma in the present" distinguishes this from the Buddhas of the past and future.
[Sub-commentary] The sutra below states: "Since Amitābha Buddha attained Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed until now.
From this, we know that Amitābha is a Buddha of the present who teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; he is not among the Buddhas of the past or the future.
...also. △ Second, the detailed explanation, which has two parts. First, the division of sections.
○ Second, the detailed explanation, which has two parts. First, the environment (niśraya-vipāka), which has two parts. First, a general explanation of Sukhāvatī.

△ Second, the explanation of the sutra has two parts. First, the explanation of the secondary environment (*sāmbhogika-kṣetra*) has two parts. First, a general explanation of Sukhāvatī has two parts. First, the citation of the sutra:

"Śāriputra, for what reason is that land named 'Supreme Bliss' (*Sukhāvatī*)? Because the sentient beings in that land have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is therefore named 'Supreme Bliss.'"
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning.

[Commentary]: "In that land" and below introduces the inquiry; "That country" and below provides the general explanation. "There are no manifold sufferings" means there are no sufferings such as those of the three miserable realms (*durgati*) or the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*).
It is called "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*) because it is spoken of in contrast to the extreme suffering of the Sahā world.

[Commentary]: The Sahā world comprises the six realms of existence. Humans, devas, and asuras are called the three good paths; they take the cultivation of precepts and wholesome deeds as their cause.
Hells, hungry ghosts, and animals are called the three evil paths; they take transgressions and malice as their cause. "Path" (mārga) carries the meaning of "that which enables passage.
This refers to how all sentient beings, by performing wholesome karma, are able to pass through to the human and heavenly realms and so forth.
Regarding "destinations" (*gati*): it is because the commission of evil karma enables one to pass through to places such as the hells.
Furthermore, what are called the "three paths" are named according to their results; that is, by means of evil karma, one passes through the path of fire, the path of blades, and the path of blood.
First, the realm of hell (*niraya-gati*): this place is located beneath the earth and within the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), and there are eight [hells].
The eight cold hells and the [eight] hot hells and so forth: sentient beings who have committed extremely heavy evil karma fall into these realms;
therefore, they are called the hell realm (*niraya-gati*). Second, the hungry ghost realm (*preta-gati*) has three types:

first, those whose sinful karma is most extreme do not hear the names of water or drink for many eons (*kalpa*); second, those who merely seek out human dwellings to consume pus and blood; [and third, those who roam in the air].
Feces and filth. Furthermore, those of the next rank may occasionally find a single meal, yet they are subjected to blades and staves and driven to fill rivers and block seas.
These are beings who have created evil karma; due to their stinginess and greed, they are born into this realm. Third is the realm of animals.
This refers to those with hair and horns, those with scales, shells, or feathers; those with four legs, many legs, or neither feet nor legs;
and those that move through water, on land, or in the air—all such beings who have created evil karma and, due to their ignorance, are born into these realms.

Regarding the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), all eight locations are characterized by obstacles and hindrances. Although there are differences in the suffering or pleasure experienced as karmic retribution in these eight places, [they are all considered difficult states].

Yet none of them are able to see the Buddha or hear the True Dharma; therefore, they are collectively termed "difficulties. First is the difficulty of the hells. The explanation of its meaning is the same as before.
Within the hells, there is perpetual darkness throughout the long night, and one undergoes uninterrupted suffering, which obstructs seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma;
for this reason, it is called a difficulty. Second is the difficulty of the animal realm. The explanation of its meaning is the same as before. Within the path of animals...
They undergo suffering without end. It obstructs the seeing of the Buddha and hearing of the Dharma; therefore, it is called a "difficulty. Third is the difficulty of the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

The explanation of the meaning is the same as before. Within the realm of hungry ghosts, one undergoes immeasurable suffering. It obstructs the seeing of the Buddha and hearing of the Dharma; therefore, it is called a "difficulty.
Fourth is the difficulty of the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*). This refers to the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), whose lifespan is five hundred *kalpas*.
Within the fourth dhyāna is the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*). It is called "non-conception" because mental consciousness does not function, like fish in ice or hibernating insects.
Many practitioners of external paths are born in that place; it obstructs the seeing of the Buddha and hearing the Dharma, and for this reason it is called a "difficulty.
Fifth is the difficulty of Uttarakuru. *Uttarakuru* in Sanskrit means "Superior Place" in Chinese. That is to say:

This place is where karmic retribution is experienced; it is superior to the three continents of the east, west, and south. Its inhabitants have a lifespan of one thousand years and do not suffer premature death.
However, because they are attached to pleasure, they do not accept instruction or transformation. For this reason, the Sages do not appear therein, and they cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma;
thus, it is called a "difficulty. Sixth is the difficulty of being blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired, referring to such individuals.

Although one may be born in a central land, if one’s karmic obstructions are profound and heavy—being blind, deaf, mute, or lacking the full set of faculties—one will encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world yet be unable to see him;
and although the Great Dharma is preached, one will be unable to hear it. Therefore, this is called a "difficulty."
Seventh is the difficulty of being possessed of worldly wisdom and eloquence. This refers to those in the world whose false intelligence is sharp and keen;

they devote themselves solely to the study of non-Buddhist scriptures and do not believe in the supramundane True Dharma. Therefore, this is called a difficulty. Eighth is the difficulty of being born before or after a Buddha.
This means that when a Buddha appears in the world as a Great Teacher, he causes all sentient beings to depart from [suffering]... [text truncated].
The suffering of birth and death and the bliss of attaining nirvana are encountered only by those who possess the necessary conditions.
Those born before or after a Buddha’s appearance do so because their karma is heavy and their conditions are thin;

having neither seen a Buddha nor heard the Dharma, this is called the difficulty of being born before or after a Buddha. "Equal to all sufferings" refers to the eight sufferings of the human realm. First, birth...

There are five kinds of suffering. First is conception in the womb; this refers to the time when consciousness enters the mother’s womb, remaining within the narrow and impure space of the maternal belly.
Second is the seed; this refers to consciousness taking up the physical remains of the parents as its seed-consciousness.
First, it follows the mother’s breath in its inhalation and exhalation, lacking any autonomy. Second, it grows;

that is, while remaining in the mother’s womb for ten months, it is boiled by internal heat, and its physical form gradually develops, dwelling between the stomach (*āmāśaya*) below and the small intestine (*pakvāśaya*) above, as if trapped in a prison.
Fourth, it emerges from the womb; that is, immediately upon birth, there is a cold wind and [a hot wind].
The wind blows upon the body, and when clothing and other things touch the physical form, the skin and flesh are so tender that it feels as if they are being pricked by objects.

Fifth is the suffering of birth (*jāti-duḥkha*): this refers to the human condition of having wealth or poverty, nobility or lowliness, and physical appearance that may be impaired or beautiful, ugly.
Second, the suffering of old age (*jarā-duḥkha*) has two aspects. The first is growth (*vṛddhi*), which refers to the transition from childhood to youth, and from youth to...
Reaching old age, one’s physical strength becomes frail and diminished, and one’s movements become unsteady;

this is the second form of destruction, wherein vigor departs and decay arrives, the spirit is depleted, and life grows shorter until one gradually reaches ruin—this is called the suffering of old age.

Third, the suffering of illness has two types: first, physical illness, which refers to the disharmony of the four great elements and the simultaneous assault of various maladies. If the earth element...
When the water element is disturbed, the entire body becomes heavy. When the fire element is disturbed, the entire body becomes feverish and hot.
When the wind element is disturbed, the entire body becomes stiff and rigid. Second are mental illnesses, which refer to harboring distress, anxiety, and sorrow within the mind;
these are called the suffering of illness. Regarding the suffering of death, there are two kinds: first, the suffering of terminal illness.

The first is death due to illness, where one dies because one's lifespan has come to an end. The second is death due to external conditions, where one dies upon encountering adverse circumstances or meeting with calamities such as water or fire;

this is called the suffering of death. Fifth is the suffering of separation from the beloved, which refers to being separated from those whom one constantly cherishes and loving, so that they cannot remain together; this is called the suffering of separation from the beloved. Sixth is the suffering of [encountering] enemies...

The suffering of encountering what is loathed refers to those who are one's constant enemies or whom one detests; though one originally seeks to distance oneself from them, they instead gather around one.
This is called the suffering of fearing the encounter with the loathed. Seventh is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, which refers to all worldly things and phenomena.
That which the mind loves and delights in, yet one seeks and cannot obtain—this is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.

Eighth is the suffering of the intense burning of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). The five aggregates are form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. "Aggregate" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of "covering" or "obscuring."
This means that it can cover and conceal the true nature, preventing it from manifesting. "Intense" (*cchi*) carries the meaning of being vast and flourishing;

it refers to the accumulation of various sufferings, such as birth, old age, sickness, and death, which occurred in previous lives. Therefore, it is called the suffering of the "intense blazing of the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha-paridāha*).

It is termed "Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*) in contrast to the extreme suffering of the Sahā world. This is because the sentient beings of Ultimate Bliss do not possess the aforementioned [sufferings] of the Sahā world.
Venerable sir, it is called "Ultimate Bliss" because it is free from all manner of extreme sufferings. To explain this further:

for the sentient beings of Ultimate Bliss, every object encountered by the six sense faculties is nothing but subtle and exquisite. Whether it be forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tactile objects, none fail to give rise to contemplative insight and the resolve to take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Consequently, there is no cause for the three poisons, and thus no karma of malice or rebellion is created. Therefore...

There is no suffering as the fruit of the three evil paths. There are no obstacles or difficulties of the three realms of existence. Having heard the Dharma and entered meditative concentration, one does not fall into the state of non-conception;
thus, there is no difficulty of the long-lived heavens. Although one experiences ultimate bliss, one constantly receives instruction and transformation;
thus, there is no difficulty of the continent of Uttarakuru. With the six sense faculties purified, clear, sharp, and wise, there is no blindness, deafness, or muteness.

There is no difficulty regarding the mute, for all sentient beings born there belong to the stage of those fixed in rightness (samyaktva-niyāma); thus, there is no difficulty regarding worldly wisdom or eloquence.
Amitābha Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma, having done so for immeasurable kalpas; Avalokiteśvara shall succeed him in that position.
He is titled the Buddha King of the Mountain of Universal Radiance and Merit; thus, there is no difficulty regarding the existence of a Buddha before or after another.

Entrusting his essence to a lotus bud, he is free from the suffering of birth. Unmoved by cold or heat, he is free from the suffering of aging. His body is not subject to segmentation, so he is free from the suffering of illness.
His lifespan is immeasurable, so he is free from the suffering of death. Having no parents, wife, or children, he is free from the suffering of being separated from those one loves.
It is suffering that all these supreme virtuous beings gather together; there is no suffering of association with the hated. They naturally enjoy celestial flowers and fragrant food;
there is no suffering of not obtaining what one seeks. They contemplate and realize the emptiness of the aggregates; there is no suffering of the skandhas.
△ Second, the specific explanation of the two types of adornments, in two parts. First, the division of sections.
○ Second, the specific demonstration of the adornments, in five parts. First, the railings and rows of trees.
△ Second, the commentary on the sūtra, in two parts. First, the railings and rows of trees, in two parts. First, the citation of the sūtra.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the land of Ultimate Bliss is surrounded on all sides by sevenfold railings, sevenfold decorative nets, and sevenfold rows of trees, all made of the four precious substances. For this reason, that land is called Ultimate Bliss.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has four parts. First, the explanation of the *railing* (*lángshǔn*).

[Commentary]: "Railing" (*lán*) refers to a balustrade. That which runs horizontally is called a *lán*; that which runs vertically is called a *shǔn*. It adorns the jeweled trees and encircles the clusters of flowers.
△ Next, the net is explained. [Commentary]:
As for the "net," it refers to jeweled nets that cover [the structure], their radiant colors shimmering and shining as they hang down all around, serving as a magnificent adornment.
△ Third, the explanation of the rows of trees.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "rows of trees," the *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Each tree is eight thousand yojanas high, with flowers and leaves made of the seven treasures."
There is nothing that is not fully possessed.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the four treasures.
[Commentary] The four treasures are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
[Commentary] To speak briefly: throughout the precious ground of Sukhāvatī, from every single jewel to the exterior of each pavilion, there are no places where jeweled trees are not arrayed.
Surrounding these jeweled trees are railings, and atop these jeweled trees and railings, they are further covered by nets.
That each is measured by sevenfold repetition is intended to symbolize the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
Furthermore, as for the trees, railings, and nets, all being made of the four jewels, these serve to symbolize that the seven factors of enlightenment are not separate from the four noble truths.
In the Sahā world, the residences of kings and ministers are not without such adornments;
however, speaking of the trees, they do not exceed mere groves; speaking of the railings, they do not exceed wood and stone; and speaking of the nets, they do not—
Regarding silk and hemp: in terms of the ground, it does not exceed soil and stone; in terms of causes, it does not exceed human effort.
Although the heavens share these qualities, they do not possess the proclamation of the Dharma-sound found in the Pure Land.

That the Pure Land and the defiled land differ, and that what is produced naturally and what is produced through effort vary—how could there not be a reason for this? The commentary cites the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Kuan-ching) as follows: 1. [The first point...]
Each tree is eight thousand *yojanas* high, fully endowed with flowers and leaves made of the seven treasures.

By analogy with this, it can be known that the adornments are not limited to the four treasures alone. I shall now cite the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* and the *Contemplation Sūtra* in full, listing each detail one by one;
this is not because I delight in prolixity, but rather to provide further support for those who seek rebirth in the Pure Land.

"Earth" refers merely to one's faith and joy. The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "As for contemplating the jewel trees, contemplate each one individually, forming the perception of rows of trees made of the seven treasures.
Each tree is eight thousand yojanas high. All these jewel trees are fully endowed with flowers and leaves of the seven treasures.
Each flower and leaf displays the colors of various jewels; from within the color of lapis lazuli, gold emerges."
From the glass-colored light, red light emerges; from the agate-colored light, mother-of-pearl light emerges;
from the mother-of-pearl-colored light, green pearl light emerges. All manner of jewels, such as coral and amber, serve as radiant ornaments.
Exquisite nets of pearls completely cover the trees, with seven layers of nets upon each individual tree. One by one...
Within the lattice-work, there were five hundred billion exquisite flower-palaces like those of the Brahma King.
Within them, celestial youths appeared spontaneously. Each youth wore five hundred billion Śakrābhilagna-maṇi jewels as necklaces;
the radiance of these maṇis illuminated a hundred yojanas, appearing as if ten billion suns and moons had been gathered together.

They may be described by name; they are interspersed with various jewels and are of the most excellent color. These jewel-trees stand in rows facing one another, with leaves following one after the other.
From among the many leaves grow exquisite flowers, and upon these flowers there are naturally fruits made of the seven precious substances.
Each leaf of every tree is exactly twenty-five yojanas in length and breadth. These leaves possess a thousand colors.
There were a hundred kinds of paintings, like celestial necklaces, adorned with various wonderful flowers of Jāmbūnada gold.
Like whirling fire-wheels, they turned gracefully among the leaves, from which various fruits sprang forth.
Like the vase of Śakra, they emitted great radiance and transformed into banners and streamers, as well as precious canopies. Within these precious canopies, the trichiliocosm was reflected.
All Buddha-activities and the Buddha-lands of the ten directions likewise appear therein. Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya* states:
"There are also seven kinds of jewel-trees. As for those trees consisting of a single jewel, their roots, trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all made of that one jewel."
Regarding two jewels forming a single tree: the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are interspersed with the two jewels. Regarding three jewels forming a single tree:
the roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are interspersed with the three jewels. Regarding four jewels forming a single tree: [the same applies].
The roots, stems, branches, and leaves each consist of one jewel; the flowers and fruits are identical to the roots and stems.
A tree composed of five jewels has its roots, stems, branches, leaves, and flowers each consisting of one jewel, while the fruit is identical to its root.
A tree composed of six jewels has its roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits each consisting of one jewel. A tree composed of seven jewels...
The trees were likewise so; they were distinguished only by their added joints and increased by one additional jewel.
Thus, these various trees were each different, yet row met row, stem faced stem, branch corresponded with branch, and leaf turned toward leaf.
Flower upon flower accorded with one another; fruit upon fruit corresponded with its like.

They were arranged in such rows, numbering hundreds of thousands of layers, interspersed with jeweled ponds in the same manner, extending even throughout the entire world. Their vibrant colors and brilliant radiance were beyond the power of the eye to behold.
△ Second, the Flower Pond and the Pavilion. Part One: Sectioning the Text.
○ Second, the Flower Pond and the Pavilion. Part One: The Direct Explanation. △ Second, the Exegesis of the Sutra.
Part One: The Flower Pond and the Pavilion. Part One: The Direct Explanation. Part One: Listing the Scriptural Text.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the Land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
The bottoms of these ponds are entirely covered with golden sand, and their four sides and steps are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Above are multi-storied pavilions, likewise adorned with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, mother-of-pearl, red pearls, and agate.

Within the ponds, lotus flowers are as large as chariot wheels; those that are blue emit a blue radiance, those that are yellow emit a yellow radiance, those that are red emit a red radiance, and those that are white emit a white radiance—subtle, wondrous, fragrant, and pure.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has six parts. First, the explanation of the seven-jeweled ponds.
[Commentary]: Regarding the seven-jeweled ponds, the *Amitābha-sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Each and every pond is composed of the seven jewels.
These jewels are soft and supple, produced from the king of wish-fulfilling gems."
[Commentary]: The "Seven-Jeweled Pond" derives its name from the water. Therefore, it cites the pond water of the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Kuan-ching) to explain it as being formed from the seven jewels.
However, does the Sahā world lack water? It arises from the element of water (*ap*), and thus its substance is not the seven jewels. Does it lack jewels?
They arise from the element of earth (*pṛthivī*), and thus their substance is not soft and supple. [This is the case] in the Pure Land.
The water of this [Pure Land] is supple yet not yin; it is precious yet not rigid. This is how purity and impurity are distinguished. Not only this:
that scripture further states that its mani-water flows among the flowers, ascending and descending along the trees.
Precisely because its substance is not identical to that of heaven, it can not only flow downward but also upward. This is how the coarse and the subtle are differentiated.
Moreover, it does not end there. That sutra further states: "Its sound is subtle and wondrous, expounding suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, as well as the various pāramitās.
Furthermore, there are those who praise the marks and signs of the Buddhas, like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels."

Golden light of subtle brilliance surged forth; this light transformed into birds of a hundred jewel-like colors, warbling together with harmonious and elegant tones, constantly praising mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha.
This is precisely because the essence is solely mind; it is for this reason that insentient things preach the Dharma, yet suffering and pleasure remain distinct.
△ Next, the eight meritorious qualities of the water are explained.
[Commentary] As for the eight qualities: according to the Tang translation, they are: first, clarity and purity; second, coolness; third, sweetness; fourth, lightness and softness.
Five: it is moistening. Six: it is harmonious and soothing. Seven: it eliminates hunger and thirst. Eight: it nourishes and develops the sense faculties.

[Commentary] This differs slightly from what is listed in the *Amitābha-sūtra*. That text says: lightness, coolness, softness, deliciousness, lack of odor, being temperate when drinking, and having no ailment after drinking.
The sub-commentary further correlates these eight qualities with the five sense objects (*pañca-āyatana*); "clear" corresponds to visible form (*rūpa*).

[The water] enters. Its lack of foul odor is the fragrance-sphere (gandha-āyatana). Its lightness, coolness, and softness are the touch-sphere (spraṣṭavya-āyatana). Its deliciousness is the taste-sphere (rasa-āyatana).

Its being temperate and free from affliction is the mental-object sphere (dharma-āyatana). The *Miaozongchao* states: "The commentary explains these eight virtues and correlates them with the five spheres, as well as the aforementioned teaching of the Dharma."

This refers precisely to the sense-base of sound (*śabda-āyatana*). Although it constitutes one of the six sense-bases, there is nothing therein that is not a wondrous realm; thus, it causes the practitioner to swiftly realize the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpāda*).
Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] states: "The water of eight virtues fills [the ponds] to the brim, being serene, pure, fragrant, and clean, with a flavor like nectar (*amṛta*).
Therein, those bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and other superior virtuous persons bathe and cleanse themselves within the pools of the seven treasures."
Regarding his physical form, he intended for the water to reach his feet; the water immediately reached his feet. He wished for it to reach his knees; the water immediately reached his knees.
He wished for it to reach his waist, his armpits, and even his neck; the water did likewise. When he wished to pour and drench his body, it was entirely according to his will.
When he wished for the water to return to its original state, it immediately returned to its original state. He could harmonize its temperature, whether warm or cold, exactly as he desired.

Everything is harmonious and agreeable. The spirit is opened and the body is liberated; emotional anxieties are washed away, becoming clear, bright, and pure. It is as translucent as if it had no form.
△ Third, explaining "the ground strewn with golden sand."
[Commentary]: Regarding "the ground is strewn with golden sand," the *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "The channels are made of gold;
beneath the channels, the bed-sand consists entirely of various colored diamonds (*vajra*)."
[Commentary] This sutra merely states that "the ground is strewn with golden sand. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sutra) says, "diamonds serve as the bottom sand.
These descriptions are still somewhat abbreviated. To speak fully, it should be as stated in the *Mahāsukhāvatī-vyūha*: "As for the golden ponds, their bottoms consist of white silver sand;
as for the crystal ponds, their bottoms consist of lapis lazuli sand; as for the coral ponds, their bottoms consist of amber sand. There are two [versions].
Regarding those ponds composed of a single jewel: their bottoms likewise consist of two jewels. If the pond consists of gold or silver, its sandy bottom is made of coral and amber.
If the pond consists of coral or amber, its sandy bottom is made of tridacna shell and agate.
If three, four, or even up to seven jewels together form a single pond, then as for the sandy bottom—
It is also thus. Among these jewel ponds, there are those that are forty li square, those fifty li square, and those sixty li square;
in this manner they increase in size successively until they reach twenty thousand four hundred and eighty li square, like the great ocean.
These various ponds are all the abodes of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and other superior beings.
It is the dwelling place where virtuous people are born and raised; at times they bathe therein.
That Buddha-pool is twice as large as this one, and is composed of the seven treasures interspersed together. White moon-jewels, bright moon-jewels, and maṇi-jewels form its sandy bottom.
△ Fourth, the explanation of the four jewels.
[Commentary]: *Vaiḍūrya* is here translated as "Not Far. Because this jewel exists not far from the city of Vārāṇasī, it is named accordingly.
*Sphaṭika* is here translated as "Water-Jade" (*shuiyu*).
[Commentary] *Vaidūrya* is a Sanskrit term. In full, it is called *vaidūrya*, which here means "not far" (*avidūra*). Therefore, its original character was written as 流離 (*liúlí*).
Because this is a Sanskrit word, later generations, seeing that it resembled a type of jade, changed it to 琉璃 (*liúlí*).
*Bōlí* (*bōlī*) is also a Sanskrit term; in its complete form, it should be *sphatika*. Its appearance is similar to that of this region [of China].
Crystal (*sphatika*). It has three colors: red, white, and blue. Its character should originally follow the *po-li* (玻離) reading;
because people saw it resembled jade, it was changed to follow *bo-li* (玻璃). *Caruka* is a Sanskrit term; in its full form, it should be called *mukhagarbha*.

This is translated as "blue-white precious gem. The *Shangshu Dazhuan* (Great Tradition of the Book of Documents) states: "The great conch shell is like the rim of a large chariot. "Rim" (*qu*) refers to—
The wheel-rims are made of red pearls. The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that they are produced by red insects.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that pearls are found within the bellies of fish, within bamboo, and within the brains of snakes; they do not necessarily arise solely from the spawn of oysters.
*Musāragalva* is the Sanskrit term for agate. This is translated as "the color of the agate gem. It is so named because its color resembles the brain of a horse. The orthography is ancient.
It was originally written as "maṇi" (agate), but later scribes changed it to follow the characters for "jade" and "stone.
△ Fifth, the explanation of the *kūṭāgāra* (pavilion).
[Commentary] Regarding the pavilion: the *Amitābha Sūtra* states that in each of the realms of the land of various jewels, there are five hundred billion [pavilions].
As for the jeweled pavilions, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The lecture halls, vihāras, palaces, and towers were all adorned with the seven treasures and manifested spontaneously.
Furthermore, they were draped and covered above with nets of pearls, moon-bright maṇi jewels, and various other precious gems."
[Commentary] The Larger Sutra further states: "The lecture halls and monasteries of Amitābha Buddha are all composed of the seven treasures interspersed with one another.
Furthermore, there are towers and railings made of the seven treasures;
additionally, there are necklaces made of the seven treasures suspended as ornaments on their sides. Moreover, white pearls, moon-bright pearls, and maṇi jewels are used to interlace them."
It was draped and covered all over its surface, exceptionally wonderful and beautiful, pure and radiant beyond words.

The palaces and residences of the other bodhisattvas and śrāvakas were likewise so. The palaces, towers, and pavilions inhabited by those devas and worldlings corresponded to their respective forms, colors, heights, and dimensions; some were made of a single jewel, others of two jewels.
...up to immeasurable varieties of precious jewels, all of which are manifested through transformation.
△ Sixth, the explanation of the four flowers.
【Commentary】 Lingzhi says: "The size of the wheels is difficult to establish as a fixed standard. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The wheel..."
The King’s thousand-spoked wheel is fifteen *li* in circumference and blue in color below.
The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that within each pond there are sixty billion lotus flowers made of the seven treasures; thus, they are not limited to four colors.
Each lotus flower is perfectly round and twelve *yojanas* in diameter; they are not merely like chariot wheels. The *Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya* states: "Within the ponds are lotus flowers."
Or [one may see it as] one *yojana*, yet come to know it as hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*; this is simply because what is perceived differs according to the capacity of the individual.
[Commentary]: Regarding the jeweled ponds and lotus flowers, one view considers them as adornments within the Pure Land, while another views them as objects of mindfulness.
The Buddha is one who has taken birth by entrustment. Because the sentient beings of Sukhāvatī are devoid of sexual desire, there are no males or females.
Because there are no males or females, there are no parents. Because there are no parents, there is no womb-birth. Since there is not even womb-birth...
How could there be egg-birth or moisture-birth? It is appropriate that all are of transformation-birth (*upapāduka*).
However, the Pure Land currently discussed is a "transverse" exit from the triple world, situated at the same level as the Sahā world.

Therefore, while beings who are born there primarily do so by transformation, the other three modes of birth seem to be present as well. This is because they take up their physical form within the womb of a lotus flower, which rests upon the water.

This is because it is the supreme [state]. Thus, the *Mūla-sūtra* says: "In the countless worlds of the ten directions, all devas and humans, down to the crawling and wriggling insects, who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha, are all born by transformation within lotus flowers in ponds of the seven treasures.
They grow naturally without anyone to nurse them, and they all eat..."

They partake of this food. Their countenances and physical forms are upright, pure, and beautiful; they are certainly beyond comparison with those of the mundane world, nor can they be compared even to devas or humans.

As for those born in the highest grade, they ride upon a vajra pedestal and, upon arrival, behold [the Buddha].
The Buddha did not traverse the path of birth to realize non-birth; there is indeed a profound reason for this. To explain:
the differences in the quality of what is perceived according to the capacities of beings likewise stem from this.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that buddha-land celestial music constantly plays, and the ground is made of gold. Six times throughout the day and night, it rains celestial *māndārava* flowers.

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has six parts; first, the explanation of celestial music.
[Commentary]: Regarding "celestial music," the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "Immeasurable devas perform celestial musical performances.
Furthermore, there are musical instruments suspended in the void like celestial jeweled banners that resonate spontaneously without being struck. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says:
"There are also ten thousand kinds of natural musical performances; moreover, every sound of music is the Dharma-sound—pure, soaring, plaintive, resonant, subtle, and harmonious."
Elegant. It cannot be matched by any sound whatsoever. [Commentary]:
Regarding "cannot be matched by any sound whatsoever," the *Daben* (Great Version) states:
"Just as the ten thousand kinds of music possessed by a worldly monarch do not equal even a single note of beauty among the various musical sounds of a Wheel-Turning Sage King. A hundredfold.

A million-fold difference exists between the ten thousand kinds of music of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*) and a single note of exquisite beauty among all the music of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;

a hundred thousand million-fold difference exists between the ten thousand kinds of music of the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and a single note of exquisite beauty among all the music of the King of the Sixth Heaven.

The ten thousand kinds of musical instruments of the Sixth Heavenly King do not equal even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of the beauty of a single sound from the various seven-jeweled trees within the land of Amitābha Buddha. Furthermore, there are natural and manifold exquisite melodies,
whose sounds are none other than the sublime Dharma— clear, resonant, piercing, subtle, harmonious, and elegant throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
