[The ground] is interspersed with the seven treasures to demarcate its boundaries; what is here called "golden" refers merely to the adornment of the surface.
[Commentary]:
The current *Smaller Sūtra* is abbreviated; if explained in detail, it is as stated in the *Larger Sūtra*: "Amitābha Buddha..."
Within each of these lands, there are naturally occurring seven treasures—namely gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva.
Their substance is gentle and supple. These seven treasures form the ground, either interspersed with one another or composed of a single treasure throughout.
Their radiance shines brilliantly; they are marvelous, pure, and surpass those of the ten directions. One.
The entire world is vast and expansive, so wide and boundless that it cannot be exhausted. The ground is entirely level and even;
there is no Mount Sumeru, nor the Diamond Iron Ring Mountains, nor any other mountains whatsoever. There are neither great oceans, small seas, nor pits, hollows, wells, or valleys.
Furthermore, there is no place of gloom or darkness.
△ Third, the explanation of the *māndārava* flower.
[Commentary]: The *māndārava* flower is here translated as "white flower" (*pāṇḍurapuṣpa*) and also as "pleasing to the mind" (*manojña*).

However, because that land is constantly illuminated by its own radiance and does not rely on the sun and moon, there is no distinction between day and night. According to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the opening of the flowers and the singing of the birds serve as the markers for these times.
At dawn, the lotuses close and the birds settle for the night. There are no four seasons—spring, autumn, winter, or summer; it is neither cold nor hot, but always temperate and harmonious.

[Commentary] "White flowers that please the mind" refers to one among the four types of flowers, cited here as a representative example. In full, it should be understood according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The heavens rained down four kinds of flowers: first, the *māndārava*, which is this small white flower;
second, the *mahāmāndārava*, which is called the "great white flower"; the *mañjūṣaka*, which is called the "small red flower";
and the *mahāmañjūṣaka*, which is called the "great red flower. Furthermore, the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] states: there are celestial *utpala* flowers and *padma* flowers.
The *mālatī* flower, the *kuvalaya* flower, and the *puṇḍarīka* flower are all celestial flowers.

Because that buddha-land—both its primary and attendant features, as well as its environment and inhabitants—is entirely luminous, it has no sun or moon, nor yin and yang, cold or heat, nor the four seasons.

Nevertheless, they take the blooming of flowers and the singing of birds as dawn, and the closing of lotuses and the roosting of birds as night. I fear this may still be [the realm of] ordinary beings.
The atmosphere of the Land of Peaceful Coexistence with Sages is at a point where it is about to forget, yet has not yet forgotten, its connection to the defiled land.
This is because those sentient beings who are born there mostly do so while still carrying their karmic burdens; such a characteristic does not exist in the [other] three higher lands.
△ Fourth, the explanation of *yīkè* (衣裓).
[Sū] The *yīkè* is the lapel of a robe.
[Chão] Paramārtha states that it is a flower container used in foreign lands. There are two interpretations preserved; the first interpretation is correct because...
The *kai* (裓) is originally the lapel of a robe; how much more so when it rains down celestial flowers? Why must one seek out a vessel?
One simply gathers them in the lapel of the robe, picks up the flowers at the lapel and scatters them, and having scattered them, lets go of the lapel and forgets about them.
This is precisely what is most agreeable in this Pure Land.
△ Fifth, the explanation of making offerings.
[Commentary] Regarding "making offerings to ten trillion buddhas," the *Mahāvaipulya* (Dàběn) states: "By virtue of the Buddha’s majestic power, in the space of a single meal..."
They travel to immeasurable worlds in the ten directions to reverently make offerings to all Buddhas.
[Commentary] This is still an abbreviated text. To cite it in full, the sutra states:

Within the land of Amitābha Buddha, the bodhisattvas, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, travel throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions in the time it takes to eat a single meal to make offerings.

For all Buddhas, whatever their hearts desire—whether flowers, incense, music, robes, canopies, banners, or countless other articles of offering—these naturally manifest before them through transformation.
Exquisite, wondrous, and extraordinary, they are unlike anything found in the world; these are then immediately offered to the Buddhas.
As for the various bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas who wished to offer flowers, these immediately transformed into flower canopies in mid-air.
The smallest were forty li in circumference, or fifty li, or sixty li;
thus they gradually increased in size until some reached six million li. Each, according to its smallness or greatness, remained suspended in the sky.
In the center, they formed a perfect orb; their momentum all directed downward, forming an act of worship.

Their radiant colors shone brilliantly, and their fragrant scents pervaded everywhere beyond description. Once they had been employed, they dissolved one after another in succession according to their order.
Then, the bodhisattvas again played celestial music in the air, singing praises of the Buddha’s virtues with subtle and exquisite sounds. Listen!

Having received the Dharma of the sutra, he experienced immeasurable joy. Once he had made his offerings, he suddenly rose up lightly and returned to his own land, as if it were still before his meal.
△ Sixth, the explanation of the time for eating.
[Commentary] "The time for eating" refers to the morning. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When one wishes to eat, bowls made of the seven precious substances appear naturally before one;
food and drink of a hundred flavors fill them naturally; and upon seeing their color and smelling their fragrance, one is naturally satiated."
The body and mind are supple and soft; they have no attachment to flavors. Once the meal is finished, [the bowl] transforms and disappears; when the time comes, it appears again.
[Commentary] The *Mahāvaipulya* version states in full: "At the time of eating the rice, some desired a silver bowl, while others desired a golden bowl."
Some desired bowls made of lapis lazuli or crystal; some desired bowls made of coral, amber, tridacna shell, or agate;
others desired bowls made of moon-pearls, maṇi-jewels, white jade, or purple gold—each according to their own wishes.
Transformed food appears before them, filled with a hundred flavors. Whether sour, salty, pungent, or bland, each is exactly as desired;

if there is much, it does not exceed what is needed, and if there is little, nothing is lacking. Furthermore, they do not eat in excess for the sake of indulgence in flavor, but only to sustain and benefit their vital energy.
Once eaten, it naturally dissolves without leaving any residue. Or, they may see only its color.
They smell fragrances and take them as food; they are naturally satiated and content, without any attachment to flavors.
Their bodies and minds become clear and sharp. Once used, they naturally vanish. When they wish to eat again, [the food] reappears as before. This is the case throughout that buddha-field.
Pure, tranquil, and secure; subtle, wondrous, and blissful. Next is the path of unconditioned Nirvana.

△ Second, the explanation of the Chapter on the Path (Mārgavarga) has two parts. First, the actual explanation has four parts.

First, the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). [Commentary]: The five faculties are: first, faith; second, diligence; third, mindfulness; fourth, concentration; and fifth, wisdom. These are able to give rise to the Noble Path.
Therefore, they are called "roots.
[Commentary]: The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*) are like a tree. First, hearing the Dharma serves as the seed;

reflection and cultivation serve as the watering of that seed—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), and the three... [text fragment].
When one does not lose the proper timing and the conditions are fulfilled, the five faculties can arise.

Once these faculties have gained strength, they are able to dispel the five hindrances of the thick earth and spread the branches and leaves of the seven factors of enlightenment, thereby producing the flowers and fruits of the samādhi of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Thus, beginning from the Sahā world, one becomes a great tree of coolness. Therefore, in the *Dharmadhātu-krama*...

The commentary on the first gate states: First is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). This refers to having faith in the right path and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*);

by doing so, one is able to give rise to all untainted meditative concentrations (*anāsrava-dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*). This is called the faculty of faith. Second is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).

This refers to having already gained faith in the correct contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) and the various wholesome factors conducive to enlightenment; consequently, one redoubles one's exertion and diligently seeks them.
The uninterrupted continuity of this is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*). Third is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*):

it means recollecting only the right path and its various auxiliary factors, contemplating them with a single mind so that no false or delusive thoughts may enter; this is called the faculty of mindfulness. Fourth is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*):

it means gathering the mind upon the right path and its various auxiliary factors, remaining in a state of one-pointed tranquility and stability without distraction; this is called the faculty of concentration.

The fifth is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). This refers to the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), which is subsumed by the factors of concentration (*samādhi-dharma*). It is self-illuminating by its own nature and does not depend on knowledge from another;
this is called the faculty of wisdom.
△ Next, the five powers (*pañcabala*) are explained.
[Commentary] The names of the five powers are the same as those of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Because they are able to eliminate karmic obstructions, they are called "powers.

[Sub-commentary] First is the power of faith (*śraddhābala*). This refers to faith in the right path and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*). If the faculty of faith increases, then one is able to...
It obstructs all afflictions and is not shaken by the various doubts of the partial or inferior vehicles; therefore, it is called the power of faith. Second is the power of diligence (*vīrya-bala*).

This means that when practicing this right path and the auxiliary dharmas of the path, if the faculty of diligence increases, one is then able to destroy all laziness and negligence, thereby bringing all the right and auxiliary dharmas of the path to completion. This is diligence.
The power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*). This refers to the time when one recollects this right path and the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
If the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) increases, one is then able to destroy all false conceptions and accomplish all supramundane merits of right mindfulness.

This is the power of mindfulness. The fourth is the power of concentration (*samādhibala*). This refers to collecting the mind upon the right path and the factors conducive to enlightenment. If the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*) increases, then...
The power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*) is that which can destroy all distracted thoughts and give rise to meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) regarding both phenomena and principles.
The fifth is the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*), which refers to the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). This wisdom illuminates and comprehends all dharmas;

when the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) increases, one is able to eliminate all attachments to what is false and erroneous, and to shatter all biased or limited forms of wisdom. Therefore, it is called the power of wisdom.
△ The Seven Factors of Enlightenment.
[Commentary] *Bodhi* here means "enlightenment" (*jue*). It is also called a "limb" (*zhī*). They are: 1. mindfulness-enlightenment; 2.
investigation-of-dharmas-enlightenment; 3. diligence-enlightenment; 4. joy-enlightenment; 5. pliancy-enlightenment; 6. concentration-enlightenment; 7. equanimity-enlightenment.

[Commentary] "A single thought of awakening. "Thought" (nian) refers to recollection. This means that when practicing the various dharmas of the Path, one should skillfully awaken to and understand them, constantly ensuring that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are balanced.

When the mind is dull or sinking, one should apply the three factors of awakening—discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*)—to observe all dharmas and prevent the mind from becoming dull. When the mind is agitated or floating, one should...

The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) removes faults of body and speech. The factor of enlightenment of equanimity (upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga) relinquishes [clinging to] contemplative wisdom.
The factor of enlightenment of concentration (samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) enters correct meditative absorption (dhyāna), gathering the distracted mind so that it does not fluctuate;

this is called a factor of enlightenment. Second is the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga). "Investigation" means discernment; that is to say, when one uses wisdom to observe all phenomena.

It is called the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) because it is well able to discern the true from the false, and thus does not erroneously grasp at deceptive dharmas.
Third is the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). "Purity" (*pra*) signifies being unmixed; "advancement" (*vega*) signifies continuity.

This means that when practicing the various path-dharmas, one is well able to awaken to them clearly, refraining from performing useless ascetic practices while constantly [applying oneself] to all the true dharmas.
Applying the mind with single-minded focus, without interruption, is therefore called the factor of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*). Fourth is the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-sambodhyaṅga*):

"joy" refers to rapture; it means that when the mind accords with and realizes the true Dharma and attains rapture, one is able to clearly discern and understand that this joy does not arise from inverted phenomena, but abides in the joy of the true Dharma—therefore, it is called the awakening factor of joy. Fifth is pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), also known as "removal."

The factor of enlightenment called *prahāṇa* (abandonment). "Abandonment" refers to the act of severing; that is, at the time of severing the afflictions of various views, one is skillfully able to discern and eliminate false and deceptive phenomena, thereby increasing genuine roots of goodness.
Therefore, it is named the *prahāṇa-saṃbodhyaṅga*. Sixth is the factor of enlightenment called *samādhi*.

"Samādhi" refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). That is, at the time of giving rise to meditative concentration, one is skillfully able to discern all dhyānas so that [distractions] do not arise.
The conceptualization of afflictions is called the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Seventh is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*):

this refers to being detached from objects of perceived attachment, skillfully awakening to their falsity and unreality, and never again recollecting them; therefore, it is named the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
△ Four: The Eightfold Noble Path.
[Commentary] Regarding the Eightfold Noble Path, various sūtras refer to it as the Eightfold Right Path (*aṣṭāṅga-mārga*). 1. Right View; 2. Right Thought; 3. Right Speech;
4. Right Action; 5. Right Livelihood; 6. Right Effort; 7. Right Mindfulness; 8. Right Concentration.

[Commentary] These eight factors are called "right" (*samyak*) because they do not proceed by way of partiality or deviation; they are called "path" (*mārga*) because they can lead directly to *nirvāṇa*.

First is right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). This means that when a person cultivates the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), they perceive the Four Noble Truths with clarity and destroy the various false views of non-Buddhists, such as those concerning existence and non-existence. This constitutes right view. Second is right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
When a person perceives the Four Noble Truths, they engage in right mindfulness, reflection, observation, and deliberation, causing their insight to increase;

this is called right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). Third is right speech (*samyag-vāc*): when a person, through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), constantly restrains their verbal karma and remains far removed from all false and unreal speech; this is right speech. Fourth is right action (*samyak-karmānta*): when a person...
Untainted wisdom consists of cultivating and gathering the mind, abiding in pure right action, and severing all forms of false and deluded conduct;

this is called right action. Fifth is right livelihood, which means that those who have left the household life always distance themselves from the five kinds of wrong livelihood for gain and sustenance, and always maintain their lives by begging for food; this is called right livelihood. Sixth is right effort.
7. Right Effort (*samyag-vīrya*): This refers to a person diligently cultivating the path of morality, concentration, and wisdom with single-minded devotion and uninterrupted persistence;

this is called right effort. 8. Right Mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*): This refers to a person recollecting the right path of morality, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the five methods for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana*) and other factors conducive to the path, thereby being capable of advancing toward *nirvāṇa*; this is called right mindfulness. 9. Right Concentration (*samyak-samādhi*): This refers to...
When a person gathers all scattered thoughts, the body and mind become tranquil, and they abide correctly in the principle of true emptiness, remaining resolutely immovable;
this is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
△ Second, pointing out deficiencies.

[Commentary]: Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), because the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), and the three categories (*triskandha*) are omitted, it says "and so forth" (*ādi-dharma*).

[Commentary] Since the sutra is incomplete, although this commentary does not supplement it, I shall now fully set forth its meaning to serve as an aid for later students in their contemplative practice.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*): "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to the observing subject, while "foundation" (*upasthāna*) refers to the observed object.
This means that all sentient beings give rise to the four inversions regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Regarding...

Regarding form (*rūpa*), there is a frequent arising of the inversion of purity; regarding sensation (*vedanā*), there is a frequent arising of the inversion of pleasure; regarding perception (*saṃjñā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*), there is a frequent arising of the inversion of self;

and regarding the mind (*citta*), there is a frequent arising of the inversion of permanence. To cause sentient beings to cultivate these four contemplations in order to eliminate these four inversions, they are called the "four foundations of mindfulness" (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
First, one contemplates the impurity of the body. The body has an internal and an external aspect; one's own body is called the "internal body," while that of others...
A person’s body is called the "external body. These internal and external bodies are both formed by taking up the physical remains of one's parents.
From head to foot, if one examines each part individually, they are entirely impure substances; yet sentient beings, being deluded and inverted, cling to them as pure.
Because one gives rise to craving and attachment, one is thus led to contemplate the impurity of the body. Second, contemplating that feeling (*vedanā*) is suffering:

that which experiences is called "feeling. There are internal feelings and external feelings. Feelings of the mental faculty (*manas*) are called internal feelings; feelings of the five [physical] faculties are called external feelings.
Each individual faculty has agreeable feelings, disagreeable feelings, and neither-agreeable-nor-disagreeable feelings. Regarding objects that accord with one's inclinations, then [craving] arises...

Pleasurable sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) gives rise to painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*) when encountering objects that are contrary to one's inclinations; it gives rise to neither-painful-nor-pleasurable sensation (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*) when encountering objects that are neither contrary nor favorable.
Pleasurable sensation is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); painful sensation is the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*);

and neither-painful-nor-pleasurable sensation is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Because sentient beings are inverted and take what is suffering to be pleasure, they are led to contemplate sensation as suffering.
Third, contemplate that the mind is impermanent. The "mind" here refers to the sixth consciousness. This means that the essence and nature of this conscious mind are in constant flux;
whether coarse or subtle, internal or external, it arises and ceases from moment to moment, and is entirely impermanent. Fourth, contemplate that phenomena are without self.
Phenomena include both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas. People all rely upon these phenomena to calculate a self, saying, "I am able..."

One practices both good and evil deeds. Within the phenomena of good and evil, there is fundamentally no self (*ātman*). If the good phenomenon were the self, then the evil phenomenon would have to be without a self;
if the evil phenomenon were the self, then the good phenomenon would have to be without a self. Sentient beings, being inverted in their views, falsely reckon that there is a self;

therefore, they are caused to contemplate the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). As for the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*): first, one causes already arisen evil [phenomena] to...
"Permanent severance" refers to the five hindrances and other afflictions that shroud the mind and cause one to be separated from the five roots of goodness;

therefore, with single-minded diligence and vigor, one employs skillful means to eliminate them so they do not arise again. Second, "not allowing unarisen evil to arise" refers to the evil dharmas of the five hindrances and other afflictions;
although these have not yet arisen at present, if they were to arise later, they would be able to obstruct the five [roots of goodness].
3. Regarding the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence and skillful means in their cultivation so that they never arise again.

4. Regarding the increase of already arisen goodness: this refers to the five kinds of roots of goodness and other wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*). Although these have already arisen, one must guard them and cause them to increase;
therefore, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence and skillful means in their cultivation so that they do not decline or be lost. 4.
To cause unarisen wholesome states to arise refers to the five kinds of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

Although they have not yet arisen, one applies oneself with single-minded diligence and vigor, practicing skillful means so that they may arise. As for the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*): first is the base of power of desire (*chanda*).
"Desire" refers to the longing, aspiration, and joyful inclination toward the adornment of those dharmas; thus it is called desire. That is to say, for an ordinary person...

Regarding all phenomena that are cultivated: if one lacks the mind of aspiration (*chanda*), the task will certainly not be accomplished; if one possesses aspiration, all that is wished for will be attained.
This is the basis of psychic power consisting of aspiration (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*). Second is the basis of psychic power consisting of mindfulness (*smṛti-ṛddhipāda*):

"mindfulness" refers to focusing the activity upon that object and dwelling with single-mindedness and right presence; thus it is called mindfulness. That is to say, if one is not single-minded, one cannot contemplate phenomena.

If one can sever [distractions] and unify the mind, all that is wished for will be attained; this is the basis of psychic power of mindfulness (*smṛti-ṛddhipāda*). Third is the basis of psychic power of diligence (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*):
it means observing the principle with exclusive concentration so that there is no intermingling of thoughts; therefore, it is called diligence.
Regarding all dharmas that are practiced and cultivated, if there is no diligence, the task will certainly not be accomplished. If one is able to be diligent, then whatever is wished for—
All are attained; this is the basis of psychic power of diligence (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*). Regarding the basis of psychic power of reflection (*citta-ṛddhipāda*):

it refers to deliberating and scrutinizing that object; thus it is called "reflection. In all practices one cultivates, if there is no reflection, nothing will be attained and none will be accomplished.
If one is able to reflect, all that is wished for will be attained. This is [the basis of psychic power of reflection].
Contemplating the bases of psychic power.
△ Fifth, the explanation of right mindfulness.
[Commentary] Gushan says: "Mindfulness of the Buddha is like a king of physicians; mindfulness of the Dharma is like a skilled physician; mindfulness of the Sangha is like a nurse."

When these three conditions are complete, the disease of afflictions can be cured. Furthermore, observe your own mind: when it is quiescent yet constantly luminous, all phenomena are vividly manifest;

this is called mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). When it is luminous yet constantly quiescent, not a single phenomenon can be apprehended; this is called mindfulness of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*).
The non-duality of stillness and illumination is precisely "existing yet being absent," which is termed "mindfulness of the Sangha. This is the Three Jewels as a single essence.
[Commentary] Mount Gu shan explains the Three Jewels based on two meanings: first, their distinct characteristics; second, their single essence.

Within the category of distinct characteristics, he merely sets forth the reasons for mindfulness of the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and does not describe the characteristics of the Three Jewels themselves. As for the mention of the "King of Physicians" and so forth:

Indeed, regarding the root of the disease of birth and death for sentient beings, if one wishes to treat this ailment within the afflictions and desires, none other than the Great King of Physicians, the Buddha, can know the disease and recognize the medicine to provide the appropriate remedy. Therefore, he places the Jewel of Mindfulness of the Buddha at the beginning.
However, even if one has seen him, if one does not hear the Dharma to seek its therapeutic methods, [the cure] cannot be achieved. Thus, [he next] joins...
If one takes [the medicine] but does not wear it, the illness cannot be cured. Therefore, the next step is to practice mindfulness of the Jewel of the Dharma.

Even if one can contemplate and cultivate according to the Dharma, if one lacks the excellent companionship of Bodhisattvas as fellow practitioners, as external protectors, as those who regulate one's diet, and as those who point out what is to be avoided, the illness likewise cannot be cured. Therefore, the next stage adds mindfulness of the Jewel of the Sangha. If...
If you wish to know: that which is fully endowed with the three bodies and four wisdoms constitutes the Buddha Jewel;
the twelve divisions of the teachings spoken [by him] constitute the Dharma Jewel; and the bodhisattvas of the forty-one stages constitute the Sangha Jewel.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there further arose the "institutional Three Jewels," wherein images cast in metal or carved from wood serve as the Buddha Jewel, and the palm-leaf manuscripts brought from the West [serve as the Dharma Jewel].
The Dharma Jewel consists of the teachings, while the Sangha Jewel consists of those who have shaved their heads and donned dyed robes.
If one can take refuge in and keep these two in mind, then the root disease of afflictions (*kleśa*) can be cured, and the fruit of the disease of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) can be healed.
Second, as for "the single essence," this refers to the text which says: "Furthermore, observe that one's own mind is quiescent yet constantly illuminating" (and so forth). This is because...

The Buddha is named "Awakening" (*buddha*), and awakening is precisely illumination. Therefore, this mind is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; that all phenomena (*dharma*) are vividly manifest is called the Jewel of the Buddha.
"Dharma" is named "non-awakening," and non-awakening is precisely quiescence. Therefore, it is through illumination that it is constantly quiescent.
That which cannot be apprehended is called the Dharma Jewel. "Sangha" means harmony. The non-duality of quiescence and illumination is the meaning of harmony;
therefore, that which is the non-duality of quiescence and illumination—neither existing nor perishing—is called the Sangha Jewel.
△ Sixth, explaining the arising of the mind.
[Commentary] Lingzhi says: "The mind in this realm is defiled, constantly contemplating the five desires; the mind in that land is pure, single-mindedly mindful of the Triple Gem.
The difference between the elevation and submergence of these two lands can be seen herein."
[Commentary]: Now, when the mind arises in response to objects, even Buddhas and sages cannot avoid it;
they simply seek its correctness. In this Sahā world, sensory objects are coarse and powerful; therefore, the mind that arises in response to these objects dwells upon them but is not correct.
Only in the Pure Land is everything heard nothing but wondrous sounds; thus, all who hear these sounds...

They all gave rise to a profound mind of mindfulness toward the Triple Gem. This is precisely what is meant by "giving rise to the mind while abiding nowhere," and "abiding nowhere while giving rise to the mind.

[Commentary] Gushan says: "Though there are jeweled towers and golden ponds, they serve as objects for pleasing the eyes, yet they are not colors that delude or dissipate the mind;

[Commentary] Those in the world who weary of disturbance must block their sight and hearing from what they perceive, thereby falling into the error of partiality and neglect.

In this world of the five turbidities, both the faculties and their objects are defiled.
If one lacks the contemplation of the emptiness of essence and lacks the method of analyzing form, whether advancing or retreating, who can avoid transgression?

Such is the wondrousness of the Pure Land, wherein one proceeds with ease through the Middle Way. To hear of it and yet not seek rebirth therein is the mark of one who is no true man.

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has three parts. First, citing the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] to clarify that the radiance is immeasurable.

[Commentary] This is but a brief citation. Were it to be cited in full: the radiance of Amitābha Buddha is brilliant, exquisite, and most profound;

Thus, he is titled the Buddha of Immeasurable Life (Amitāyus), and is also titled the Buddha of Immeasurable Light (Amitābha) and the Buddha of Boundless Light (Anantābha). No...
Buddha Obstructing Light; Buddha Unopposed Light; Buddha King of Blazing Light; Buddha Pure Light; Buddha Joyful Light;

Wherever their radiance shines throughout incalculable worlds, all places of darkness and gloom are forever filled with great light.
The gods, humans, birds, beasts, and all classes of wriggling and crawling creatures, upon seeing this radiance, were without exception filled with joy and gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness.
Those who were lustful, wrathful, or deluded, upon seeing this radiance, were without exception moved toward goodness.

They shall no longer suffer affliction; after their lives end, they shall all attain liberation.
It is not only I who now praise the light of Amitābha Buddha, but also the countless Buddhas of the ten directions, along with the assemblies of Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.

It is exactly the same; all shall offer praise in this manner. If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing of the majestic power and meritorious virtues of this light, take refuge day and night and praise it without ceasing, they will surely be born in that land according to their vows.
Furthermore, they shall likewise be praised by all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas. Thus do I speak of Amitābha Buddha.
The majesty and spiritual power of this radiance are so lofty and sublime that even a day and night, or an entire kalpa, would not suffice to exhaust its description;

Next, I shall cite the *Amitābha Sūtra* to clarify the function of this radiance.

He possesses eighty-four thousand secondary marks of excellence. Within each mark, there are further eighty-four thousand rays of light.

This refers to the fact that the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—pervade everywhere without exception. It further says: "Therefore..."

this mind creates the Buddha, and this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Tathāgatas, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, arises from the mind’s thoughts.

[Commentary]: Śrāvakas pertain to both teachings. Those of the Two Vehicles consist of the practitioners of the Tripitaka Teaching who analyze form to contemplate emptiness, and those of the Shared Teaching who take form as the substance to contemplate emptiness.

those of the Distinct Teaching who practice the *sands-of-the-Ganges* Dharma-gates; and those of the Perfect Teaching who practice the wondrous conduct of non-action. All of these...

upon being born in that land, they each follow their original habitual tendencies, whether as Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, or as partial or perfect, beholding the Buddhas of the four teachings and hearing the Dharma of the four teachings.

△ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts. First, single-mindedness of phenomena.

[Commentary]: Regarding "single-mindedness in practice" (*shishi ichinen*): the practitioner binds their attention and recollects the Buddha Amitābha, his physical marks (*lakṣaṇa*), secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*), and radiance, without any intention to scatter the mind.
To be thus uninterrupted from moment to moment is called single-mindedness in practice.
[Commentary]: "Binding the object of focus through mindfulness" refers to contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). "Amitābha Buddha and so forth" refers to the object (*ālambana*).

"Without a distracted mind, maintaining uninterrupted mindfulness moment after moment" means that the power of mindfulness is so vigorous that it can dispel miscellaneous thoughts, ensuring that no internal states arise and no external objects intrude.
Although the following text clarifies the single-mindedness within the principle (*li*), one must first rely upon the practice of maintaining the object within phenomena (*shi*).

Single-mindedness is taken as its foundation. Within this principle, one need only employ the power of understanding to harmonize and penetrate it, ensuring that no phenomena remain obstructed, thereby establishing the cause for supreme excellence.
If one were lacking even slightly in this, how could one possibly achieve the merit of subduing delusions within a single thought?
△ Next, the explanation of the principle of the single mind and the two [aspects]. First, clarifying the three contemplations within the single mind.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "single mind of principle," it means to thoroughly realize that both the contemplating mind and the Buddha who is contemplated are devoid of intrinsic nature.
Although it is originally empty and quiescent, there is a mutual resonance between the response and the stimulus, like reflections in a mirror or the moon in water.
Spontaneously manifesting benefit, it is empty in its very locus; it is entirely provisional, yet neither extreme can be found and the Middle Way does not exist.
The three truths are perfectly interfused, transcending thought and meaning; this is called the single mind of principle.

[Commentary] The section below clarifies the meaning of "immediately empty" (*jìkōng*). To say that both the "one who recollects" and the "object recollected" are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) refers to the four types of nature (*catuḥ-svabhāva*), through which one realizes their non-arising (*anutpāda*).
One should further state that they also lack extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*), common nature (*sāmānyasvabhāva*), and causeless nature (*ahetusvabhāva*);
these are omitted from the text. In this context, it is appropriate to take the fact that the mind which recollects is fundamentally empty as its lack of intrinsic nature.

That which is contemplated—Amitābha—is fundamentally empty, for he lacks a nature of otherness (*parabhāva*). The mutual resonance of cause and response is like a reflection in a mirror or the moon in water;
it lacks a common nature (*sabhāva*). It spontaneously manifests benefit, for it lacks a nature of no-cause (*ahetuka-bhāva*).

This is the method of subsuming the latter into the former to clarify that there are no four natures. Next, from "Although it is originally empty and quiescent" onwards, it clarifies its provisional nature (*prajñapti*). Above...
The first two lines clarify the provisional nature [of phenomena] by means of dharmas; the latter two lines clarify the provisional nature by means of analogies.

Here, the form and the water are used as metaphors for the stimulus (*gan*), while the mirror and the moon are used as metaphors for the response (*ying*). The mirror and the moon are fundamentally without intention, yet images naturally appear within them;
the form and the water likewise have no volition, yet they spontaneously evoke the mirror and the moon. When this efficacy reaches the point of rebirth, it occurs through effortless spontaneity.

This reveals the benefit. That "all things in their respective places are empty" means that existence is itself emptiness. That "the entire body is itself the provisional" means that emptiness is itself existence.
Since existence is itself emptiness, existence is not existence; since emptiness is itself existence, emptiness is not emptiness.
When it is neither emptiness nor existence, the Middle Way is manifest. When it is both emptiness and existence, even the Middle Way vanishes. Therefore, it is said:

The two extremes cannot be found, and the middle way does not exist. Thus, the object of contemplation consists of the three truths in perfect fusion, while the contemplating mind is beyond thought and beyond discourse.
The two gates of phenomena and principle have already been briefly indicated in the section on "Understanding.
If one wishes to further clarify this intent, there are two different aspects: the horizontal and the vertical. Regarding the horizontal exposition of the three contemplations:
The subject that can recollect belongs to the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), while the object that is recollected belongs to the three truths (*tisraḥ satyāni*).

For example, at the very moment one correctly utters the name, one realizes that the mind which performs the recitation is neither internal nor external, and is without form or appearance; this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Although it lacks internal or external form and appearance, [it nevertheless exists].
This mind that is capable of mindfulness is vivid and distinct; this is the contemplation of the conventional (parikalpita).

Yet this capacity for mindfulness does not exist apart from the conventional, nor does the conventional exist apart from emptiness (śūnyatā). This simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination is the contemplation of the middle way (madhyamaka).
The name of the Buddha and its sound are like an echo in a valley or the moon reflected in water; they are utterly ungraspable.
This is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Although it is ungraspable, the Buddha’s name and voice are vividly present in the mouth and clearly manifest to the ear.
This is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore, this which is being contemplated is neither conventional apart from the ultimate, nor is it ultimate apart from the conventional;
they both exist and both are forgotten. This is the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). This is the horizontal exposition of the three contemplations and the three truths. If...
Regarding the vertical discourse: taking "the single mind in non-distraction" and "the simultaneous stilling of all conditions" as the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*);
and taking "the six-character sacred name being recited with clear and distinct articulation" as the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).

Although the capacity to recite is empty, the one who recites is vividly present; although that which is recited is provisional, it is like an echo and lacks substantiality. Thus, it is emptiness itself, yet not empty.

Emptiness is itself the provisional; the provisional is not merely provisional. The provisional is itself emptiness. Both are negated and both are illuminated. Subject and object, as well as contemplation, are both forgotten.
That which is called the "wondrous provisional" is the object, and that which is called "emptiness" is the contemplation. When object and contemplation are both forgotten, this is the Middle Way.
How could there ever be a sequence between forgetting and illumination? Within the single mind, all is fused and severed, leaving no trace whatsoever. If it is thus, one seeks birth in the Pure Land.
For such a person, it is simply by means of single-mindedness without distraction that they hold fast to the Name;

yet, in the very act of holding fast to the Name, there is single-mindedness without distraction. Within this lies the entirety of boundless, wondrous meaning. This inconceivable contemplation is not separate from its own essence;
it may be said that cultivation arises entirely from nature, and cultivation is entirely present within nature. Furthermore, one must understand that within the sutra...
The intent is to ensure that cause and effect correspond in name and reality by maintaining a single mind without distraction.
By upholding the Name, one seeks to bring about the mutual resonance between the living being and the Buddha. Regarding the correspondence of cause and effect in name and reality:

the Land of Ultimate Bliss is called the Pure Land; it is only when the mind is pure that the Buddha-land becomes pure. Thus, the principle that "the mind is pure and the land is pure" is profound indeed.
2. Penetration. When the five stages of dwelling are completely subdued and the three delusions are completely destroyed, this is termed "purity of mind.
This purity of mind brings about the purity of the Buddha-land, which encompasses all four lands in their entirety; in this case, it refers specifically to the Pure Land of Shared Residence.
It requires only one day up to seven days of single-mindedly holding the Name without distraction to serve as the cause for rebirth through the purity of mind. 2.
Regarding the mutual resonance between the living practitioner and the Buddha: Amitābha’s wondrous response is that of one who has attained the fruit of Buddhahood;
furthermore, he possesses past vows that cause me to hold his name. Therefore, it is essential to maintain the recitation of the name as the cause for rebirth through mental purity.
Thus, "single-mindedness without distraction" and "maintaining the recitation of the name" are two meanings that require one another; neither can be dispensed with.
Therefore, the core teaching of this sutra must be analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1.

**It is single-mindedness, but not the recitation of the name.** This refers to ordinary cultivation of dhyāna as well as the single-minded cultivation of various other practices that lack dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and the making of vows. None of these are the direct cause for rebirth [in the Pure Land]. 2.

**It is the recitation of the name, but not single-mindedness.** This refers to reciting the name with a distracted mind; although it is indeed the Buddha’s [name], [it lacks the necessary concentration].

First, planting seeds by relying on conditions is also not the direct cause for rebirth there. Third, those who are neither single-minded nor engaged in the practice of holding the Name are ordinary people acting in a leisurely and distracted manner;
even though they perform various virtuous deeds, these are likewise not the cause for rebirth there. Fourth, it is being single-minded and engaged in the practice of holding the Name.

This is precisely the primary cause for rebirth as taught in this sutra. If we consider this sutra according to its classification within the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings, which encompasses the capacities of the four vehicles to discern the single mind, there are four distinct types of practitioners: first, those of the Tripitaka Teaching (zangjiao).
The Buddha within the mind truly exists; it is merely by way of conventional phenomena that we judge the mind to be undistracted.

Taking this as the cause and augmenting it with faith and aspiration, when the fruit ripens at the moment of death, one immediately attains rebirth in the Pure Land. Ordinary people of today have not yet penetrated the ultimate principle;
they merely shut off the six sense-faculties so that there is neither exiting nor entering, single-mindedly reciting the Name. Or, they may employ the mind to investigate various matters.

Analysis: These all refer to the single-minded recitation of the Name by those of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao). Second, as for those of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), they are well able to thoroughly comprehend that both mind and Buddha are like illusions and transformations.
Since the Buddha is fundamentally non-existent, how could the mind exist? Sounds are like echoes in a valley; Buddhas are like reflections in a mirror.
Understanding and realizing it in this way, one realizes non-arising in the very place [of occurrence]. This is the single-mindedness of those of the Shared Teaching.
This refers to upholding the name. Third are those of the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagdeśanā). They first are able to penetrate emptiness and are also able to penetrate the provisional.
Using the mind of emptiness to construct the provisional Buddha, they do not think that the Buddha exists alone while the mind does not;

rather, by using the mind of emptiness to recollect the provisional Buddha, emptiness is no longer empty and the provisional is no longer provisional. Being neither provisional nor empty, they perceive the Middle Way. This is the Separate [Teaching].

This teaches people to single-mindedly hold the name. Fourth, those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) are able to realize that the Pure Land is mind-only and that Amitābha is one's own original nature;

that this is the Middle Way between the ultimate and the conventional; that within contemplation it is empty and yet provisional; that whether with thought or without thought, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-nature;

and that whether there is no Buddha or there is a Buddha, all is True Suchness (Tathatā). Thus, throughout the day they have thought, yet throughout the day they are without thought, contemplating by means of non-thought.

The characteristics possess the characteristic of characteristics; non-arising yet arising, arising yet non-arising—this is the single-minded holding of the name by one of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

This interpretation according to the meaning is thus for the period of the Vaipulya (fangdeng) sutras. If, however, it concerns the Lotus Sutra (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*) which reveals the Real by opening the Provisional, one should harmonize the preceding teachings so that they all return to the Perfect and Sudden.
For those of the Tripitaka Teaching, who have their six sense-faculties closed and whose minds are restrained...
Non-disorder is my Perfect Teaching: the single mind within phenomena. The Shared Teaching’s "like an illusion" is my Perfect Teaching: the single mind as emptiness.
The Distinct Teaching’s "transcending the mundane" is my Perfect Teaching: the single mind as the provisional. The Perfect Teaching is the fundamental mutual identity of these aspects.
There is no need for reconciliation. Because the *Lotus Sūtra* is sublime, it possesses both types of sublimity.

While the previous Perfect Teaching’s single mind was the "sublimity of mutual dependence" (*xiāngdài*) as discussed in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the present comprehensive synthesis is the "sublimity of absolute non-dependence" (*juédài*) as discussed in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Therefore, practitioners of the Perfect Teaching, having already heard the Sublime Dharma and profoundly awakened to the Perfect Principle, give rise to the Perfect School through such functional power.

They are perfectly interfused and unimpeded. When phenomena are fully understood, they are phenomena that are identical with principle; when principle is realized, it is principle that is identical with phenomena.

Therefore, when one holds the name with a single mind, it may be the single mind of phenomena, it may be the single mind of principle, and it may be the single mind in which phenomena and principle are mutually identical.
Every thought-moment is nothing other than the Dharma-realm; every mind is identical with the true and eternal. Thus one should contemplate.

The Buddha possesses the greatest merit; he is able to subdue the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling, to shatter the three delusions within the single mind, to purify the four kinds of pure lands, and to perceive the Amitābha of the three bodies. This is inconceivable mindfulness;
this is effortless mindfulness. Yongming [Yanshou] said: "To possess both Chan and Pure Land is like a tiger with horns. In this present age...
"To be a teacher of men; to become a Buddha or a patriarch in a future life. This verse is specifically for those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching who single-mindedly hold the Name.
△ Next, the fundamental doctrine of the inherent nature is explained.
[Commentary: One must thoroughly realize that the dharma-realm is mind-only and that there are no objects external to the mind. Amitābha’s marks and signs are originally one's own mind;
the hundred trillion lands do not transcend the present thought-moment. Because all phenomena are inherently complete within nature, they are not obtained from another.
[Commentary] The Dharma-realm has three meanings: first, the inherent nature (*xingju*), which refers to the three thousand realms and the ten realms;
second, the essential body (*xingti*), which refers to the "pure and fundamental" true suchness-dharma-realm; third, the capacity of nature (*xingliang*), which refers to the one true dharma-realm.

This is the measure of the vertical and horizontal pervasiveness of the realm. The nature of the three kinds of dharma-realm is entirely such that the faculties and objects of sentient beings correspond;
it is but a single thought-moment of the discriminating consciousness. Therefore, apart from the mind there is no object, and apart from the object there is no mind.
For this reason, the marks and signs of Amitābha are the Amitābha of one’s own original nature, and the ten thousand billion lands are the Pure Land of one’s own *cittamātra* (mind-only).
Therefore, it is said that they are originally one’s own mind, not exceeding the present thought-moment.
Thus, the conclusion states: "Because they are inherent in one's nature, they are not obtained from another."
△ Fourth, the explanation of the titles in the root sūtra.
[Commentary] Furthermore, it should be known that Amitābha has already realized the ultimate *paramārtha-satya*. To once invoke his auspicious name...

The myriad virtues manifest simultaneously; transgressions are extinguished across kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, and blessings become equal to empty space. How much more so for those who practice for one day up to seven days!

This is truly due to the fundamental vows of Dharmākara: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings of the ten directions, with sincere heart, faith, and joy, desire to be born in my land, and even have ten recitations—if they should not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Having already received these [vows]...

Through the power of the vows made during his causal stage, the Buddha’s radiance in the state of fruition upholds those who recite his name; their merit is immeasurable, and they will certainly behold the Buddha at the time of death, without any doubt.
[Commentary] In the previous explanation of the matter, "a single thought-moment" was spoken of in reference to recollecting the Buddha’s physical marks, minor characteristics, and radiance;
this might seem to overlap with the practice of visualizing the Buddha as taught in the *Contemplation Sūtra*. Although the mental application is the same, the objects of focus differ.

Here, however, it specifically points to the grasping and upholding of the Name as the object of focus; therefore, it is said: "A single invocation of the auspicious Name [engenders] the ten thousand virtues."

To clarify both points, the text here addresses the latent doubts of certain critics. These critics ask: "The Buddha possesses ten thousand virtues and should be contemplated as the three bodies (trikāya).
Why is it that merely invoking his name allows one to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]? Therefore, he earnestly demonstrates this by saying:
Furthermore, one should know that "and so forth" [refers to] the following. The text explains the doubt by means of two points:

first, the correspondence between name and reality; second, the original vows of the Dharma-treasury. Regarding the first, the correspondence between name and reality, the *Sijiao yi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states:
"All names belonging to the fruit of perfect consummation are not empty in the slightest, but are ultimately accomplished. Indeed, all that they summon..."
Because it is the ultimate reality, the Great Sutra states: "In the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is only name and no actual substance;
in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is both name and actual substance.

Since the Buddha is the ultimate ultimate truth, and since Amitābha has now already realized this ultimate ultimate truth, the ten thousand virtues are simultaneously manifested by a single invocation of his auspicious title. Thus, [Amitābha]...

The sun of wisdom of the myriad virtues has already manifested both its essence and its radiance simultaneously. Thus, the darkness and karmic stains of sentient beings shall naturally vanish in a single thought, even across kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.

Since the nature of sin is fundamentally empty—being void and unreal—once that which is void and unreal has vanished, the merit and blessings equal to space, arising from the recitation of the Buddha’s name, will spontaneously manifest.
If such is the case for a single invocation of the Buddha’s name, how much more so is this true otherwise?
From one day to seven days, if one holds the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction, then there is no sin that will not be extinguished and no merit that will not arise.
At the time of death, one will be reborn in the Pure Land; this is certainly not in vain.
This is because, as stated below, the second section shows the Original Vow of Dharmākara, and so forth. Indeed, the original vows of all Buddhas are [immeasurable].
There is no falsehood. Because Amitābha, during his causal stage, had already made forty-eight vows, he then spent incalculable eons practicing to fill the ocean of vows.
Once that ocean of vows was full, immeasurable dharma-treasures manifested all at once.
Therefore, I now take up the Land of Ultimate Bliss to gather and sustain sentient beings.

The beings of this Sahā world have already placed their faith in this matter and have further made vows to be reborn there, casting themselves into the ocean of aspiration. They further cultivate the practice of invoking the Name to increase the mountain of conduct;
just as the ten thousand streams returning to the sea share the same salty taste, and as Mount Sumeru gathers all things within its single azure hue.
This occurs spontaneously and is not the result of forced effort. Therefore, at the conclusion of the commentary on the text, the two meanings are combined to resolve the root of doubt, stating:

"Since one has received the power of the vows made by that Buddha during his causal stage, and because the light of his land of fruition, the upholding of his name, and the virtues of his kalpa are immeasurable, one will see the Buddha at the moment of death; of this there is no doubt."
△ Five: Correcting Errors and Omissions in This Sutra (3). First, presenting the ancient edition. [Commentary:
The *Lingzhi Shu* records the stone edition from Xiangyang, which states that after "single-mindedly not being distracted," there is the following passage: "Diligently hold fast to the Name;
because one invokes the Name, all transgressions are extinguished; this is precisely the causal condition of many roots of goodness and merit."
△ Next, the correction of errors and omissions.
[Commentary] That Stone Sutra edition was transcribed by people of the Six Dynasties period. I privately suspect that the current edition has undergone transmissional errors and omissions.

[Sub-commentary] Since it is stated in the *Jie* (Exegesis) that "the current transmission contains errors and omissions," all those who read and practice it should rely on the ancient edition to supplement them.
Correcting this. △ Third, illustrating the holding of the name by way of comparison.
[Commentary]: How much more so for me, Amitābha, who welcomes beings through their names. When heard by the ear and recited by the mouth, the boundless holy virtues are gathered and brought within.
The consciousness-mind shall forever become the seed of Buddhahood; it will instantly eliminate the heavy sins of billions of kalpas and attain the realization of unsurpassed Bodhi.
One should know with certainty that this is not due to meager roots of goodness, but is truly the result of manifold merit.

[Commentary]: Generally, when the response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of all Buddhas engage with sentient beings, there are four types of benefit. First, benefit through form, which is the manifestation of the body.
Second, benefit through light, which is the emission of radiance. Third, benefit through sound, which is the preaching of the Dharma.
Fourth, benefit through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), which is the manifestation of psychic feats. However, for Amitābha alone, beyond these four benefits, he further adds—
It is called "receiving beings by name" because it fulfills the vows originally made at the time [of Amitābha’s practice].
Among the other four ways of receiving beings, their capacity to gather sentient beings is narrow; only the reception by name has a broad capacity to gather them.

Since Amitābha receives beings by means of their names, sentient beings are able to hear them with their ears and recite them with their mouths—not merely once, but repeatedly invoking his auspicious title.
Thus, the myriad virtues manifest simultaneously; furthermore, the boundless sacred merits are gathered into the consciousness-mind, becoming forever the seed of Buddhahood.
To eradicate transgressions and realize the Way is inconceivable; how could the merit of these roots of goodness be anything but immense?
If one privately examines the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, that which it reveals is one and the same; it is only the methods of cultivation that differ, for although its gates are many.
If one summarizes their ultimate destination, it does not exceed two types: first, correct cultivation; second, auxiliary practices. Within correct cultivation, there are two methods:
first, visualization; second, the recitation of the name. If one concentrates the mind on visualization, the text is recorded in the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
If one concentrates the mind on the recitation of the name, the text is recorded in this sūtra. As for visualization and the recitation of the name, if both are practiced together—
As for the practice, it is recorded in the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*. Now, if one wishes to clarify its meaning, there are five points of distinction.

First is the distinction between name and reality. "Name" refers to the provisional designation of the Buddha-realm; "reality" refers to the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and the land of the Buddha-realm.
When one contemplates the real dharmas of the five aggregates, one contemplates the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas shown in the sūtra as they proceed through the three grades.

Regarding the nine contemplations beginning with "arising" (*jāti*), when contemplating the *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive environment), one contemplates the six objects shown in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, such as the sun, ice, earth, and trees.
If, however, one follows what is shown in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*, one contemplates only the Buddha’s body, which is the actual retribution (*samyag-vipāka*) of the true dharma.
In the present sutra, however, one merely maintains the provisional name; therefore, it says: "Upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha, one grasps and holds his name."
This practice is cultivated in reliance upon this very sutra; it takes merely the six-syllable sound of the Buddha’s name as its object of focus.

One does not contemplate the Buddha’s physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), lest it confuse the central tenet of the sutra—namely, that a single recitation of his auspicious name [is sufficient].
The myriad virtues manifest simultaneously; by raising up the provisional names, the ultimate reality is fully encompassed.

Thus, one knows that what this sutra demonstrates is a dharma-gate that grasps the main principles and the essential points. Second, there are differences in urgency, as shown in the *Amitābha Sūtra* regarding the sixteen sublime contemplations:
when first practicing the contemplation of the sun, one must wait until it is perfected before changing the contemplation to contemplate water, and then contemplating ice.
...and so forth. Proceeding gradually, one accomplishes this in a single lifetime. The method for holding the name shown in this sutra requires an extremely long period—up to seven days;
next, six, five, or even a single day of reciting the name with a single mind and without distraction.
This includes the "lower grade" rebirth described in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* and the ten [recitations] at the moment of death in the *Mahā-amitābha Sūtra*.
By merely recollecting [the Buddha], one immediately attains rebirth. Thus, we know that the teaching shown in this sutra is a dharma-gate that excels in urgency over slowness.
Third, the difficulty and ease differ: the meditative contemplations (*guan*) of the *Amitābha-sūtra* are intended for ordinary persons whose mental conceptions are weak and inferior.
Therefore, the practice first demonstrates the visualization of the sun facing west to collect the mind.
Once the mind has become still and subtle, one then visualizes water and ice, until the visualization of the image is perfected. Only then does one visualize the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*).
This must be practiced by those whose faculties have been matured through long-term cultivation. As for the ordinary beings at the initial stage shown in this sutra, they possess only the words.
It can be recited; those with faith and the capacity for mindfulness may all practice it. Thus we know that this sutra reveals even the most concise and easy-to-practice Dharma-gate.
Regarding the four types of pure and quiet places and the sixteen contemplation gates, these are for practitioners at the initial stage.

One may contemplate [the object] after entering meditative absorption in the full lotus posture; however, it is not its proper sphere when emerging from concentration and traversing sensory conditions.
If one upholds the Name, there is no distinction between leisure and busyness, nor restriction by movement or stillness; it can be practiced while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down.
Thus, one knows that this sutra reveals a dharma-gate that is even more swift and direct. Fifth, the ways of gathering sentient beings differ.

If one practices according to what is taught in the *Contemplation Sūtra*, it is intended only for those of superior faculties; thus, the practitioners for whom such practice is designed are narrow rather than broad.
The method of invoking the Name makes no distinction between the wise and the foolish, nor does it select between men and women;
whether poor or wealthy, noble or lowly, all may practice it. Therefore, we know that this sūtra demonstrates a dharma-gate that encompasses practitioners most extensively.
Thus, regarding the object and contemplation elucidated in this sutra, it is sufficient to take solely the holding of the Name as the object of contemplation.

Whether the matter concerns phenomena or principle, all practice is explained through this; there is no need to further incorporate the contemplation of the Buddha’s physical marks and signs as an adjunct.
△ III. Receiving the Fruit of Maturation. This has two parts. First, the section headings. ○ III. Receiving the Fruit of Maturation. This has two parts.
First, receiving the welcome of the sages. △ II. Explanation of the Sūtra. This has two parts. First, receiving the welcome of the sages. This has two parts. First, listing the sūtra passages.
When that person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha, together with the assembly of holy ones, will appear before them.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning, in four parts. First, according to what is evoked by the chapter.

[Commentary] Lingzhi said: "The assembly of holy beings appearing before one is also of many kinds; they may be true Buddhas or transformation Buddhas, such as Avalokiteśvara and Śrī-Ārya-Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, according to one's spiritual rank.
This is detailed in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*."
[Commentary]: The True Buddha is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Amitābha. This is of two kinds: first, the superior response-body; second, the inferior response-body.
The transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) emanates from the response-body and further manifests its form to come and guide sentient beings.

By analogy, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta likewise possess both true and transformed bodies. According to the spiritual practices of those in this land who recite the Buddha’s name, they destroy their delusions.
Subduing the afflictions: by manifesting as what kind of body does [the Buddha] receive and guide them?
△ Second, refuting erroneous interpretations, in two parts. First, describing the errors.
【Commentary】 Some claim that seeing the Buddha at the time of death is a manifestation of Māra; others say it is merely the appearance of one's own karma and that, in reality, there is no [Buddha].
Regarding the statement "other Buddhas come":
[Commentary] This is a common assertion among those who have only a shallow realization of the worldly gates of dhyāna and who have erroneously inherited the traditions of the garden of teachings.
△ Second, the refutation of this error.

[Commentary] This is likely because they do not understand that the living being and the Buddha are of one essence, and that their mutual resonance through the Way is profound. To obstruct oneself and others constitutes a fault that is no small matter.

[Sub-commentary] Whenever one sees the Buddha, one must discuss the principle of resonance and response (*ganying*). If, during one's daily practice of Chan meditation or the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness, one...
If one sweeps away all sectarian tenets, even the Buddha cannot be established. If there is any view held, it is entirely a realm of Māra.

Śāriputra, in the worlds of the northern direction, there are Buddhas such as Flame-Shoulder Buddha, Most Victorious Sound Buddha, Unassailable Buddha, Sun-Born Buddha,
and Net-Luminosity Buddha. These and other Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, each within their own lands,
extend the mark of the broad and long tongue, completely covering the trichiliocosm.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has five parts. First, the explanation of the Buddha Arciṣkandha. [Sūtra Commentary]:
"Arciṣkandha" (Flame-Shoulder) means that he simultaneously illuminates both the ultimate and conventional truths, like flames erupting from his shoulders. [Sub-commentary]:

The two shoulders symbolize the two wisdoms of the provisional and the real; now, the fact that flames erupt from his two shoulders symbolizes the radiant light of these two wisdoms illuminating [all things].
This refers to the two principles of the ultimate and the conventional.
△ Next is the explanation of the Buddha Supreme Sound (*Varaghoṣa*).
[Commentary]: "Supreme Sound" means that his Brahma-voice is profound and wondrous, transcending and surpassing all others.
[Commentary]: Whenever the Buddha expounds the Dharma, he proclaims it through the eight qualities of his voice and the four types of analytical eloquence.
The principles thus elucidated are most profound and subtle; they cannot be compared by any ordinary person. Therefore, they are said to be "supreme."
△ Third, the explanation of the Buddha who cannot be obstructed or destroyed.
[Sūtra Commentary] "Obstructed or destroyed" means that the Dharma-body is firm and solid, and cannot be obstructed or ruined.

[Sub-commentary] The Buddha is endowed with the three bodies; to mention one is to include all three. Since the Dharma-body is already firm and solid, the Reward-body and Response-body must likewise be so.
It is the same. In short, none of these can be obstructed or destroyed.
△ Fourth, explaining the Buddha born from the sun.
[Commentary] "Born from the sun" means that just as the sun first rises, there is no darkness it does not illuminate.

[Commentary]: The Buddha-sun travels through the void and is able to illuminate all that is obscure. However, it is the meaning of illuminating the obscure that is particularly manifest on the first day of its rising;
therefore, this is what is specifically mentioned. △ Fifth, the explanation of Jālinīprabha Buddha.
[Commentary] As for "Jālinīprabha" (Net-Luminosity): his wisdom-light is like a net that universally covers the ten realms. [Sub-commentary] The Buddha’s light of wisdom is like Indra’s net;

as it mutually reflects and adorns one another without end, so too does it universally cover the ten directions without exception, symbolizing how his compassion provides shelter and protection to the ten realms.

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has six parts. First, the explanation of the Buddha Siṃha (Lion).
[Commentary] "Siṃha" is like a lion king who subdues the various beasts.
[Sub-commentary] The lion is the king among the hundred beasts; its physical strength is fierce and majestic, its roaring sound is powerful and resonant, and its power is able to subdue them.

The beast’s roar can split the brain; this is a metaphor for the Buddha manifesting supernormal powers from the wheel of mind and preaching the Great Dharma with the wheel of speech, such that no sentient being fails to take refuge and all malevolent spirits are utterly subdued.
△ Next, the explanation of the name "Renowned Buddha" (Mingwenfo).
[Commentary] "Renowned" means that his fame is heard throughout immeasurable worlds.
[Sub-commentary] The Buddha possesses immeasurable virtues; thus he must have immeasurable names, each of which corresponds to the reality of its designation. One by one...

It is not in vain. Each and every one of these names is heard throughout immeasurable worlds, such that there are none among those who hear them who do not look up to the name, partake of its virtue, and thereby obtain benefit.
△ Third, the explanation of the name *Prabhāsa* (Light-Radiance) Buddha.
[Commentary] Regarding the "name-light": the name is like sunlight, universally illuminating all things.
[Sub-commentary] That is, the light of wisdom constitutes the "name-light. Wisdom follows the name in its pervasiveness, while the light relies upon wisdom for its illumination.
△ Fourth, the explanation of Dharma-Buddha.
[Commentary] "Dharma" is translated as "Dharma" (the Teaching/Reality). It refers to the Dharmakāya that is realized, which serves as the norm and sustainer for the myriad transformations.

[Sub-commentary] Just as the warm spring reaches everywhere and all things consequently come to life, so too does the Dharmakāya pervade everywhere and all things follow its norm, responding to conditions.
He does not deviate from the rules and measures. Suchness is unchanging and inconceivable.
△ Fifth, the explanation of the Buddha Dharmadhvaja.
[Commentary] "Dharmadhvaja" (Dharma-Banner): the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like a banner, rising high above all mundane existence.

[Commentary]: "The dharma-nature (dharmatā) that eminently transcends" refers to the dharma-nature that has emerged from the entanglements (*saṃkleśa*). It is for this reason that Buddhas and sentient beings are both identical and distinct.
△ Sixth, the explanation of the Buddha who Upholds the Dharma.
[Commentary] "Upholding the Dharma" means that by means of the true wisdom of the Middle Way, one upholds the dharmas of the two extremes.

[Sub-commentary] If emptiness and existence cannot uphold the reality of the Middle, it is because that which is below cannot govern that which is above; yet, when there is the reality of the Middle, it can...
Regarding "maintaining the two extremes": this means that the superior is able to govern the inferior. Thus, one neither loses the Middle Way nor loses the two extremes.
