[Commentary]: "Brahma" means purity. The Dharma-sound is pure and subtle; those who hear it find it refreshing and pleasing.
[Commentary]: The Buddha, having personally realized the pure and wondrous Dharma, speaks with the eightfold voice and four types of analytical eloquence to gladden the hearts of beings;
his teachings accord with both principle and capacity, such that there is nothing that does not bring satisfaction.
△ Next, the explanation of the Buddha Nakṣatrarājasaṃkusumitābhijña.
[Commentary] "Nakṣatrarāja" (Lord of the Constellations): like the moon illuminating the night, he is the king among the constellations.
[Sub-commentary] The noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles are like the constellations; the Buddha, the pure moon, is like the king among the constellations, because of his purity.
Pure Dharma. It shields one from all afflictive heat.
△ Second, the explanation of the Buddha "Fragrance Surpassing" (Xiāngshàng).
[Commentary]: Regarding "Fragrance Surpassing," his manifold virtues are like fragrance; he transcends all causal stages.
[Commentary]: The Buddha possesses the fragrance of the five bodies (pañcakāya), which can encompass all myriad virtues and surpasses what humans are capable of attaining;
therefore, he is praised with the epithet "Supreme Fragrance."
△ Fourth, the explanation of the Buddha Fragrant Light (Gandhaprabhāsa).
[Commentary] "Fragrant Light" refers to the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body, which, like light, dispels darkness.
[Sub-commentary] The Buddha is named "Adorned with Fragrant Light" because he possesses the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body, which universally illuminates the Dharma.
The realm. It is because it shatters the impure darkness of all sentient beings.
△ Fifth, the explanation of the Buddha Mahārciskandha.
[Commentary] "Great Flame Shoulder" means that great wisdom emits light, illuminating both truths simultaneously.
[Commentary: The true nature of all phenomena does not transcend the ultimate and the conventional; therefore, the wisdom that illuminates them consists solely of the provisional and the real.
Thus, flames issue from both shoulders to manifest that the realm of wisdom is inconceivable.
△ Sixth, the Buddha Adorned with Precious Flower Ornaments.

[Commentary] "Adorned with precious flowers" means that the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices adorn the body of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā-kāya) just as jewels provide ornamentation.

[Commentary]: That the Buddha-body is adorned with the various marks as its manifold jewels precisely symbolizes the fruition-virtue (*phala-guṇa*), for it is adorned by the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices (*daśasāhasra-pratipatti*).
Since he has thus adorned his body, he further adopts these as his titles so that sentient beings, upon beholding these marks, may all aspire to emulate him.
△ Seventh, the explanation of the Buddha Śālarāja.
[Commentary] *Śāla* means "firm" or "solid" (*dṛḍha*) in this language, serving as a metaphor for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is subject to no change or transformation.
[Sub-commentary] In India, the *śāla* is considered the king among trees; in the land of China, it is found only at Mount Emei, Mount Wangwu, and Mount Tian.
It is recorded in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*: "The tree possesses five virtues: first, it provides vast shade; second, its dense canopy forms a scale-like mosaic;
third, it does not wither in winter or summer; fourth, its trunk is firm and solid; fifth, its flowers are beautiful in color and fragrant. For these reasons, it is called the king among trees.

It may be used as a metaphor for the Tathāgata, whose great compassion universally covers all, who is fully endowed with myriad virtues, who eternally abides in quiescence, and who has reached ultimate [enlightenment]."
Ultimately firm and adorned with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), one extracts the meaning of "firmness" from within these [qualities] to serve as a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*,
because it is able to unify all virtues.
△ Eighth, the explanation of the Buddha Ratnapuṣpadhvaja.
[Commentary] His four virtues are like jewels and like flowers in full bloom.
[Sub-commentary] Among all that the Buddha treasures, nothing is more precious than these four virtues; they are fragrant and resplendent, like flowers in full bloom.
△ Ninth, the explanation of the Buddha Sarvārthadarśin.
[Commentary] “Seeing all meanings” means penetrating the profoundly deep meaning of all phenomena (*dharmas*).
[Sub-commentary] “All phenomena” refers to the ten realms. “Meaning and intent” refers to the three truths. Only a Buddha and a Buddha can thoroughly investigate them.
Exhausted. Therefore, he is called the Buddha who perceives all meanings (*sarvārthadarśin*).
△ Tenth, explaining the Buddha Like Mount Sumeru.
[Commentary]: "Like Mount Sumeru" means like the Wondrous High Mountain (*Sumeru*), the most honored among all sages.
[Commentary]: Mount Sumeru is composed of the four precious substances; therefore, it is called "wondrous" (*miao*). It stands out above all other mountains; therefore, it is called "high" (*gao*).
This serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s ultimate permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity, which no sentient being can surpass.

Śāriputra, if there are good sons or good daughters who hear this sutra and accept and uphold it,
or who hear the names of the various Buddhas, all these good sons and good daughters shall be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas,
and they shall all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has four parts. First, the explanation based on three sutras. [Commentary]:
"One who hears this sutra" refers to the Sutra of Teaching. "One who receives and upholds it" refers to the Sutra of Practice.

"Not regressing from Bodhi"—Bodhi is the inherent nature-virtue; this is the Sutra of Principle. These three sutras are precisely the secret treasury of the three virtues, which is perfectly all-encompassing.
All of it: when unfolded, it pervades and encompasses the Dharma-realm; when rolled up, it is contained within a single scripture.
Thus, those who receive and uphold it are protected and remembered by Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and they shall never regress from Bodhi.

[Commentary] "Hearing this" and below explains and establishes the three sutras. "The three sutras" and below converge them into the three virtues (*triguṇa*). The sutra of principle is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
the sutra of practice is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*); the sutra of teaching is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*). That which perfectly encompasses all things—
This clarifies that the three virtues are not lacking in anything. To unfold them is to encompass the entire dharma-realm;
this is "the one is all. To roll them up is to condense them within a single sutra; this is "all is the one.
If one can realize it in this way, then the single sutra of Amitābha may indeed fill the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm of the ten directions is entirely endowed with this.
The Sūtra is acceptable; furthermore, one must thoroughly understand the Sūtra of Teaching, Practice, and Principle. To mention one is to include all three, and the other two are easily understood.
Here, we clarify only the Sūtra of Practice: for example, upholding the Name with single-mindedness and without distraction. This practice is the Sūtra of the Virtue of Prajñā.
The Name upheld, wherein the myriad virtues are fully manifested, is the Sūtra of the Dharma-body, the virtue of Principle. In every thought-moment, one eliminates and eradicates [afflictions].
It is the teaching of the sūtra that liberates one from the grave sins of birth and death. For those who receive and uphold it, the Tathāgata will protect and mind them;
does his protection and mindfulness not reside herein?
△ Next, the explanation according to the text [is as follows].

[The *Shu*] states: Lingzhi says, "Those who hear this sutra and uphold it" refers back to the passage concerning the adornments of the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the causes and effects of cultivation and realization;
"and those who hear the names of the Buddhas" refers back to the passage concerning the praises offered by the Buddhas of the six directions. To protect...
This means to provide protection so that one is not disturbed by Māra; "recollection" (smṛti) means to keep it in mind so as not to let it fall away. The Tang translation states:

"Having heard this sutra, one will give rise to profound faith and understanding, and will certainly be sustained by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of ten Gaṅgā rivers."
[Commentary] This can be understood from the text.
△ Third, the explanation according to the title of the fruit.
[Subcommentary] *Anuttara* means "unsurpassed" (*wu-shang*). *Samyak* means "correct and equal" (*zheng-deng*). *Sambodhi* means...
"Perfect Enlightenment" (Zhengjue) is the title for the fruit of Buddhahood.
△ Fourth, the explanation by way of function.

[Commentary] Lingzhi said: "Ordinary worldlings at the level of common ground are bound by karma and afflictions, transmigrating through the five realms of existence for hundreds of thousands of millions [of lifetimes]."
After kalpas, one suddenly hears of the Pure Land and resolves to seek rebirth there. By reciting the name for a single day, one immediately transcends to that land;

protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas, one proceeds directly toward Bodhi. This may be called a rare encounter, difficult to meet even in ten thousand kalpas, occurring but once in a thousand lifetimes.
[Commentary]: Encountering [this teaching] is difficult even in ten thousand kalpas; it is met but once in a thousand lifetimes. Furthermore, there are various degrees of difference.

For instance, although one may hear the Great Dharma and plant roots of goodness, one is not necessarily able to transcend birth and death immediately, because it is difficult to escape from the cycle of saṃsāra.

This is because the Great Way is difficult to accomplish. The Dharma now being taught—if one believes, accepts, and practices it—its merit in a single day will surpass that of three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
That the Buddhas protect and keep one in mind truly depends upon this.

The Buddhas protect and sustain them; thus, these three conditions are complete. If one possesses even a modicum of faith, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is exceedingly easy.
It is like crossing the great ocean: having obtained a massive vessel, with a capable guide, and further aided by a favorable wind, one will surely reach the other shore swiftly.
If, however, one refuses to board the ship and lingers on the perilous path, whose fault is it?
[Commentary] "Relying on the power of others" (*parāśraya*) is stated here by taking the majority of cases as the basis for the expression.

This is because in the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, the practice consists merely in reciting the Name, and the time limit is only seven days. If one were not to extensively rely on the power of others, how could one attain birth in the Pure Land?
There are three aspects to this power of others: first, the encompassing vow of Amitābha, which is likened to a great vessel; second, the exhortation of Śākyamuni.
The praise is like that of a skilled guide; the protection and mindfulness of the three Buddhas are like a favorable wind.

It is precisely because of this that one arrives swiftly. Yet, though the compassionate vessel is prepared, you are unwilling to board it, choosing instead to dwell contentedly in the land of rākṣasa demons.

△ Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts. First, a general clarification that all Buddhas praise [Śākyamuni] in common.
[Commentary]: Those Buddhas and others likewise praise me; thus, Amitābha also joins all the Buddhas in praising Śākyamuni.

[Commentary]: Although each praises the other, that which is praised is fundamentally different. For example, when Śākyamuni praises Amitābha, he emphasizes his ability to bestow happiness through great compassion and to take in and sustain beings by means of his pure land.

When Amitābha praises Śākyamuni, he emphasizes his ability to uproot suffering through great compassion and to subdue beings by manifesting his land. Although there is mutual application of these qualities, they are in fact distinct from one another.

Because it benefits others, one seeks to uproot suffering and truly desires to bestow happiness; through the arousal of joy, one truly desires to uproot suffering, thus compassion and kindness provide simultaneous relief.
Bestowing happiness and uprooting suffering are applied together, like a stern father and a compassionate mother; the Way proceeds as a unified practice without mutual contradiction.

second, preaching the Dharma that is difficult to believe for the sake of sentient beings.
[Commentary] The reason Śākyamuni is called "The Capable One" (Nengren) is that he possesses two kinds of capability.
First, in a land where it is difficult to attain bodhi, he attained this very bodhi; for this reason, he is titled "The Silent One" (Jimo).
This is because he was capable of attaining the silent bodhi within a realm that is neither silent nor mute. This is the first capability. Second, regarding those who are stubborn and fierce...
In this defiled and evil land where people lack understanding, he preaches this wondrous Dharma; for this reason, he is titled "The Capable One" (Śākyamuni).
Indeed, because he is able to preach this difficult-to-believe Dharma to those who have little faith and little understanding, he is titled "The Capable One."
These two are the capacities [of the Buddha].
△ Third, the explanation of the lands to be converted has two parts. First, the explanation of Sahā.
[Commentary]: In Sanskrit, it is *Sahā*; here it is translated as "Endurance" (*Kāṃsahana*). This is because sentient beings are capable of enduring the three poisons and all...
"Because of afflictions (*kleśa*).

[Commentary: The 'three poisons' are greed, hatred, and delusion. They collectively encompass the five sharp-faculties afflictions (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) and the five dull-faculty afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*), as well as the eighty-eight afflictions of the stage of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) and the eighty-one grades of the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). All are termed 'afflictions' because 'affliction' is like a feverish heat."
Affliction (*nirvedana*) is precisely that which causes distress; one cannot attain even a moment of coolness or sovereignty.
It may indeed be called extreme suffering, yet one endures it with placid composure—not only not regarding it as suffering, but even taking pleasure in it.
This is why it is called "Endurance" (Sahā).
△ Second, the explanation of the five turbidities has two parts. First, the general explanation. [Commentary:
Regarding the five turbidities, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like clear water into which sand and earth are thrown; the earth loses its quality of obstructing and retaining."
Water loses its purity; it becomes turbid and muddy. Due to these five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the water of principle loses its clarity.

[Commentary]: Clear water is a metaphor for the principle of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Sand and soil are metaphors for the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), as well as the resultant form they summon.
When one principle and one delusion interweave to falsely constitute existence, because of this, the water loses its purity and the delusions lose their obstructive nature. Therefore, it is said:
Due to these five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), the water of principle loses its clarity; thus they are called "turbid.

However, the five turbidities in this sutra differ from those in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in terms of coarseness and subtlety, and their phenomena and principles are entirely distinct. If one brings them together and returns to their source, they are both different and the same.
△ Next, the five [corruptions] are explained individually. First, the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (corruption of the eon).

[Commentary]: *Kalpa* is the Sanskrit term for *kalpa*; this is translated here as "period of time. From the time when human lifespan during the *apacaya-kalpa* (decreasing eon) reaches twenty thousand years, one enters the *kalpa-kaṣāya*.
The four corruptions increase and intensify, congregating at this time. Hostility increases, leading to the calamity of war.
As they arise, famine occurs when greed intensifies; pestilence occurs when delusion intensifies.
Because these three calamities arise, afflictions flourish twofold and various views blaze ever more fiercely. The various turbidities converge like waters rushing toward a dark abyss.

[Commentary] A *kalpa* (劫) is termed a "period of time" (*kāla-bhāga*) and takes the world as its substance. The world undergoes the four great periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness.
Each of these periods consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease. The present is the end of the period of decrease within the kalpa of abiding.
At the beginning of this period of decrease, human lifespan was eighty thousand years; it decreases by one hundred years for every passing century.
From a lifespan of one *kalpa*, it decreases until it reaches twenty thousand years; at that point, the *kalpa-kṣaya* (the defilement of the eon) enters.

While the defilements have not yet increased to their peak, from that time onward, the three poisons of sentient beings increase day by day and flourish month by month. By the time of Śākyamuni, the human lifespan was one hundred years;

therefore, it is said that the four defilements (*catur-kaṣāya*) intensified and converged during this period. As for "weapons and so forth," these refer to the minor three calamities (*tri-saṃvarta*). One is born into this very time.

The arising of calamities is not constant; it is invariably brought about by the influence of the three poisons within the human mind. Nevertheless, these have not yet reached the point of extreme severity.
It is only when the human lifespan has decreased to ten years that these minor three calamities may be said to reach their peak. Thus it is with the sentient beings of the world.
When there were no survivors, it was said that the son’s virtue diminished his father’s virtue and the son’s lifespan diminished his father’s lifespan;
only then did the hearts of people grow weary of suffering, gradually enabling them to turn toward goodness. From this point on, another hundred years passed, and the lifespan increased by one year.
As the lifespan continued to increase, goodness likewise progressed, until it reached eighty thousand years and then ceased. This is called the son’s virtue increasing his father’s.
The son’s age is twice that of his father’s; thus it continues for twenty cycles.

Thereafter, one enters the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), where the three great calamities of water, fire, and wind successively manifest. This process repeats for another twenty such cycles.
It was precisely at the beginning of the empty kalpa (*śūnya-kalpa*). During the twenty cycles of emptiness, the world likewise underwent twenty cycles of formation.
Only then did it enter the abiding kalpa (*sthiti-kalpa*). At the time of Śākyamuni, it was during the ninth cycle of decrease within the period of abiding; therefore, it is said:
"Able [to appear] in this world of five turbidities," and so forth.
△ Next, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) is explained.

[Commentary: "Views" refers to the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); that is, the five sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*), up to the sixty-two views, and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*): it refers to the false conceptualization of a self within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), forcibly establishing a sovereign master and constantly giving rise to the view of "I," clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self.
This is called the view of a self-identity. Regarding the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*): it refers to reckoning one's own body as either annihilated or eternal;
clinging to annihilation and not eternity, or clinging to eternity and not annihilation, grasping only at one extreme. This is called the view of extremes. Regarding precepts...

"Grasping at precepts" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) refers to mistakenly regarding what is not the true precept as being the precept, and stubbornly clinging to it as superior and sublime while seeking its attainment and progress;
this is called grasping at precepts. "Grasping at views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa) refers to mistakenly calculating that which is not the truly sublime Dharma to be nirvāṇa.
The mind gives rise to grasping and attachment, falsely reckoning what has been acquired as superior; this is called the "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).

As for "false view" (mithyādṛṣṭi), it refers to grasping at principles with a perverted mind, holding inverted and deluded views, disbelieving in cause and effect, severing all roots of goodness, and practicing the conduct of an icchantika.
This is called false view. It is stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Regarding the sixty-two views:
this refers to non-Buddhists who, within the five aggregates (*skandhas*) of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, give rise to four types of views for each aggregate.

These are: reckoning that the self is great and form is small; that the self is within form; that the self is great and form is small; and that form is within the self; and that the self is distinct from form.
"Form is the self. Just as it is with the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), so it is with the other four; thus, twenty views are established.

When these are discussed in relation to the three periods of time—past, present, and future—they become sixty views. Adding the two root views of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) completes the total.

The original text contains sixty-two [items] in total, as extracted from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Regarding the "five sharp messengers" (*pañca-tīkṣṇa-dūta*): "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) carries the meaning of being keen and acute;

it refers to these five kinds of delusive afflictions that arise the moment a thought stirs and are constantly present even in the briefest interval. "Messenger" (*dūta*) carries the meaning of one who drives or dispatches;
it means that all sentient beings, driven by these five kinds of delusive afflictions, have their minds and spirits pursued, causing them to transmigrate through the three realms.
Because there is no time of emergence, they are called "proclivities" (*anuśaya*).
△ Third, the explanation of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
[Commentary]: "Afflictions" refers to greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt—the five dull proclivities—as well as the hundred and eight afflictions, and so forth.
It is so. [Commentary]:

Greed (*lobha*) means to grasp and take without satiety. This refers to sentient beings who are attached to the worldly forms, desires, and treasures, indulging their minds and emotions without ever reaching fulfillment.
Anger (*dveṣa*) means fury; this refers to sentient beings regarding that which is disagreeable...
In terms of their functions: anger gives rise to various forms of malice, vexing and disturbing both oneself and others;
delusion is confusion and a lack of clarity, meaning that sentient beings, by perceiving objects with a deluded mind, are unable to understand all phenomena;
pride is self-reliance and the disparagement of others, meaning that sentient beings, relying on their own lineage, wealth, status, virtue, or talent, treat others with contempt.
"Doubt" refers to hesitation and indecision; it means that sentient beings, with deluded minds, deviate from principle and are unable to penetrate the characteristics of dharmas.

Regarding the "five dull afflictions," "dull" means sluggish; these five kinds of delusive confusion do not arise immediately upon a movement of thought, nor are they constantly present at every moment, and for this reason they are called "dull. As for the "one hundred and eight afflictions," they are characterized by darkness...
The nature of affliction (*kleśa*) is to disturb and agitate the mind; therefore, it is called "affliction.

Specifically, when the six sense faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—encounter the six objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—each of these encounters three distinct types:

the agreeable, the disagreeable, and the neutral. Thus, eighteen afflictions are formed. Furthermore, within these, there arise the feelings of suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Regarding pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), there are further eighteen types, making thirty-six in total.
When these are further categorized according to the three periods of past, present, and future, there are thirty-six types for each period, totaling one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
△ Fourth, the explanation of the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
[Commentary] "Sentient beings" (*sattva*) refers to that which grasps the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the fruit of views and pride; this provisional name is established for such a thing.

[Sub-commentary] "Many" (*sattva*) means "multitude. One grasps the real dharmas of the five aggregates and establishes the provisional name "sentient being. As for "views and pride": [text continues]

Regarding "fruition" (*vipāka*): its meaning is defined as the result being induced by a cause. "Views and conceit" refer to the causes—the past two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely the sharp and the dull.
"Fruition" refers to the result—the present five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

△ Fifth, the explanation of the defilement of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). [Commentary] "Lifespan" refers to momentary arising and ceasing; it destroys years and shortens longevity. [Sub-commentary] Explanation:
When Kāśyapa appeared in the world, the human lifespan was eighty years. Although this is called "short," compared to other ages it was still long. Furthermore, by...
Comparing years by means of months, and comparing months by means of days, one gradually compares them down to the *kṣaṇa*.
A single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) contains sixty *kṣaṇas*, and each *kṣaṇa* contains sixty births and cessations. As it is said:
"Not only do years change, but months also pass away. This is illustrated by the metaphor of fire turning to ash; every thought-moment perishes, and this process of decay and extinction never ceases.

One must decisively realize that this body ultimately undergoes transformation and extinction. Generally, the lifespan of worldly people is displaced by the eight marks—namely, the four minor marks and the four major marks.
Therefore, it is said that there is arising and ceasing at every *kṣaṇa*, and years are crushed while life is shortened.
△ The four concluding sections all arise from compassionate vows.
[Commentary] The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "By the power of my original vow of great compassion, I dwell in this turbid, evil, and impure land."
[Commentary]: That the sentient beings in this turbid and evil land suffer in grief and pain corresponds precisely to the compassionate vow of Śākyamuni;

that is to say, they harmonize with the six realms of beings below, sharing the same sorrowful longing. As for the sentient beings in the Pure Land who look up in joy, this corresponds precisely to the compassionate vow of Amitābha;
that is to say, they harmonize with the Buddhas of the ten directions above, sharing the same power of compassion.
However, Śākyamuni’s compassion does not exclude loving-kindness, and Amitābha’s loving-kindness does not exclude compassion.
It is only because we are currently contrasting the two lands—the pure and the defiled—that we speak of them from one particular perspective alone.
△ Five Objections Regarding Difficult-to-Believe Teachings. [Commentary]:

Now, as for the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation, it does not distinguish between the worthy and the foolish; it does not select between the noble and the lowly; it makes no account of the long or the short;

it does not differentiate between the good and the evil. It requires only resolute faith. Even those facing the evil omens at the moment of death can attain rebirth through ten recitations. This is...
That ordinary, ignorant beings bound by all fetters, even those of the lowest class such as butchers and wine-sellers, can transcend [samsara] in a single instant and attain Buddhahood—
this Dharma may indeed be called something extremely difficult for the entire world to believe.
[Commentary]: Now, the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma is of a single flavor and equal; it certainly makes no distinction between the wise and the foolish, or the noble and the lowly.

If one were to say that the appearance of evil omens at the moment of death and rebirth through ten recitations of the name occur only within the single gate of the Pure Land, this would be truly difficult for all the world to believe.
It may be called the Mahāyāna among Mahāyānas, the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) within [the section].
△ Second, revealing that it is not in vain, in two parts. First, restating the topical outline.
○ Second, revealing that it is not in vain.
△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra has two parts. First, the citation of the sūtra:
"Śāriputra, you should know that in this world of five turbidities, I have performed this difficult task:
having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, I preach this dharma so difficult to believe for the sake of all the world. This is exceedingly difficult."
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning, in two parts. First, it clarifies that Śākyamuni was endowed with two difficulties.
[Commentary] Guishan said: "To attain Bodhi while practicing difficult practices within a world of the five turbidities is already difficult;
furthermore, to preach this Dharma which is difficult to believe—to perform these two tasks simultaneously is exceedingly difficult. All Buddhas...
"To praise me—how could these words be empty? [Commentary]:
That all Buddhas praise Śākyamuni together is because he possesses two difficulties: first, being able to attain enlightenment in a land where it is difficult to achieve;
second, preaching this Dharma to people who are difficult to inspire with faith. This is stated in contrast to [other lands].
The Buddhas, then, have made these two [paths] easy.
△ Next, the difficulty and ease of practice in the two lands are revealed.
【Commentary】Ciyun says: It is difficult to attain the Way amidst the five turbidities; in the Pure Land, practice is easy.
[Commentary] Master Ciyun said: "There are ten difficulties for attaining the Way in this Sahā world: first, not frequently encountering a Buddha;
second, not hearing the preaching of the Dharma; third, being entangled by evil associates; fourth, being disturbed and distracted by various māras; and fifth, the cycle of saṃsāra never ceasing."
Sixth, it is difficult to escape the evil realms. Seventh, worldly conditions obstruct the Path. Eighth, one’s lifespan is short. Ninth, there is regression from practice.
Tenth, it is difficult to achieve realization over many kalpas. There are ten advantages to practicing in a Pure Land: First, one constantly beholds the Buddha.
Second, one constantly hears the sound of the Dharma. Third, holy sages assemble there. Fourth, one remains far removed from demonic activities. Fifth, one does not undergo cyclic existence.

Sixth, one is forever separated from the evil realms. Seventh, one receives superior conditions that assist the Path. Eighth, one’s lifespan is immeasurable. Ninth, one enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Tenth, one attains birth in the presence of Buddhas. Eleventh, one fulfills the practices. Such are the clear explanations regarding the characteristics of the difficult and the easy [paths]. How could one not abandon the difficult and take up the easy?
△ Second, the two assemblies joyfully receive and practice [the teaching]. This has two parts: first, the summary of the section;
second, the two assemblies joyfully receive and practice.
△ Second, the explanation of the sūtra. This has two parts: first, the listing of the sūtra.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Śāriputra, the bhikṣus, and all the world— including devas, humans, asuras, and others—
having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced, accepted it with faith, prostrated, and departed.
△ Second, the explanation of the meaning has five parts. First, the inclusion and exclusion based on the capacities of the audience.

[Commentary]: "All worlds" generally includes the fourfold assembly and the ten realms. Specifically, the three fortunate destinies are mentioned because they constitute the primary audience for conversion.
"Heaven" refers to the heavens of Brahmā, Śakra, the desire realm, the form realm, and so forth. Asura is translated here as "non-[god]."

"Devas": though they share the same heaven as the wealthy and noble, they are full of flattery and deception because they lack deva-conduct (*devacara*). "Etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to the eight classes of spirits and deities;
they constitute the assembly of listeners.
[Commentary] In the explanation, it clarifies the capacities for hearing the Dharma as described in the sutra; there is both inclusion and exclusion.
"All worlds" refers to the comprehensive inclusion of the fourfold assembly and the ten realms. The fourfold assembly are, of course, those who regularly hear the Dharma;
the ten realms further include the four miserable destinies—thus, the scope of the included capacities is so vast. "Devas, humans, and asuras," however, excludes [the miserable destinies].
Regarding the other realms, only the three fortunate paths are mentioned; this is because the number of sentient beings who are to be transformed is so vast.
This explanation is made for the time being based on a general summary according to other sutras.

However, as for the Dharma-gate of Ultimate Bliss, as described in the *Larger Sutra*, even when the signs of the hells appear at the moment of death, down to the smallest crawling insects, all are gathered in by the power of their vows.

...thereby causing them to be born in that land. Thus, as for the capacities of beings to be gathered, it is truly appropriate that the fourfold assembly and the ten realms of existence should be included without exception.
△ Next, the reason for this benefit is explained.
[Commentary] Gushan said: Because he heard what he had never heard before, he received it with joy and faith; because he revered the Dharma and honored his teacher, he paid obeisance and departed.
△ Third, the depth of the benefits obtained.

[Commentary] The term "joyful" (*pramuditā*) encompasses both profound and shallow meanings. It may refer to attaining the benefit of joy, or it may refer to realizing the principle and entering the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
[Sub-commentary] "Attaining the benefit of joy" is a judgment made according to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint). "Entering the Stage of Joy" is, according to...
This is the judgment according to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
△ Fourth, citing evidence for the profound benefit.
[Commentary]: Therefore, at the conclusion of the Great Sūtra, it is recorded that immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds on Bodhi, and *nayuta* of people attained...
"Purity of the Dharma-eye" [Commentary]:
To resolve upon Bodhicitta belongs to the stage of the Mahāyāna; there one attains the benefit of entering into principle and gains purity of the Dharma-eye.

To belong to the stage of the Hīnayāna is to attain the benefit of entering into principle. The Sūtra further states: "Believing, accepting, and practicing accordingly," whereby one further attains the capacity for human existence.

The *dāna-siddhānta* provides the benefit of generating goodness; however, it lacks the benefit of the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, which destroys evil. Since there are these three benefits, [the *siddhānta*] should also encompass them.
△ Fifth, the perpetual circulation.
[Commentary] Proclaimed throughout the ten directions and handed down for ten thousand generations, it shall provide inexhaustible benefit and joy until the end of the future.
[Sub-commentary] There are two essential aspects to the method of circulation: first, self-cultivation; second, transforming others. Regarding self-cultivation, there are again two types:
first, practicing according to the teaching—namely, holding the Name for seven days with a single mind without distraction; second, reading and reciting.

Regarding the scriptural text, I shall explain its meaning according to the passage. Formerly, during the Liang dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Daolin, who once practiced the visualization of water while reciting the Buddha’s name at Mount Lu.
Suddenly, he dreamed that the river waters were overflowing and a multitude of people were boarding a boat, saying they were traveling to the Western Land.
Daolin said, "I, Daolin, have cultivated the practices for the Western Land throughout my life; you may board with me. The person on the boat replied, "Dharma..."
"Although the Master’s lectures on the sutras were very extensive, he had not yet recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Nianfo Wangsheng Zhou* (Recitation for Rebirth), nor had he bathed the monks;
his pure karma was not yet perfected, so you must not go. At this, Zhen wept with emotion.

After waking from the dream, he abandoned his lecturing duties to devote himself exclusively to reciting this sutra and the *Wangsheng Zhou*, while also arranging for the monks to bathe. When the night drew toward its end, a wondrous radiance appeared.
It illuminated the mountain peak as if thousands of torches were arrayed there. A divine being arrived carrying a precious platform and invited the Master to be reborn [in the Pure Land].
Thus, one knows that the vow for rebirth through the circulation [of this scripture] cannot be fulfilled without recitation. Second, regarding transforming others:
this means exclusively expounding this sutra for others, exhorting them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and to vow to be reborn in Sukhāvatī; or, one may transcribe and explain it.
Commentary: There is no practice that he does not perform. He dedicates the merit of his work in transforming others toward the Pure Land and makes a vow to be reborn there.
Formerly, Zan Xueyu of Siming constantly used woodblock prints of the *Bekko-zu* (The Diagram of the Grid) to distribute as gifts, encouraging people to recite the Buddha’s name.
There was a man named Ji Gong, an ironworker from Taoyuan, who was nearly seventy years old and had lost the sight of both eyes. When he first received one of these diagrams, he began to recite...
When he had completed three hundred and sixty thousand recitations, his two eyes became clear and bright upon reaching the fourth diagram.
He continued in this manner for three years until he had completed seventeen diagrams. One day, while reciting the Buddha’s name, he suddenly lost consciousness;

after half a day, he revived and said, "I saw the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who commanded that six diagrams be given to the District Magistrate Zan, as he was the leader in encouraging others, and that one diagram be given to another."
He entrusted his son with this letter and diagram, instructing him to go and thank the Academician Xue.
Having finished speaking, he bathed, sat facing west, and passed away. Observing this, one sees that encouraging others to recite the Buddha’s name is itself an act of rebirth in the Pure Land.
Since the Academician Zan was able to encourage others, how could he not have been able to recite for himself? This is the merit of benefiting both oneself and others.
The merit for rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss will doubly increase, and one’s rank therein will surely be high.
*Abridged Explanation of the Amida Sutra: A Commentary on the Perfect and Round*, Scroll Lower (End).
Appendix.
The Divine Incantation for Eradicating the Root of All Karmic Obstructions and Rebirth in the Pure Land:
*Namo Amitābhāya* (1) *Tathāgatāya* (2) *Tiṣṭhate* (3) *Amitiṭu* (4) *Bhavi* (5) *Amitita* (6) *Siddham bhavi* (7) *Amiti* (8)
Tadyathā (8) vighnāntakṛt (9) amṛte (10) vighnāntaka (11) ghaṇṭe (12) gagane (13) jitakāli (14) svāhā (15). The Master You said: This mantra is in the Sanskrit language.
The people of this land recite it without receiving transmission from a teacher, resulting in errors and corruptions.

It is indeed many. This mantra is contained in the section on the character "Yang" (養). Scribes have introduced errors in the phrasing and punctuation, and later generations have followed these mistakes, thereby losing its original correctness.
Works such as the *Longshu Jingtuwen* (Pure Land Texts of Longshu) and the *Lebang Wenlei* (Classified Writings on the Land of Bliss) fail to investigate the underlying reasons;

they stubbornly maintain their own versions as correct while conversely treating the authentic version as erroneous. To hear a righteous teaching and not follow it is an extreme error. Please consider this in light of the *Lengyan Jing*...

The arrangement of the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* and so forth can be understood through comparison. Now, we rely on the authentic edition for publication and printing, universally encouraging its recitation and retention so that the esoteric words may circulate without losing their correctness. ○ I, [the author], say:

since Master You has already standardized the divisions and punctuation of the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* according to the *Lengyan jing*, then the fourth phrase should, like the sixth phrase, consist of four characters per phrase; thus, the fifth [phrase] should be moved [to the end of the fourth].
The phrase *dū* (都) and the character *zì* (字) combine to form *Amṛtadū*. The fifth phrase consists of the two characters *tuópí* (怛婆毗).

Furthermore, in the *Jìngtǔ zhǐguī* (淨土指歸) compiled by the Master [Tánwù], this dhāraṇī is also recorded therein. It states that although the character *chā* (哆) is pronounced as *duō-hé* (多曷), it must not be called with an entering tone (*rùshēng*) or with emphasis;
rather, its sound should be identical to that of the character *dài* (帶). This, too, is profound.
There is a reason for this. Generally, if the character "哆" (duō) were to follow the rhyme categories (*piānyùn*), it should be read as "侈" (chǐ).

That it is now pronounced with the *duō-hé* (多曷) initial and read as "帶" (dài) is due to the retroflex sound of the Sanskrit phonetic system; this is because the characters of the Eastern Flower [China] lack sounds for retroflex articulation.
Therefore, whenever a translator encounters a retroflex sound, they add the character for "mouth" (口) to it in this local script;

however, whenever the character for "mouth" appears, it must always be pronounced with a retroflex articulation. For instance, when the character *ca* (哆) is joined with the character for "mouth," it is read as *ṭa*, thereby producing the retroflex sound.
The postscript to the *Yuanzhong chao* (Excerpts from the Center of the Carved Circle) concerning the Buddha’s discourse on the Single Sūtra of Amitābha Buddha is as follows:

It is like the household meal recipes, the inventories of furnishings for the halls and chambers, the pattern records for clothing, or the catalogs of flowers in the gardens of a wealthy and noble family; it merely records the facts directly.
I entrust this to those of our own house, so that they may guard it without loss and employ it without exhaustion.
Why, then, must I further burden it with footnotes or clutter it with commentaries? My only concern is that young people, weary of rich delicacies, might fail to distinguish between beans and wheat.

They indulge in silks and brocades while remaining ignorant of mulberry trees and hemp. Thus, at the side of the Elder, his ministers, assistants, officials, and commoners who record notes on scrolls and slips were permitted to take up their pens and advance.
When I first ascended the lecture seat, I used Master Quan’an of Wumen’s *Brief Commentary* as my starting point.

It has been transcribed for beginners as a commentary on the "Perfect and Sudden" [teachings], establishing that the Pure Land is Mind-only and that Amitābha is one's own original nature. Those who regard this as mere straw dogs must surely be lost;

for those who seek the correct path from the Clear and Tranquil [Dharma], this will not fail to provide some small benefit. Thus says Yuanfu, a Dharma-descendant of Yansheng of Siming, who raised funds to carve this woodblock for circulation.
I concur. I admire his aspiration to benefit himself and others; therefore, I have once again composed this colophon for him.
Recorded by a monk who transmits the Tiantai "Inexhaustible Lamp" in the winter of the fifth year of the Ming Tianqi era.
